knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Łojasiewicz Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PL regime bounds objective suboptimality by a constant multiple of the squared gradient norm, without assuming convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f_*\) be a reference minimum value attained in \(U\). The Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with constant \(\mu>0\) on \(U\) is
\[
\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge \mu\bigl(f(x)-f_*\bigr)
\]
for every \(x\in U\) with \(f(x)\ge f_*\). This condition does not require convexity; it directly bounds objective suboptimality by the squared gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f_*\) is an attained reference minimum value on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f_*)\) for every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth local PL inequality normalized by one-half the squared gradient norm.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard smooth PL condition with a clear normalization and the correct content kind, but no authoritative locator is supplied for the definition, normalization, or nonconvex scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Dominance Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PL geometry excludes suboptimal stationary points, but by itself gives neither convexity, uniqueness, nor a distance-to-solution error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f\) satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality with \(\mu>0\) and minimum value \(f_*\) on \(U\). Then
\[
f(x)-f_*\le \frac{1}{2\mu}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
\]
for every \(x\in U\). Consequently, every stationary point \(x\in U\) satisfies \(f(x)=f_*\); thus the region contains no stationary points having strictly suboptimal objective value. The assertion concerns objective values and does not, without additional assumptions, imply convexity, uniqueness of minimizers, or a distance error bound to the minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the PL condition with constant \(\mu>0\) on \(U\).
\(f_*\) is the minimum value referenced by that condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and \(x\in U\) imply \(f(x)=f_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric consequences of PL gradient dominance on a reference region.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Exclusion of strictly suboptimal stationary points follows directly from the displayed PL inequality. The broader boundary claims concerning convexity, uniqueness, and distance error bounds require an authoritative source or explicit sourced counterexamples.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Exponent Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the stated exponent convention, the local PL inequality is exactly the smooth KL inequality with exponent one-half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable and let \(f_*\) be the local minimum value. Under the KL-exponent convention
\[
\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge c\bigl(f(x)-f_*\bigr)^\theta
\]
for nearby points satisfying \(0<f(x)-f_*<\eta\), the exponent \(\theta=\tfrac12\) is equivalent to the local PL inequality. Precisely, PL with constant \(\mu>0\) gives \(c=\sqrt{2\mu}\), while a KL inequality with \(\theta=\tfrac12\) and constant \(c>0\) gives PL with \(\mu=c^2/2\) on the same punctured objective neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta=\tfrac12\), \(c=\sqrt{2\mu}\), and \(\mu=c^2/2\) identify the two inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under the KL convention using a power exponent on objective excess.

notation.meaning: KL exponent in the gradient lower-bound convention

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The constant conversion is algebraically correct under the explicitly stated gradient lower-bound convention. Because KL exponent conventions differ across sources, an authoritative locator confirming this convention and its local domain is required.

children.title: KL Construction Stability Calculus
children.top_down_role: Operations and transformations used to assemble recognizable KL models.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix an o-minimal structure \(\mathcal R\) over the real field. Let \(\mathscr F_{\mathcal R}\) denote the proper lower-semicontinuous functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces whose epigraphs are definable in \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition packages model-building operations through definability. It asserts class preservation, not preservation of a numerical KL exponent or constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite construction rule \(\mathcal O\) is KL-stable over \(\mathcal R\) if, whenever its input functions and constraint sets are definable in \(\mathcal R\), every output function \(g=\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m;C_1,\ldots,C_q)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable. A KL-stable construction calculus is a collection of such rules closed under finite composition. Since every proper lower-semicontinuous definable function has the KL property at every point of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial g\), membership of the output in \(\mathscr F_{\mathcal R}\) is the recognition certificate. Typical rules are finite sums, finite maxima or minima when lower semicontinuity is retained, Cartesian separable sums, composition with definable continuous maps, addition of definable indicators, and definable marginalization when the marginal is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KL-stable construction calculus is a collection of finite model-building operations that keeps proper lower-semicontinuous definable functions inside the same definable class. The output is therefore KL wherever its limiting subdifferential is nonempty. The definition deliberately separates qualitative KL recognition from quantitative preservation of exponents and constants.
assumptions_latex: Every input function and set is definable in one fixed o-minimal structure \(\mathcal R\).
Each output is required to be proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_i,C_j\text{ definable and admissible}\Longrightarrow \mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m;C_1,\ldots,C_q)\in\mathscr F_{\mathcal R}\Longrightarrow\text{the output has the KL property}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The graph or epigraph description produced by each rule is definable and the resulting extended-real function is proper and closed.
special_cases_latex: Taking \(\mathcal R\) to be the semialgebraic structure yields the semialgebraic construction calculus.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any finite expression tree made solely from admissible rules has a KL objective at every subdifferential-domain point.
boundary_notes: Pointwise limits, infinite suprema, and arbitrary perturbations are not included merely because every finite stage is definable.
A common KL exponent is not implied by qualitative definability.

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of a set when used in a construction.

review_flags: No inspected local source gives one precise locator supporting the complete closure calculus and all stated admissibility qualifications.
A source on definable KL functions and o-minimal closure operations is required before review promotion.

children.title: Finite Model Construction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional model-building operations and separable constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{j=1}^q\mathbb R^{n_j}\), fix an o-minimal structure \(\mathcal R\), and let \(f_i\) and \(C_j\) be definable functions and sets of compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only finite-dimensional, finite-arity expressions are covered. Properness and lower semicontinuity are explicit admissibility requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite model construction is an extended-real function \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) represented by a finite rooted expression tree whose leaves are definable functions, constants, coordinate projections, or indicators \(\delta_C\) of closed definable sets, and whose internal nodes apply finitely many of the operations \[u+v,\quad au,\quad \max_{1\leq i\leq m}u_i,\quad \min_{1\leq i\leq m}u_i,\quad u\circ G,\quad \sum_{j=1}^q u_j(x_j),\] where \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(m,q<\infty\), and \(G\) is continuous and definable. The expression is admissible when its final value is proper and lower semicontinuous. The finite model construction calculus is the smallest class containing the leaves and closed under these admissible operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite model is built from finitely many definable primitive functions, coordinate maps, constants, and closed-set indicators using finite arithmetic, maxima, minima, compositions, and separable sums. The resulting expression belongs to the calculus only when it defines a proper lower-semicontinuous extended-real function.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive object is definable in the same structure \(\mathcal R\).
Every composition is dimensionally compatible and uses a continuous definable inner map.
The final function is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an admissible finite definable expression and hence is a proper lower-semicontinuous definable function.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\) is the value at the root of a finite directed acyclic expression graph with admissible definable operations.
special_cases_latex: A block-separable model has the form \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_q)=\sum_{j=1}^q f_j(x_j)+\delta_C(x_1,\ldots,x_q)\).
A finite minimax model has the form \(F(x)=\max_{i\leq m}f_i(x)\) or \(F(x)=\min_{i\leq m}f_i(x)\), subject to lower semicontinuity.
immediate_consequences_latex: When the primitives are semialgebraic, every admissible finite construction is semialgebraic.
boundary_notes: Countably infinite sums and suprema are excluded.
A finite minimum of lower-semicontinuous functions need not be lower semicontinuous without an additional check.

notation.meaning: Zero on \(C\) and positive infinity outside \(C\).

review_flags: The mathematical class is explicit, but no inspected source locator supports this exact packaged construction calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Definable Model Expressions
Finite Aggregation Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite sums and finite maxima of continuous semialgebraic functions remain continuous semialgebraic and therefore possess the KL property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous semialgebraic functions. For coefficients \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\), both
\[
F_{\mathrm{sum}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i(x),\qquad F_{\max}(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m} f_i(x)
\]
are continuous semialgebraic functions. Hence each aggregate is proper, lower semicontinuous, and satisfies the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at every point of its limiting-subdifferential domain. The claim concerns finite aggregation; arbitrary infinite sums or suprema require separate definability and regularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sum}}\) and \(F_{\max}\) are continuous semialgebraic KL functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL stability obtained from finite semialgebraic sums and maxima.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Finite sums and maxima preserve continuity and semialgebraicity under the stated assumptions, and the property kind fits the construction leaf. No source is supplied for the semialgebraic closure facts and the resulting nonsmooth KL assertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Product Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a finite Cartesian product equals the sum of the factor indicators; closed semialgebraic products therefore inherit the KL property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) be nonempty closed semialgebraic sets for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and set \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\). For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), the indicator of the product satisfies
\[
\delta_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}(x_i).
\]
Consequently, \(C\) is closed and semialgebraic, and \(\delta_C\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous semialgebraic function. It therefore has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at every point of \(C\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_{\prod_i C_i}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i\delta_{C_i}(x_i)\), and this indicator is a KL function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian-product indicators represented by separable sums.

notation.meaning: indicator taking zero on C and positive infinity outside C
Cartesian product of the factor sets

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The product-indicator identity and semialgebraic closure statement are coherent, and representation is an appropriate content kind. The asserted KL conclusion lacks an inspectable authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous semialgebraic outer function composed with a continuous semialgebraic mapping remains semialgebraic and KL, though exponents need extra hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous semialgebraic mappings. Then the composite \(F=g\circ h\) is continuous and semialgebraic. In particular, \(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous and satisfies the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at every point in its limiting-subdifferential domain. This closure assertion does not supply a KL exponent or a subdifferential chain rule; quantitative exponent transfer requires additional regularity and nondegeneracy assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=g\circ h\) is a continuous semialgebraic KL function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semialgebraic composition as a sufficient KL construction rule.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative semialgebraic-composition closure claim is precise and properly avoids exponent-transfer and chain-rule claims. An authoritative source is still needed for the closure and KL implications.

children.title: Elimination Value-Function Calculus
children.top_down_role: Recognition after partial minimization or variable elimination.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), let \(H:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(C\subseteq X\times Y\). Define the fiber \(C(x):=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns elimination by infimum in finite dimensions. KL recognition additionally requires an admissible definability and closedness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The elimination or marginal value function associated with \((H,C)\) is \[v(x):=\inf_{y\in C(x)}H(x,y),\qquad \operatorname{dom}v:=\{x:-\infty<v(x)<+\infty\}.\] Its argmin mapping is \(M(x):=\operatorname{argmin}_{y\in C(x)}H(x,y)\). The elimination is attained on \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}v\) if \(M(x)\neq\varnothing\) and \(v(x)=H(x,y)\) for every \(y\in M(x)\), \(x\in D\). It is KL-admissible on \(D\) when \(H\) and \(C\) are definable, the infimum is finite and attained there, and the resulting restriction of \(v\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. In that case elimination produces a definable KL value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable elimination replaces a joint objective and feasible relation by the infimum over the eliminated variable. The associated solution mapping contains the minimizers in each fiber. For KL recognition, the data must be definable and the marginal must remain finite, attained, proper, and lower semicontinuous on the parameter region under consideration.
assumptions_latex: \(H:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) are given.
For KL-admissibility, \(H\) and \(C\) are definable and \(v\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on the declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=\inf\{H(x,y):(x,y)\in C\}\), with \(M(x)=\{y\in C(x):H(x,y)=v(x)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}v=\{(x,t):\exists y\in C(x)\text{ with }H(x,y)\leq t\}\) when the infimum is attained at the relevant level.
special_cases_latex: Unconstrained partial minimization corresponds to \(C=X\times Y\).
A parameterized nonlinear program is obtained when \(C(x)=\{y:g_i(x,y)\leq0,\ h_j(x,y)=0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Under definability and attainment, the epigraph of \(v\) is obtained by a finite-dimensional definable projection.
boundary_notes: Infima equal to \(-\infty\), nonattainment, or loss of lower semicontinuity fall outside KL-admissible elimination.
Subdifferential formulas for \(v\) require additional qualification conditions and are not part of this definition.

notation.meaning: Argmin mapping of the eliminated problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a continuous semialgebraic function over a fixed compact semialgebraic set produces a continuous semialgebraic, hence KL, value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, compact, and semialgebraic, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times K\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and semialgebraic. Define
\[
v(x)=\min_{y\in K}F(x,y).
\]
The minimum is attained for every \(x\). Moreover, \(v:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and semialgebraic; consequently, it is a proper lower-semicontinuous Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz function. Compactness is a sufficient uniform level-boundedness condition and is essential to this stated version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=\min_{y\in K}F(x,y)\) is attained, continuous, semialgebraic, and KL.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact semialgebraic minimization preserves continuity, definability, and KL structure.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: For a fixed nonempty compact semialgebraic set, attainment, continuity, and semialgebraicity of the value function are plausible under the stated assumptions. The combined Berge-type continuity, definable elimination, and KL conclusions require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact smooth minimization model has a directional derivative obtained by minimizing active partial gradients; a unique minimizer yields the ordinary gradient formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty and compact, and suppose \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times K\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous with \(\nabla_xF\) continuous. Define \(v(x)=\min_{y\in K}F(x,y)\) and \(M(x)=\operatorname{argmin}_{y\in K}F(x,y)\). Then \(M(x)\) is nonempty and compact, and the one-sided directional derivative satisfies
\[
v'(x;d)=\min_{y\in M(x)}\langle\nabla_xF(x,y),d\rangle.
\]
If \(M(x)=\{y_x\}\), then \(v\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(\nabla v(x)=\nabla_xF(x,y_x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v'(x;d)=\min_{y\in M(x)}\langle\nabla_xF(x,y),d\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Danskin directional formula for a compact smooth minimization model.

notation.meaning: one-sided directional derivative in direction d

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The minimization-form Danskin formula has the expected minimum over active gradients and fits the geometry leaf. A precise theorem locator is required to confirm that the stated continuity assumptions suffice for the directional derivative and unique-minimizer differentiability conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noncompact elimination can destroy lower semicontinuity: minimizing the polynomial (xy−1) squared over y yields a value function discontinuous at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Marginalization over a noncompact variable need not preserve lower semicontinuity, even for a polynomial joint objective. Let
\[
F(x,y)=(xy-1)^2,\qquad v(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y).
\]
For every \(x\ne0\), choosing \(y=1/x\) gives \(v(x)=0\), whereas \(v(0)=1\). Hence
\[
\liminf_{x\to0}v(x)=0<v(0),
\]
so \(v\) is not lower semicontinuous at zero. Thus continuity and semialgebraicity of \(F\) alone do not justify the standard proper-lower-semicontinuous KL calculus for its marginal; compactness or suitable local uniform level-boundedness is needed.
assumptions_latex: The eliminated variable ranges over the noncompact set \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=0\) for \(x\ne0\), \(v(0)=1\), and \(v\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of lower semicontinuity under noncompact elimination.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial counterexample is correctly computed, demonstrates failure of lower semicontinuity under noncompact elimination, and is correctly classified as a failure boundary. No inspectable source is provided for the general stability-boundary conclusion or the stated level-boundedness remedy.

children.title: Parameterization Stability Classes
children.top_down_role: Behavior under regular changes of coordinates and redundant parameterizations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(P:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(C^1\), set \(g=f\circ P\), and fix \(\bar z\) with \(\bar x=P(\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The principal class consists of locally bi-Lipschitz \(C^1\) coordinate changes. Redundant parameterizations are separated because rank loss can destroy slope comparability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parameterization \(P\) is locally KL-stable at \(\bar z\) if there are neighborhoods \(V\ni\bar z\), \(U\ni\bar x\), constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\), and a \(C^1\) inverse \(Q:U\to V\) such that \(P:V\to U\) is bijective, \(Q=P^{-1}\), and \[m\|h\|\leq\|DP(z)h\|\leq M\|h\|\qquad\forall z\in V,\ h\in\mathbb R^m.\] Thus \(m=n\) and \(P\) is a local \(C^1\) diffeomorphism with uniformly conditioned Jacobian. Under the applicable subdifferential chain rule, slope residuals of \(f\) and \(g=f\circ P\) are comparable locally, so a KL inequality transfers after rescaling its desingularizer by a positive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable coordinate parameterization is a local continuously differentiable diffeomorphism whose Jacobian and inverse Jacobian are uniformly bounded. Such a map changes distances and slopes only by fixed factors, so qualitative KL behavior transfers between an objective and its pullback. A redundant or rank-deficient parameterization is not in this class unless a separate transverse-slope condition is supplied.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has a \(C^1\) local inverse near \(\bar z\).
The singular values of \(DP(z)\) are uniformly bounded above and away from zero locally.
The limiting-subdifferential chain rule is valid for \(f\circ P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is locally KL-stable, and KL inequalities for \(f\) at \(\bar x\) and \(f\circ P\) at \(\bar z\) transfer up to multiplicative changes in the desingularizer.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P\) and \(P^{-1}\) are locally Lipschitz and \(DP(z)\) is nonsingular throughout a sufficiently small neighborhood.
special_cases_latex: An invertible affine change \(P(z)=Az+b\) is KL-stable, with constants determined by the extreme singular values of \(A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Power-type KL exponents are unchanged by such a reparameterization, although constants may change.
boundary_notes: A surjective map with a nontrivial kernel is redundant and is not covered by the diffeomorphic definition.
A map whose smallest singular value tends to zero may flatten gradients and invalidate slope comparison.

notation.meaning: Uniform lower and upper Jacobian bounds.

review_flags: A precise inspected source for KL invariance under local diffeomorphisms and the required limiting-subdifferential chain rule is missing.
knowledge_statements.title: KL-Stable Local Reparameterization
Coordinate-Change Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally nonsingular smooth coordinate transformation preserves the KL property, with only a multiplicative change in the desingularizing function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), and let \(T:V\to U\) be a \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism between neighborhoods of \(\bar y\) and \(\bar x=T(\bar y)\). Suppose \(f\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\) with desingularizing function \(\varphi\), and \(\sup_{y\in V}\|DT(y)^{-1}\|\le M<\infty\). Then \(g=f\circ T\) has the KL property at \(\bar y\); specifically, after shrinking \(V\), \[ (M\varphi)'(g(y)-g(\bar y))\,\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial g(y))\ge 1 \] whenever \(g(\bar y)<g(y)<g(\bar y)+\eta\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and KL at \(\bar x\).
\(T\) is a local \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism with uniformly bounded inverse derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\) is KL at \(T^{-1}(\bar x)\), with desingularizer \(M\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local invariance of the KL property under a nonsingular smooth change of coordinates.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Coordinate-Change Stability and its scaling by M is consistent with the expected limiting-subdifferential chain rule for a local C1 diffeomorphism. No cited source verifies that chain rule or the precise local hypotheses, so the candidate cannot be accepted yet.

knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterization Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular increasing transformation of objective values preserves the KL inequality after explicitly reparameterizing its desingularizing function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have the KL property at \(\bar x\) with desingularizer \(\varphi\), and let \(\rho\) be \(C^1\) and strictly increasing on a neighborhood of \(f(\bar x)\), with \(\rho'(t)>0\). Define \(g=\rho\circ f\) and, for sufficiently small \(s\ge0\), \[ \psi(s)=\varphi\!\left(\rho^{-1}(\rho(f(\bar x))+s)-f(\bar x)\right). \] If the limiting-subdifferential chain rule \(\partial g(x)=\rho'(f(x))\partial f(x)\) holds locally, then \(g\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\) with desingularizer \(\psi\).
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is locally \(C^1\), strictly increasing, and has positive derivative.
The local limiting-subdifferential chain rule is valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=\rho\circ f\) is KL at \(\bar x\) with desingularizer \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL stability under a regular increasing scalar transformation of objective values.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Reparameterization Stability, and the displayed desingularizer is formally consistent with a positive-derivative scalar change of objective values. An authoritative locator is needed for the limiting-subdifferential chain rule and its required regularity assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Parameter Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a quadratic with a power map whose derivative vanishes can worsen its optimal KL exponent arbitrarily close to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(m\ge2\), let \(f(x)=x^2\), \(T_m(t)=t^m\), and \(g_m=f\circ T_m=t^{2m}\). At the origin, \(f\) satisfies the gradient KL inequality with exponent \(1/2\), since \(\lvert f'(x)\rvert=2\lvert f(x)\rvert^{1/2}\). In contrast, \[ \lvert g_m'(t)\rvert=2m\lvert g_m(t)\rvert^{1-1/(2m)}, \] and no gradient KL inequality \(\lvert g_m'(t)\rvert\ge c\lvert g_m(t)\rvert^\theta\) can hold locally with \(\theta<1-1/(2m)\). Thus the degenerate map \(DT_m(0)=0\) worsens the optimal exponent.
assumptions_latex: The gradient KL exponent convention is \(\|\nabla h\|\ge c|h-h(\bar x)|^\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal exponent changes from \(1/2\) for \(f\) to \(1-1/(2m)\) for \(f\circ T_m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent deterioration caused by a parameter map whose derivative vanishes.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and is the correct content kind for Degenerate Parameter Maps: direct differentiation gives the stated optimal power threshold. The record nevertheless supplies no inspectable source for the KL-exponent convention or optimality claim.

children.title: KL Transfer Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of transferring KL properties through perturbation, approximation, or limiting operations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform KL Transfer for a Function Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_k,f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be compact, and suppose each \(f_k\) has a KL inequality near \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates the uniform data needed for passage through approximation or a limit. It does not assert that ordinary pointwise or epigraphical convergence preserves KL.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((f_k)\) is uniformly KL-transferable to \(f\) along \(K\) if there exist \(\eta,\delta>0\) and one concave \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb R_+\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\in C^1(0,\eta)\), and \(\varphi'>0\), such that: (i) \(f_k\to f\) with value consistency at points approaching \(K\); (ii) limiting subgradients are graphically outer-stable, meaning \(x_k\to x\), \(f_k(x_k)\to f(x)\), and \(v_k\in\partial f_k(x_k)\), \(v_k\to v\), imply \(v\in\partial f(x)\); and (iii) for all large \(k\), \[\varphi'(f_k(x)-f_k(\bar x_k))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_k(x))\geq1\] whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<\delta\) and the value gap lies in \((0,\eta)\). Loss of any common neighborhood, common desingularizer, value consistency, or subgradient-graph control is a KL transfer boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of objectives admits stable KL transfer only when its KL inequalities are uniform and its values and subgradient graphs converge compatibly near the reference set. Merely knowing that every approximating function is KL is insufficient. The stability boundary is crossed when neighborhoods shrink, constants degenerate, desingularizers vary without control, or limiting subgradients cannot be recovered.
assumptions_latex: One pair \((\eta,\delta)\) and one desingularizer \(\varphi\) work for all sufficiently large \(k\).
Function values and limiting-subdifferential graphs satisfy the stated consistency conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family possesses uniform KL data suitable for transfer to the limiting objective; absence of uniformity or graph consistency lies outside the transfer class.
special_cases_latex: If \(f_k=f\) and the reference set is compact with constant objective value, the definition reduces to a uniformized KL inequality along \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A common power desingularizer \(\varphi(s)=cs^{1-\theta}\) prevents degeneration of the KL exponent along the approximating family.
boundary_notes: Pointwise convergence alone does not control subgradients.
The definition supplies transfer hypotheses; it is not itself a theorem that the limit is KL without a closed passage argument.

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of the kth objective.

review_flags: The node describes a boundary rather than a universally standardized named definition.
A source proving a KL stability theorem under the selected variational convergence and graph conditions is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform KL Transfer for a Function Family
Perturbation Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparable value gaps and a lower subgradient bound transfer a power-form KL inequality to a perturbed objective with the same exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=f+r\) near \(\bar x\), with \(f(\bar x)=g(\bar x)\). Assume that for all relevant \(x\) near \(\bar x\), \[ a\bigl(f(x)-f(\bar x)\bigr)\le g(x)-g(\bar x)\le b\bigl(f(x)-f(\bar x)\bigr) \] for constants \(0<a\le b\), and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial g(x))\ge c\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\) for some \(c>0\). If \(f\) has a power-form KL inequality \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge\mu(f(x)-f(\bar x))^\theta\), then \[ \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial g(x))\ge c\mu b^{-\theta}(g(x)-g(\bar x))^\theta. \]
assumptions_latex: The value gaps of \(f\) and \(g=f+r\) are locally comparable.
The perturbed subgradient distance is bounded below by that of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) satisfies a power-form KL inequality with exponent \(\theta\) and constant \(c\mu b^{-\theta}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantitative sufficient condition transferring a KL inequality through a perturbation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Perturbation Stability, and the constant follows algebraically from the stated value-gap and subgradient comparisons. A source is still required for this formulation as a KL perturbation-transfer condition and for the intended domain of the relevant points.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common KL inequality passes to a limit when both value gaps and subgradient distances possess suitable recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_k,f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(\bar x_k\to\bar x\) and \(f_k(\bar x_k)\to f(\bar x)\). Suppose all \(f_k\) satisfy, on common value and spatial neighborhoods, \[ \varphi'(f_k(x)-f_k(\bar x_k))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_k(x))\ge1 \] for one desingularizer \(\varphi\). Assume every relevant \(x\) admits \(x_k\to x\) such that \(f_k(x_k)-f_k(\bar x_k)\to f(x)-f(\bar x)\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_k(x_k))\to\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\). Then \(f\) satisfies the same KL inequality at \(\bar x\).
assumptions_latex: The approximants share one KL desingularizer on uniform neighborhoods.
Base points and base values converge.
Value gaps and subgradient distances admit simultaneous recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\) with desingularizer \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Passage of a uniform KL inequality to a variational limit under slope recovery.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Approximation Stability, but the asserted passage to the limit depends on the exact regularity of the desingularizer, uniform neighborhoods, and simultaneous value-and-slope recovery. No source is supplied to validate that these hypotheses are sufficient in the claimed generality.

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-Operation Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform limits of KL functions need not be KL when critical points with positive values accumulate at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a nonnegative \(C^\infty\) function \(f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(f(0)=0\) and positive local maxima \(x_j\to0\). Hence \(f'(x_j)=0\) and \(f(x_j)>f(0)\), so no KL inequality can hold at \(0\). By polynomial approximation, there are polynomials \(p_k\) converging uniformly to \(f\) on \([-1,1]\). Each \(p_k\) is semialgebraic and therefore KL, while the uniform limit \(f\) is not KL at \(0\). Consequently, uniform convergence without uniform desingularizers and slope control does not preserve KL regularity.
assumptions_latex: A smooth nonnegative function has positive stationary local maxima accumulating at zero.
Polynomials approximate it uniformly on the compact interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform convergence of KL functions alone does not imply that the limit is KL.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise or uniform function convergence alone does not preserve the KL property.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind and conclusion match Limiting-Operation Failures. The proposed construction is plausible, but the existence of the required smooth function and the polynomial-KL step need inspectable authoritative locators.

children.title: Abstract KL Convergence Framework
children.top_down_role: Reusable continuous- and discrete-time frameworks that convert KL geometry into trajectory convergence and rate classifications.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Abstract descent framework and applications
Analytic descent sequences

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((x^k)_{k\geq0}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded, and let \(E\) be a real-valued continuous energy on an open neighborhood of the sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an algorithm-independent discrete architecture formulated through decrease and a power-type value-gap/motion coupling. It is distinct from a particular update rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \(((x^k),E)\) satisfies the abstract power-KL descent architecture with data \((a,c,\theta,E_\infty)\) if \(a,c>0\), \(\theta\in[0,1)\), \(E(x^k)\downarrow E_\infty\), and, for all sufficiently large \(k\), \[E(x^{k+1})\leq E(x^k)-a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\] \[\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\geq c^{-1}\bigl(E(x^{k+1})-E_\infty\bigr)^\theta\] whenever \(E(x^{k+1})>E_\infty\). The first inequality converts motion into energy decrease; the second is the KL-type coupling that prevents arbitrarily small motion while a positive value gap remains. Finite termination, linear behavior, and sublinear behavior correspond respectively to \(\theta=0\), \(0<\theta\leq1/2\), and \(1/2<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The abstract architecture consists of a bounded trajectory, a continuous decreasing energy, quadratic sufficient decrease, and a KL power coupling between step length and the remaining value gap. It records only the reusable inequalities needed for convergence and rate classification, not how an algorithm computes its next iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is continuous on an open set containing the sequence.
\(a,c>0\), \(\theta\in[0,1)\), and the two inequalities hold eventually.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(((x^k),E)\) belongs to the abstract power-KL descent class with exponent \(\theta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The coupling inequality is \(E(x^{k+1})-E_\infty\leq c^{1/\theta}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^{1/\theta}\) when \(\theta>0\).
special_cases_latex: \(\theta=0\) forces a positive lower bound on every nonzero late step.
\(\theta=1/2\) is the boundary of the linear-rate regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: The sufficient-decrease inequality implies \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\).
boundary_notes: Square summability alone does not imply finite trajectory length.
This definition does not include stochastic errors, delays, or a multistep Lyapunov state.

children.title: Continuous-Time KL Trajectories
children.top_down_role: KL convergence architecture for gradient and subgradient dynamical systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(x:[0,T)\to H\) be locally absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses quadratic curves of maximal slope and a local KL inequality. It covers smooth gradient flows and suitable nonsmooth subgradient flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The curve \(x\) is a continuous-time KL trajectory for \(f\) if there is a strong upper gradient \(g\) for \(f\) such that, for every \(0\leq s\leq t<T\), \[f(x(t))+\frac12\int_s^t\|\dot x(r)\|^2\,dr+\frac12\int_s^t g(x(r))^2\,dr=f(x(s)),\] and the KL inequality holds near the trajectory's nonempty cluster set: there are \(\eta,\delta>0\) and a concave \(\varphi\in C^1(0,\eta)\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi'>0\), such that \[\varphi'(f(z)-\ell)g(z)\geq1\] whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(z,\omega(x))<\delta\) and \(0<f(z)-\ell<\eta\), where \(\ell=\lim_{t\uparrow T}f(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-time KL trajectory is a locally absolutely continuous energy-dissipating curve whose kinetic speed and slope exactly account for the energy loss, and whose limiting energy landscape satisfies one uniform KL inequality near the cluster set.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is a strong upper gradient for \(f\).
The energy identity and the uniform KL inequality hold as displayed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is an energy-dissipating curve of maximal slope operating in a KL neighborhood of its limiting set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When equality \(\|\dot x(t)\|=g(x(t))\) holds almost everywhere, the energy identity becomes \(-\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=\|\dot x(t)\|^2=g(x(t))^2\) almost everywhere.
special_cases_latex: For smooth \(f\), take \(g=\|\nabla f\|\) and \(\dot x=-\nabla f(x)\).
For suitable nonsmooth \(f\), take \(g=\|\partial^\circ f\|\), the norm of the minimal subgradient.
immediate_consequences_latex: The energy is nonincreasing and both \(\dot x\) and \(g\circ x\) are locally square integrable.
boundary_notes: A differential inclusion without a chain rule need not satisfy the energy identity.
Infinite-dimensional compactness issues are excluded.

notation.meaning: Cluster set as time approaches the terminal horizon.

children.title: Smooth Gradient-Flow Families
children.top_down_role: Continuous-time descent for differentiable objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Gradient-Flow Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth gradient flow follows the negative gradient and dissipates objective value at the squared speed of the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. A smooth gradient-flow trajectory from \(x_0\) is an absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[ \dot x(t)=-\nabla f(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T),\qquad x(0)=x_0. \] Along such a trajectory, the chain rule gives \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\nabla f(x(t))\|^2=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere. A parameterized gradient-flow family is a collection of these trajectories indexed by their initial points or by parameters entering \(f\).
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is absolutely continuous and satisfies the differential equation almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\le0\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical continuous-time descent trajectories for continuously differentiable objectives.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition and dissipation identity match Smooth Gradient-Flow Families and consistently restrict the objective to the differentiable setting. No authoritative source with a section, theorem, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth gradient flow follows the negative gradient of a differentiable objective. Its preconditioned variants multiply the gradient by a uniformly positive-definite metric field. In either case the objective decreases continuously, and in the Euclidean case the squared speed, squared gradient norm, and energy dissipation coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Subgradient-Flow Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth subgradient flow solves a differential inclusion and dissipates energy when the appropriate subdifferential chain rule holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. A subgradient-flow trajectory from \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is an absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) for which there exists a measurable selection \(v(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) satisfying \[ \dot x(t)+v(t)=0\quad\text{for almost every }t,\qquad x(0)=x_0. \] When \(f\) admits the subdifferential chain rule along \(x\), one has \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=\langle v(t),\dot x(t)\rangle=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: A measurable limiting-subgradient selection exists along the trajectory.
The subdifferential chain rule holds along \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x(t))\) is nonincreasing and \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential-inclusion descent trajectories governed by a nonsmooth limiting subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Write \(\partial f\) for its limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses an almost-everywhere differential inclusion. Energy dissipation requires a compatible chain rule and is stated as part of the admissible flow class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsmooth subgradient-flow trajectory for \(f\) is a locally absolutely continuous curve \(x:[0,T)\to H\) for which there exists a measurable selection \(v(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) satisfying \[\dot x(t)+v(t)=0\qquad\text{for almost every }t.\] It is an energy-compatible subgradient flow if \(f\circ x\) is locally absolutely continuous and obeys the chain rule \(\frac d{dt}f(x(t))=\langle v(t),\dot x(t)\rangle\) almost everywhere. Then \[\frac d{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2=-\|v(t)\|^2\] almost everywhere. The minimal-section flow additionally requires \(v(t)=\partial^\circ f(x(t))\), the minimum-norm element of \(\partial f(x(t))\), whenever that element exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth subgradient flow is an absolutely continuous curve whose negative velocity is a limiting subgradient almost everywhere. An admissible energy-compatible flow also satisfies the subgradient chain rule, so its objective decrease equals the squared speed. Choosing the minimum-norm subgradient defines the minimal-section variant.
assumptions_latex: A measurable \(v(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) exists with \(\dot x(t)=-v(t)\) almost everywhere.
For energy compatibility, the displayed chain rule holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\dot x(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) almost everywhere; under energy compatibility, \(-\frac d{dt}f(x(t))=\|\dot x(t)\|^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In a Hilbert space, a quadratic curve of maximal slope driven by the minimum-norm subgradient satisfies the corresponding gradient-flow inclusion under the stated regularity conditions.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\in C^1\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\) and the inclusion reduces to smooth gradient flow.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every constant subgradient-flow trajectory is limiting-critical: \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
boundary_notes: For a general nonconvex nonsmooth function, the chain rule is not automatic.
Clarke, convex, and limiting subdifferentials define different flow classes unless regularity makes them coincide.

children.title: Trajectory Limit-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Continuous-time counterparts of finite length and cluster-set collapse.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space and let \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) be locally absolutely continuous with metric derivative \(|x'|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The objects are purely trajectory-geometric. Criticality or KL assumptions enter only in later convergence results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The omega-limit set of \(x\) is \[\omega(x):=\{\bar x\in X:\exists t_j\uparrow\infty\text{ with }x(t_j)\to\bar x\}.\] The tail length after time \(T\) is \[L(T):=\int_T^\infty |x'|(t)\,dt,\] and the trajectory has finite length if \(L(0)<\infty\). It exhibits cluster-set collapse if \(\omega(x)=\{x_\infty\}\) and \(x(t)\to x_\infty\). For an absolutely continuous trajectory in a complete metric space, finite length implies existence of \(x_\infty\), cluster-set collapse, and the quantitative tail estimate \[d(x(t),x_\infty)\leq L(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The omega-limit set contains all limits of trajectory subsequences at times tending to infinity. The trajectory has finite length when its total metric speed is integrable. In a complete space, finite length forces the entire trajectory to converge to one point, collapses the omega-limit set to that singleton, and bounds the remaining distance by the remaining arc length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(0)<\infty\Longrightarrow\exists x_\infty:\ x(t)\to x_\infty,\ \omega(x)=\{x_\infty\},\ d(x(t),x_\infty)\leq L(t).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finite length means that the total variation of \(x\) on \([0,\infty)\) is finite.
special_cases_latex: For a differentiable Euclidean trajectory, \(|x'|(t)=\|\dot x(t)\|\) almost everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sequence \(t_j\uparrow\infty\) has the same trajectory limit when finite length holds.
boundary_notes: A bounded trajectory can have a nontrivial omega-limit set when its length is infinite.
Square-integrable speed does not imply finite length.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Trajectory Length
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform KL geometry converts energy dissipation into finite trajectory length and convergence to one critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a bounded absolutely continuous trajectory for a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f\). Suppose \(-\dot x(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) and \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere. If \(f(x(t))\downarrow\ell\) and a uniform KL inequality with desingularizer \(\varphi\) holds near the nonempty omega-limit set at level \(\ell\), then for sufficiently large \(t_0\), \[ \int_{t_0}^{\infty}\|\dot x(t)\|\,dt\le \varphi(f(x(t_0))-\ell)<\infty. \] Hence the whole trajectory has finite length and converges to a critical point.
assumptions_latex: The bounded trajectory satisfies the subgradient inclusion and exact energy identity.
A uniform KL inequality holds near its omega-limit set at level \(\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int_0^\infty\|\dot x(t)\|dt<\infty\), and \(x(t)\) converges to a critical point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL finite-length conclusion for bounded energy-dissipating subgradient trajectories.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Finite Trajectory Length, and its tail estimate is consistent with the exact energy identity, subgradient inclusion, and a uniform KL inequality. A source must verify the uniformization assumptions and the closedness conditions needed for the final criticality conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Omega-Limit Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded trajectory approaches a nonempty compact omega-limit set, which lies in one critical level under descent and asymptotic criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and continuous, and define \[ \omega(x)=\{z:\text{there exists }t_k\to\infty\text{ with }x(t_k)\to z\}. \] Then \(\omega(x)\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\operatorname{dist}(x(t),\omega(x))\to0\). If \(x\) is a subgradient-flow trajectory, \(f(x(t))\downarrow\ell\), \(f\) is constant with value \(\ell\) on \(\omega(x)\), and every cluster point is asymptotically critical, then \(\omega(x)\subset\operatorname{crit}f:=\{z:0\in\partial f(z)\}\).
assumptions_latex: Objective values converge and equal \(\ell\) at all cluster points.
Every cluster point is asymptotically critical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(x)\) is nonempty and compact, \(\operatorname{dist}(x(t),\omega(x))\to0\), and \(\omega(x)\subset\operatorname{crit}f\cap f^{-1}(\ell)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic topology and criticality of limit sets for bounded descent trajectories.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The topological omega-limit assertions fit the container and are valid for bounded continuous trajectories in finite-dimensional space. However, `asymptotically critical` is not formally defined, and no source states the precise subdifferential closedness and value-convergence hypotheses that yield critical cluster points.

knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Set Collapse
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite arc length forces an absolutely continuous trajectory to converge to one point, so its omega-limit set is a singleton; the limit is critical when all omega-limit points are critical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be absolutely continuous and suppose \[ \int_0^\infty\|\dot x(t)\|\,dt<\infty. \] Then there exists \(x_\infty\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(x(t)\to x_\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\), and the omega-limit set satisfies \(\omega(x)=\{x_\infty\}\). If, additionally, every omega-limit point is critical for a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), then \(0\in\partial f(x_\infty)\).
assumptions_latex: For the criticality conclusion, every point of \(\omega(x)\) is critical for \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)\to x_\infty\), \(\omega(x)=\{x_\infty\}\), and, under the additional criticality assumption, \(0\in\partial f(x_\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite length collapses the omega-limit set to a singleton.

children.title: Discrete Descent Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Algorithm-independent mechanisms connecting decrease, motion, residuals, and accumulation behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous and let \((x^k)_{k\geq0}\subset\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is deterministic, finite-dimensional, and algorithm independent. It separates decrease, stationarity control, and limit compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((x^k)\) is an abstract discrete descent sequence for \(f\) if there exist \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and vectors \(w^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})\) such that, for every sufficiently large \(k\), \[f(x^{k+1})+a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\leq f(x^k),\qquad \|w^{k+1}\|\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|,\] and the following compatibility condition holds: whenever \(x^{k_j}\to\bar x\), one has \(f(x^{k_j})\to f(\bar x)\). A Lyapunov descent sequence replaces \(f(x^k)\) by an auxiliary energy \(E(z^k)\) on a finite-memory state \(z^k=(x^k,\ldots,x^{k-r})\), while retaining analogous decrease, residual, and compatibility requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstract discrete descent sequence has three components: sufficient objective decrease proportional to squared motion, a subgradient residual controlled by the latest step, and continuity of objective values along convergent subsequences. A finite-memory Lyapunov version applies the same mechanism to an augmented state.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b>0\) and \(w^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})\) satisfy the two inequalities eventually.
Objective values are compatible with convergent subsequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^k)\) is a discrete descent mechanism coupling energy loss, motion, stationarity residuals, and accumulation behavior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The relative-error inequality may be written \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\).
special_cases_latex: For an exact smooth gradient step, \(w^{k+1}=\nabla f(x^{k+1})\).
In inertial schemes, the energy may be \(E(x^k,x^{k-1})=f(x^k)+c\|x^k-x^{k-1}\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(f\) is bounded below along the sequence, then \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\to0\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not itself guarantee boundedness or finite length.
Inexact and stochastic variants require explicit error sequences.

children.title: Sufficient-Decrease Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Objective or auxiliary-energy decrease as a convergence input.

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient-Decrease Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sufficient decrease charges each squared step against an energy drop, yielding square-summable increments and asymptotic regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\). The sequence satisfies quadratic sufficient decrease if there exists \(a>0\) such that \[ F(x_{k+1})+a\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2\le F(x_k)\qquad\text{for every }k\ge0. \] More generally, an auxiliary energy \(E_k\) may replace \(F(x_k)\), provided \(E_{k+1}+a\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2\le E_k\) and \(E_k\) is bounded below. In either form, \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2<\infty\), hence \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\).
assumptions_latex: The objective or auxiliary energy is bounded below along the sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete energy decrease condition used in abstract KL convergence arguments.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition is the correct content kind for Sufficient-Decrease Mechanisms. Given a lower bound on the applicable energy, telescoping yields the stated square summability and vanishing increments, but no authoritative KL descent-framework locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((Z,d)\) be a metric space, let \(E:Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \((z^k)\subset\operatorname{dom}E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an algorithm-independent deterministic decrease condition. The energy may be the objective or an augmented Lyapunov function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((z^k)\) satisfies quadratic sufficient decrease for \(E\) with constant \(a>0\) if \[E(z^{k+1})+a\,d(z^{k+1},z^k)^2\leq E(z^k)\qquad\forall k\geq k_0\] for some \(k_0\). More generally, for a nonnegative motion measure \(D:Z\times Z\to\mathbb R_+\), it satisfies \(D\)-sufficient decrease if \[E(z^{k+1})+aD(z^{k+1},z^k)\leq E(z^k).\] The mechanism is strict in the sense that \(D(z^{k+1},z^k)>0\) forces a positive energy loss. When \(z^k\) is a finite-memory algorithmic state, this defines sufficient decrease of an auxiliary energy even if the original objective is nonmonotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sufficient decrease means that every accepted motion pays for itself through a quantified drop in an objective or Lyapunov energy. The canonical KL-analysis form uses the squared step length, while a generalized form uses another nonnegative motion measure. An augmented state permits nonmonotone objectives provided that the auxiliary energy decreases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(z^{k+1})\leq E(z^k)-aD(z^{k+1},z^k)\) for every sufficiently large \(k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(D(z^{k+1},z^k)=d(z^{k+1},z^k)^2\), the decrease is quadratic in motion.
special_cases_latex: For \(z^k=x^k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(E=f\), and Euclidean distance, \(f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(E\) is bounded below, then \(\sum_{k\geq k_0}D(z^{k+1},z^k)<\infty\).
boundary_notes: Monotonicity without a quantitative motion term is not sufficient decrease in this sense.
A summable additive-error variant is a different mechanism.

children.title: Relative-Error Mechanisms

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient at each new iterate is bounded by a fixed multiple of the latest step, so vanishing steps imply vanishing stationarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x_k)_{k\ge 0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\). A relative-error mechanism holds if there exist \(b>0\), an index \(k_0\), and vectors \(w_{k+1}\in\partial F(x_{k+1})\) such that, for every \(k\ge k_0\), \[\|w_{k+1}\|\le b\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x_{k+1}))\le b\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\); hence vanishing inter-iterate motion forces the chosen stationarity residual to vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x_{k+1}))\le b\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract subgradient residual bound used in discrete KL convergence arguments.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity Residual Relative to Inter-Iterate Motion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous and let \((x^k)\subset\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exact deterministic one-step relative-error condition is primary. A finite-window and summably inexact extension is recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((x^k)\) satisfies the one-step relative-error condition for \(f\) with constant \(b>0\) if, for every sufficiently large \(k\), there exists \(w^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})\) such that \[\|w^{k+1}\|\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\] A finite-window relative-error condition of memory \(r\) replaces the right side by \(b\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\|x^{k+1-j}-x^{k-j}\|\). An inexact variant permits an additive \(\varepsilon_{k+1}\geq0\), which must be controlled separately, commonly by \(\sum_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative error bounds a stationarity residual at the new iterate by the motion used to reach it. The canonical form uses only the latest step; multistep algorithms may use a finite window of recent motions. Inexact variants add an explicitly controlled error term.
assumptions_latex: \(b>0\), and an appropriate subgradient selection exists at each relevant iterate.
For the inexact variant, \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\) and its required summability or decay is stated separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) eventually in the canonical one-step regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(w^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})\) satisfying the displayed norm bound.
special_cases_latex: For a smooth objective, \(\|\nabla f(x^{k+1})\|\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\).
For a composite objective, \(w^{k+1}\) may be assembled from the subproblem optimality residual.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\to0\).
boundary_notes: The inequality controls stationarity but does not itself imply descent.
A residual evaluated at \(x^k\) rather than \(x^{k+1}\) is an index-shifted variant and must be stated explicitly.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit–criticality compatibility for a descent trajectory
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\). Write \(\partial F\) for the limiting subdifferential and \(\omega(x^0)\) for the cluster set of the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, possibly nonsmooth and nonconvex setting; the definition records the sequential compatibility needed to identify cluster points as limiting-critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trajectory is limit–criticality compatible with \(F\) if, for every subsequence \((x^{k_j})\) converging to some \(\bar x\), one has \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)\), and there exist residual vectors \(v^k\in\partial F(x^k)\) such that \(\|v^k\|\to0\). Equivalently, the value-continuity condition along convergent subsequences and the vanishing limiting-subgradient condition jointly ensure that every \(\bar x\in\omega(x^0)\) satisfies \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory is limit–criticality compatible with the objective when objective values agree with the objective at every subsequential limit and the trajectory admits limiting subgradients whose norms vanish. In the finite-dimensional limiting-subdifferential setting, these conditions identify every cluster point as a limiting-critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\,x^{k_j}\to\bar x:\quad F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x),\qquad v^k\in\partial F(x^k),\quad \|v^k\|\to0,\quad\text{and hence}\quad \omega(x^0)\subset\operatorname{crit}F.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the infimum in the slope residual is attained, the residual condition can be written as \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^k))\to0\).
If \(F\) is continuous on a neighborhood containing the trajectory and its cluster set, the subsequential value-compatibility condition holds automatically.
special_cases_latex: For \(F\in C^1\), limiting criticality reduces to \(\nabla F(\bar x)=0\), and the residual condition becomes \(\|\nabla F(x^k)\|\to0\).
For \(F=f+g\), with \(f\in C^1\) and \(g\) proper lower semicontinuous, the stationarity inclusion is \(0\in\nabla f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convergent subsequence has a critical limit.
If the full sequence converges to \(x^\star\), then \(0\in\partial F(x^\star)\).
boundary_notes: Vanishing step lengths alone do not imply limiting criticality.
Lower semicontinuity yields only one inequality for objective values; equality along the selected subsequence is an additional compatibility requirement.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, strong or weak convergence and the applicable closedness property of the subdifferential must be specified separately.

set of limits of convergent subsequences of the trajectory

knowledge_statements.title: Limit–criticality compatibility for a descent trajectory
Continuity Routes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the objective converges along the trajectory and is continuous relative to the trajectory closure at every cluster point, then every cluster point has the limiting objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\), and define the trajectory closure \(C:=\overline{\{x_k:k\ge0\}}\). Suppose that \(F(x_k)\to\ell\in\mathbb{R}\) and that the restriction \(F|_C\) is continuous at every cluster point of \((x_k)\). Then, for every subsequence satisfying \(x_{k_j}\to\bar x\), one has \[F(x_{k_j})\to F(\bar x).\] Consequently, every cluster point \(\bar x\) satisfies \(F(\bar x)=\ell\).
assumptions_latex: The restriction of \(F\) to \(C=\overline{\{x_k:k\ge0\}}\) is continuous at every cluster point of \((x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point \(\bar x\) of \((x_k)\) satisfies \(F(\bar x)=\ell\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility obtained by continuity of the objective along convergent trajectory subsequences.

notation.meaning: limiting objective value along the trajectory
an arbitrary cluster point of the trajectory

knowledge_statements.title: Attentive-Convergence Routes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each cluster point must be reached by a subsequence whose iterates and objective values converge simultaneously to that point and its objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. A subsequence \((x_{k_j})\) converges \(F\)-attentively to \(\bar x\), written \(x_{k_j}\xrightarrow{F}\bar x\), when \[x_{k_j}\to\bar x\quad\text{and}\quad F(x_{k_j})\to F(\bar x).\] The attentive-convergence route to limit compatibility requires that each trajectory cluster point admit at least one such subsequence. If \(F(x_k)\to\ell\), this requirement implies \(F(\bar x)=\ell\) for every cluster point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every cluster point \(\bar x\), there is \((k_j)\) with \(x_{k_j}\to\bar x\) and \(F(x_{k_j})\to F(\bar x)=\ell\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequence compatibility stated through simultaneous convergence of iterates and objective values.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The attentive-convergence definition and its compatibility consequence are internally coherent and fit the route container, but the specialized variational-analysis terminology and exact formulation require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Criticality Compatibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attentive convergence plus vanishing limiting-subgradient residuals makes every corresponding cluster point critical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Suppose indices \((k_j)\), points \(x_{k_j}\), and vectors \(w_{k_j}\in\partial F(x_{k_j})\) satisfy \[x_{k_j}\to\bar x,\qquad F(x_{k_j})\to F(\bar x),\qquad w_{k_j}\to0.\] By sequential closedness of the limiting-subdifferential graph under attentive convergence, \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\). Thus an attentive cluster point is critical whenever the associated stationarity residuals vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness mechanism transferring vanishing residuals to stationarity at cluster points.

notation.meaning: selected limiting subgradients along a convergent subsequence

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The attentive closedness statement is the appropriate compatibility property, but the decisive limiting-subdifferential graph-closedness theorem has no cited source. Its precise hypotheses must be verified against an authoritative variational-analysis reference.

children.title: Trajectory Compactness Routes
children.top_down_role: Level boundedness, coercivity, and other mechanisms preventing trajectory escape.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \((x^k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\) be a trajectory satisfying \(F(x^{k+1})\le F(x^k)\). Define the initial sublevel set \(L_0=\{x\in X:F(x)\le F(x^0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic trajectories. Compactness is formulated as a property ensuring at least one cluster point and preventing escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trajectory compactness route is a verified condition implying that the tail of \((x^k)\) is contained in a compact set. Canonical routes are: \(L_0\) is compact; or \(F\) is lower semicontinuous and level bounded, so every sublevel set is compact; or the trajectory is directly known to be bounded. Under monotonicity, compactness of \(L_0\) gives \(x^k\in L_0\) for every \(k\), while direct boundedness gives compact closure \(\overline{\{x^k:k\ge0\}}\) in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory compactness route is any stated hypothesis that confines all sufficiently late iterates to a compact set. For a monotone descent sequence, compactness of the initial sublevel set is the standard route. Lower semicontinuity plus level boundedness supplies that compactness, while an independently established boundedness estimate is another route in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists K\subset\mathbb R^n\ \text{compact}\quad\forall k\ge k_0:\ x^k\in K,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \omega(x^0)\ne\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, relative compactness of \(\{x^k:k\ge k_0\}\) is equivalent to boundedness of that tail.
A function is level bounded precisely when \(\{x:F(x)\le\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\); if it is also lower semicontinuous, these sublevel sets are compact.
special_cases_latex: Coercivity, \(F(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\), implies level boundedness.
A compact feasible set confines every feasible trajectory without requiring coercivity of the objective.
immediate_consequences_latex: The trajectory has a convergent subsequence.
Its cluster set is compact and nonempty.
Any continuous quantity evaluated on the compact trajectory closure is bounded.
boundary_notes: Descent alone does not prevent an unbounded trajectory when the relevant sublevel set is unbounded.
Bounded objective values do not imply bounded iterates.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, boundedness need not imply relative compactness.

notation.meaning: sublevel set at the initial objective value

review_flags: The supplied source hints were not verified as support for the complete route definition.
A source explicitly covering level boundedness, coercivity, and trajectory precompactness is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory compactness route
Trajectory Boundedness Routes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A descending trajectory remains in its initial sublevel set and is therefore bounded when that sublevel set is bounded; coercivity is a standard sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\) satisfy \(F(x_{k+1})\le F(x_k)\) for every \(k\ge0\). Define \[L_0:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(x)\le F(x_0)\}.\] If \(L_0\) is bounded, then \(x_k\in L_0\) for every \(k\), and hence \(\sup_{k\ge0}\|x_k\|<\infty\). In particular, coercivity of \(F\), meaning \(F(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\), is sufficient for boundedness of \(L_0\).
assumptions_latex: The sublevel set \(L_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(x)\le F(x_0)\}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\in L_0\) for every \(k\ge0\), and \(\sup_{k\ge0}\|x_k\|<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient routes preventing the discrete trajectory from escaping to infinity.

notation.meaning: sublevel set determined by the initial objective value

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Global Convergence of the Basic Algorithm p. 115

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Routes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a bounded trajectory has compact closure, a convergent subsequence, and a nonempty compact cluster set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_k)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). If the trajectory is bounded, then its closure \[K:=\overline{\{x_k:k\ge0\}}\] is closed and bounded, hence compact. Consequently, \((x_k)\) has a convergent subsequence and its cluster set \(\omega(x_0)\) is nonempty and compact. More generally, it suffices that all iterates lie in any compact set \(K\). The implication from boundedness to compactness here is specific to finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\overline{\{x_k:k\ge0\}}\) is compact and \(\varnothing\ne\omega(x_0)\subset K\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness conditions guaranteeing existence of trajectory cluster points.

notation.meaning: set of subsequential limits of the trajectory
