children.title: Structured Merit Splitting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structured methods requiring method-specific merit functions or regularity before KL arguments apply.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured splitting interface equipped with a merit state
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean product space, let \(S:Z\rightrightarrows Z\) be an iteration map, and let \(\mathcal M:Z\times Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a method-specific merit function. A state may contain primal variables, multipliers, reflected variables, residuals, or delayed iterates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic interface for splitting schemes whose KL analysis is applied to a method-specific merit function rather than necessarily to the original objective. This slot defines the interface and does not claim that every splitting method admits it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trajectory \((z^k)_{k\ge0}\) has a structured merit splitting interface with constants \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and memory length \(q\in\mathbb N\) if \(z^{k+1}\in S(z^k)\) and there are residuals \(r^{k+1}\ge0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(k\), \[\mathcal M(z^{k+1},z^k)+a\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|^2\le \mathcal M(z^k,z^{k-1}),\] \[\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\partial\mathcal M(z^{k+1},z^k)\right)\le b\sum_{j=0}^{q}\|z^{k+1-j}-z^{k-j}\|+r^{k+1}.\] The interface is exact when \(r^{k+1}=0\); it is summably inexact when \(\sum_k r^{k+1}<\infty\). It is KL-compatible on a set \(K\subseteq Z\times Z\) when \(\mathcal M\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, is bounded below along the trajectory, and has the KL property at every cluster point in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured merit splitting interface consists of an iteration map, an augmented state, and a proper lower-semicontinuous merit function. Along the generated trajectory the merit must decrease by at least a positive multiple of the squared step, while the distance from zero to its limiting subdifferential must be controlled by finitely many recent steps and an optional error residual. Exact and summably inexact versions are distinguished by whether that residual is zero or summable. KL compatibility additionally requires the merit function to have the KL property at the relevant cluster points and to remain bounded below along the trajectory.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is finite dimensional and \(z^{k+1}\in S(z^k)\) for every \(k\).
\(\mathcal M\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on its effective domain.
The sufficient-decrease and relative-error inequalities hold eventually with fixed \(a,b>0\) and finite \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S,\mathcal M,(z^k))\) constitutes an exact or summably inexact structured merit splitting interface, and is KL-compatible when the stated KL and boundedness conditions also hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first inequality can be written \(E_{k+1}+a\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|^2\le E_k\) with \(E_k=\mathcal M(z^k,z^{k-1})\).
When \(q=0\), relative error reduces to \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\mathcal M(z^{k+1},z^k))\le b\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|+r^{k+1}\).
special_cases_latex: An augmented-Lagrangian splitting method may take \(z^k=(x^k,y^k,\lambda^k)\) and use a regularized augmented Lagrangian as \(\mathcal M\).
A reflection method may enlarge the state to include both a shadow iterate and a reflected iterate.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(r^{k+1}=0\), then \(E_k\) is nonincreasing and \(\sum_k\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|^2<\infty\) whenever \(E_k\) is bounded below.
The interface separates algorithm-specific verification of decrease and relative error from the later use of a KL inequality.
boundary_notes: The definition does not identify a universal merit function for Douglas–Rachford, ADMM, or alternating projections.
Boundedness of the iterates and continuity of the merit along convergent subsequences are separate requirements in many convergence results.

notation.meaning: Method-specific merit function on the augmented state.
Finite memory length in the relative-error estimate.

review_flags: No inspected source states this exact abstract merit-interface definition with both the finite-memory relative-error inequality and the exact/summably-inexact distinction.
A method-specific authoritative KL convergence source is required before promotion.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured splitting interface equipped with a merit state

children.title: Nonconvex Douglas-Rachford Interface
children.top_down_role: Reflection-splitting families with KL-compatible envelopes or merit functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Douglas-Rachford Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the two proximal maps to a point and its reflection, relax the discrepancy update, and monitor the shadow-point residual through a KL-compatible merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_x f(x)+g(x)\), choose \(z^0\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(\lambda_k\in(0,2)\). At iteration \(k\), select
\[
x^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(z^k),\qquad
y^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(2x^k-z^k),
\]
and update
\[
z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(y^k-x^k).
\]
Here \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_u\{h(u)+\|u-v\|^2/(2\gamma)\}\), interpreted set-valuedly. Stop when \(\|y^k-x^k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return the shadow point \(x^k\). A KL convergence analysis additionally requires a proper merit function with sufficient decrease and a relative-error bound.
assumptions_latex: The two displayed proximal sets are nonempty along the generated sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(y^k-x^k)\), with splitting residual \(y^k-x^k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued proximal reflection splitting for a nonconvex two-term objective.
review_flags: Nonconvex parameter restrictions and admissible KL merit functions vary by theorem.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the Douglas–Rachford interface and the set-valued update is recognizable, but admissible relaxation ranges and KL merit-function conditions in the nonconvex setting are theorem-dependent. A precise source is required before this version can be relied upon.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R^n\), let \(f,g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous functions, and let \(\gamma>0\). For \(h\in\{f,g\}\), define the possibly set-valued proximal map \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in H}\{h(u)+\|u-z\|^2/(2\gamma)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, possibly nonconvex and nonsmooth two-function splitting. The definition assumes only that the proximal selections used by the iteration exist; it makes no convexity-based single-valuedness or convergence assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relaxed nonconvex Douglas–Rachford trajectory for \(f+g\) is a sequence \((z^k,x^k,y^k)_{k\ge0}\) and a relaxation parameter \(\lambda\in(0,2)\) satisfying, for every \(k\ge0\), \[x^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(z^k),\qquad y^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(2x^k-z^k),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(y^k-x^k).\] Equivalently, with set-valued reflectors \(R_{\gamma h}=2\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}-I\), the update obeys \[z^{k+1}\in\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)z^k+\frac{\lambda}{2}(R_{\gamma g}\circ R_{\gamma f})(z^k).\] The sequence \((x^k)\) is the proximal shadow sequence. A KL-compatible Douglas–Rachford interface additionally specifies a proper lower-semicontinuous envelope or lifted merit \(\mathcal D_\gamma\) on the relevant state for which sufficient decrease, relative error, boundedness, and the KL property can be verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two proper lower-semicontinuous functions, a nonconvex Douglas–Rachford step selects a proximal point of the first function, reflects the current state through that selection, selects a proximal point of the second function at the reflected state, and moves the state by a relaxed difference of the two proximal points. Because either proximal map may be multivalued, the interface is a set-valued iteration. The equivalent reflector form averages the identity with the composition of the two set-valued reflectors. A KL-compatible version must separately identify an envelope or lifted merit satisfying the descent and subgradient-control properties required by KL analysis.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper and lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb R^n\).
For every encountered argument, both displayed proximal argmin sets are nonempty.
\(\gamma>0\), \(\lambda\in(0,2)\), and one proximal selection is made whenever a map is multivalued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inclusions and relaxed state update define a set-valued nonconvex Douglas–Rachford trajectory and its shadow sequence.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\lambda=1\), \(z^{k+1}\in\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma g}R_{\gamma f})(z^k)\).
Writing \(u^k=x^k\) and \(v^k=y^k\), the state displacement is \(z^{k+1}-z^k=\lambda(v^k-u^k)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f=\delta_A\) and \(g=\delta_B\) for closed sets \(A,B\), the proximal maps are metric projections and the method becomes Douglas–Rachford feasibility splitting.
If both functions are closed proper convex, their proximal maps are single-valued and the interface reduces to the classical convex Douglas–Rachford iteration.
immediate_consequences_latex: A fixed state with compatible selections satisfies \(x=y\); this equality is the splitting residual condition.
Nonuniqueness of either proximal subproblem can produce multiple valid successor states from the same \(z^k\).
boundary_notes: The classical convex source inspected for the iteration does not support the asserted nonconvex scope, so it is not cited as evidence for this slot.
Existence of proximal selections may require prox-boundedness and a sufficiently small parameter; these conditions are not automatic from proper lower semicontinuity.
No particular Douglas–Rachford envelope is canonical across all nonconvex models.
review_flags: An authoritative nonconvex Douglas–Rachford source is required for the exact set-valued scope and the KL-compatible envelope clause.
Inspected local sources state the displayed iteration only for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-valued nonconvex Douglas–Rachford splitting interface

children.title: Nonconvex ADMM Interface
children.top_down_role: Alternating-direction families whose KL analysis depends on additional structural control.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex ADMM Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternately minimize the augmented Lagrangian in two blocks, update the multiplier, and stop when primal feasibility and dual-change residuals are small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), choose \((x^0,z^0,y^0)\) and \(\rho>0\). With
\[
L_\rho(x,z,y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2,
\]
perform
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_xL_\rho(x,z^k,y^k),\quad
z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_zL_\rho(x^{k+1},z,y^k),
\]
\[
y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c).
\]
Stop when the primal residual \(r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\) and dual residual \(s^{k+1}=\rho A^TB(z^{k+1}-z^k)\) meet prescribed tolerances. KL convergence requires additional structural descent and boundedness control.
assumptions_latex: The displayed nonconvex block subproblems admit selected minimizers.
The matrix dimensions are compatible with \(Ax+Bz=c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^{k+1},z^{k+1},y^{k+1})\) is the next ADMM state with residuals \(r^{k+1}\) and \(s^{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-block augmented-Lagrangian splitting with explicit primal and dual residuals.

notation.meaning: Dual residual under the stated convention.

review_flags: The iteration is standard, but nonconvex KL convergence needs theorem-specific rank, penalty, and regularity assumptions.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the ADMM interface, and the displayed iteration is a standard formal ADMM update. A source is required for the stated dual-residual convention and for distinguishing the bare interface from the additional rank, penalty, regularity, descent, and boundedness hypotheses needed by nonconvex KL convergence results.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb R^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous functions, let \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^q\), and consider \(\min\{f(x)+g(y):Ax+By=c\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic two-block ADMM allowing nonconvex block objectives or domains. This is an algorithmic interface, not a convergence theorem; convergence requires additional rank, regularity, parameter, and merit-function conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a penalty \(\rho>0\), define the augmented Lagrangian \[\mathcal L_\rho(x,y,\lambda)=f(x)+g(y)+\langle\lambda,Ax+By-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+By-c\|^2.\] A nonconvex ADMM trajectory is any sequence \((x^k,y^k,\lambda^k)_{k\ge0}\) satisfying, for every \(k\ge0\), \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\mathcal L_\rho(x,y^k,\lambda^k),\] \[y^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb R^p}\mathcal L_\rho(x^{k+1},y,\lambda^k),\] \[\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+By^{k+1}-c).\] The interface is proximal ADMM when positive-semidefinite quadratic terms \(\|x-x^k\|_P^2/2\) and \(\|y-y^k\|_Q^2/2\) are added to the respective block subproblems. It is KL-compatible only after specifying a lifted or regularized augmented-Lagrangian merit that satisfies sufficient decrease and relative-error estimates along this state sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvex ADMM applies alternating exact minimization to the two primal blocks of an augmented Lagrangian and then updates the multiplier by the current linear-constraint residual. Proper lower-semicontinuous block functions may be nonconvex, so either block argmin can be set-valued. A proximal variant adds positive-semidefinite quadratic regularizers centered at the previous block iterates. Calling the interface KL-compatible additionally requires a specified augmented merit with the descent and subgradient-control properties needed by KL analysis; the unmodified augmented Lagrangian need not have those properties automatically.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper and lower semicontinuous, and the two displayed block argmin sets are nonempty at every iteration.
The coupling constraint is linear and \(\rho>0\).
When the proximal variant is used, \(P\succeq0\) and \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three displayed updates define a possibly set-valued two-block nonconvex ADMM trajectory for the linearly coupled problem.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With the scaled multiplier \(u^k=\lambda^k/\rho\), the multiplier update is \(u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+By^{k+1}-c\).
The primal residual is \(r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+By^{k+1}-c=(\lambda^{k+1}-\lambda^k)/\rho\).
special_cases_latex: Setting \(B=-I\) and \(c=0\) yields the split formulation \(Ax=y\).
If \(f\) and \(g\) are closed proper convex, the same formulas give classical two-block convex ADMM.
immediate_consequences_latex: Primal feasibility at an iterate is equivalent to a zero multiplier increment.
Nonuniqueness of a nonconvex block minimizer makes the iteration map set-valued unless a selection rule is imposed.
boundary_notes: The definition does not cover Jacobi, asynchronous, stochastic, or more-than-two-block ADMM without further state and update rules.
The formulas alone do not guarantee bounded iterates, feasibility, stationarity, or convergence.

review_flags: The source supports a structured multiblock nonconvex BCD–ADMM realization; the record presents its canonical two-block specialization.

children.title: Alternating-Projection Interface
children.top_down_role: Projection families for tame sets and regular intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Projection Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project alternately onto two closed sets using arbitrary nearest-point selections; convergence needs additional tameness and regular-intersection hypotheses in the nonconvex case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed sets, choose \(y^0\in D\), and for \(k=0,1,\ldots\) select
\[
x^{k+1}\in P_C(y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}\in P_D(x^{k+1}),
\]
where \(P_S(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in S}\|u-v\|\). Stop when \(\|x^{k+1}-y^{k+1}\|\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\|y^{k+1}-y^k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\). For nonconvex sets the projections may be multivalued; KL convergence conclusions require an appropriate tame merit function and local regularity of the intersection geometry.
assumptions_latex: A selection is made whenever a metric projection is multivalued.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued alternating projections between closed nonconvex sets.

notation.meaning: Set-valued Euclidean metric projection onto S.

review_flags: No supplied locator states the tame-set and regular-intersection hypotheses needed for a precise KL convergence theorem.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the alternating-projection interface, and closed nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space have nonempty metric projections. No source is supplied for the stated stopping interface or for the tame-merit and regular-intersection qualifications attached to KL convergence.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-valued alternating projections between closed sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed sets. For a nonempty closed set \(C\), define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|\) and \(P_C(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C}\|x-c\|\), which is nonempty but may be multivalued.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility interface for closed, possibly nonconvex sets, including tame or definable sets. Regular intersection and KL assumptions are not part of the update definition and must be added to obtain local convergence results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An alternating-projection trajectory for the ordered pair \((A,B)\) is a sequence \((a^k,b^k)_{k\ge0}\) such that \(b^0\in B\) and, for every \(k\ge0\), \[a^{k+1}\in P_A(b^k),\qquad b^{k+1}\in P_B(a^{k+1}).\] Equivalently, the \(B\)-subsequence satisfies the set-valued fixed-point iteration \[b^{k+1}\in(P_B\circ P_A)(b^k).\] A selected trajectory includes a rule choosing one element whenever a projection set is not a singleton. A local regular-intersection interface at \(\bar x\in A\cap B\) augments the iteration with a neighborhood \(U\) and a quantified transversality or error-bound condition, such as \[d_{A\cap B}(x)\le\kappa\max\{d_A(x),d_B(x)\}\qquad(x\in U),\] for some \(\kappa>0\). Tameness means that the sets, their distance functions, or an associated projection merit belong to a specified definable category.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating projections starts from one closed set, selects a nearest point in the other set, and then selects a nearest point back in the first set, repeating this ordered pair of operations. For nonconvex closed sets, metric projections can be multivalued, so a trajectory includes projection selections. The two-step process is equivalently a set-valued fixed-point iteration of the composition of the two projection maps. A regular-intersection version additionally records a neighborhood and a quantitative local error bound relating distance to the intersection to the individual set distances. Tameness or definability is extra geometric structure, not part of the basic projection update.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
Every successor is selected from the displayed metric-projection set.
For the regular local interface, \(\bar x\in A\cap B\) and the stated error bound holds on a neighborhood \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed projection inclusions define a set-valued alternating-projection trajectory, optionally equipped with a local regular-intersection certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The paired update is \(b^{k+1}\in P_BP_A(b^k)\) with the intermediate point \(a^{k+1}\in P_A(b^k)\).
Projection membership is equivalent to \(a^{k+1}\in A\) and \(\|a^{k+1}-b^k\|=d_A(b^k)\), with the analogous condition for \(b^{k+1}\).
special_cases_latex: For nonempty closed convex sets, both projections are single-valued.
For smooth embedded manifolds, projections are locally single-valued within a sufficiently small tubular neighborhood.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each half-step realizes the corresponding set distance exactly.
A common point \(x\in A\cap B\) is a fixed point under the selections \(P_A(x)=P_B(x)=\{x\}\).
boundary_notes: The inspected alternating-projection source assumes convex sets and therefore does not support this slot's nonconvex tame-set scope.
The definition does not assert that a fixed point of \(P_BP_A\) lies in \(A\cap B\) when the sets are disjoint or nonconvex.
Tameness alone does not supply a particular regularity constant or initialization neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space or smooth Riemannian manifold, let \(F:M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(\operatorname{crit}F=\{x:0\in\partial F(x)\}\), and let \(F_\star=\inf_M F\) with solution set \(X_\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_M F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract certificate object for smooth or variationally nonsmooth finite-dimensional landscapes. A concrete certificate system must choose a criticality notion and provide valid regional predicates; this definition itself is application-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonconvex landscape certificate system for \(F\) is a tuple \[\mathfrak C=(\mathcal R,\{C_r\}_{r\in\mathcal R},\{\Gamma_r\}_{r\in\mathcal R},\Pi),\] where \(\mathcal R\) is a finite index set, \(C_r\subseteq M\) are certificate regions satisfying \(M=\bigcup_{r\in\mathcal R}C_r\), each \(\Gamma_r:C_r\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\) is a mathematically quantified predicate, and \(\Pi:\operatorname{crit}F\to\mathcal T\) assigns every critical point a type in a specified taxonomy \(\mathcal T\). Validity requires \(\Gamma_r(x)=\mathrm{true}\) for every \(r\) and every \(x\in C_r\), and requires each type assignment \(\Pi(x)\) to follow from explicit local conditions at \(x\), such as value optimality, positive or negative curvature, higher-order descent, manifold degeneracy, or variational regularity. The system is complete relative to \(\mathcal T\) when every critical point receives exactly one type, and globally benign when every type not contained in \(X_\star\) carries a quantified escape certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex landscape certificate system is a finite cover of the domain by regions, together with a valid quantified predicate on each region and a taxonomy assigning every critical point a mathematically defined type. A valid system requires every regional predicate to hold everywhere on its stated region and every type assignment to follow from explicit local conditions. Completeness means that each critical point receives exactly one type. Global benignity means that every nonoptimal type has a quantified escape certificate, such as negative curvature or a higher-order descent direction. The object is independent of a particular algorithm and does not by itself assert that an algorithm can discover or exploit the certificates.
assumptions_latex: A precise criticality mapping \(\partial F\) and a finite taxonomy \(\mathcal T\) are fixed.
The certificate regions \(C_r\) cover the stated domain.
Every predicate \(\Gamma_r\) and type condition is expressed by explicit quantified equalities, inequalities, or membership conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak C\) is a valid, complete, or globally benign landscape certificate system according to the corresponding coverage, classification, and escape conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Validity is the family of inclusions \(C_r\subseteq\{x:\Gamma_r(x)=\mathrm{true}\}\) for all \(r\in\mathcal R\).
Completeness can be encoded by a disjoint partition \(\operatorname{crit}F=\bigsqcup_{t\in\mathcal T}K_t\), where \(K_t=\Pi^{-1}(t)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(F\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), predicates may use \(\|\nabla F(x)\|\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2F(x))\).
For a nonsmooth proper lower-semicontinuous function, predicates may use \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\) and subdifferential regularity.
immediate_consequences_latex: A complete certificate system prevents unclassified critical points relative to its declared taxonomy.
Overlapping regions are allowed, but their simultaneously asserted predicates must be compatible on every overlap.
boundary_notes: A list of informal landscape descriptions is not a certificate system unless its predicates and quantifiers are specified.
Completeness is relative to the chosen taxonomy and does not imply global optimality of all critical points.
No inspected source supplies this exact application-independent tuple definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order critical-point stratification of a smooth objective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(f\in C^2(U)\). Define \(K=\{x\in U:\nabla f(x)=0\}\) and write \(H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained smooth optimization. The classification is based on local value behavior and Hessian inertia; degenerate points require an additional residual class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The second-order critical-point stratification of \(f\) is the disjoint family \[(K_{\min}^{\mathrm{nd}},K_{\max}^{\mathrm{nd}},K_{\mathrm{sad}}^{\mathrm{str}},K_{\mathrm{deg}}),\] where \[K_{\min}^{\mathrm{nd}}=\{x\in K:H(x)\succ0\},\qquad K_{\max}^{\mathrm{nd}}=\{x\in K:H(x)\prec0\},\] \[K_{\mathrm{sad}}^{\mathrm{str}}=\{x\in K:\lambda_{\min}(H(x))<0<\lambda_{\max}(H(x))\},\] and \[K_{\mathrm{deg}}=K\setminus\bigl(K_{\min}^{\mathrm{nd}}\cup K_{\max}^{\mathrm{nd}}\cup K_{\mathrm{sad}}^{\mathrm{str}}\bigr).\] A value-refined stratification further divides \(K_{\mathrm{deg}}\) into local minima, local maxima, saddles, and locally constant points using the quantified neighborhood definitions: a local minimum satisfies \(\exists r>0\;\forall y\in B_r(x), f(x)\le f(y)\), a local maximum reverses the inequality, and a saddle is a critical point for which every neighborhood contains both a point of smaller value and a point of larger value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function, the critical set can be partitioned first by Hessian inertia. Positive-definite critical points form the nondegenerate-minimum class; negative-definite points form the nondegenerate-maximum class; indefinite points form the strict-saddle class; and all remaining critical points are degenerate. The degenerate class may then be refined using neighborhood value comparisons into local minima, local maxima, saddles, and locally constant points. This refinement is needed because a singular positive-semidefinite or negative-semidefinite Hessian does not determine the local type by itself.
assumptions_latex: Eigenvalue inequalities refer to the symmetric Hessian \(H(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four displayed sets are pairwise disjoint and cover \(K\); the quantified value tests refine the otherwise unresolved degenerate class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in K_{\mathrm{sad}}^{\mathrm{str}}\) iff the Hessian has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue.
The saddle neighborhood condition is \(\forall r>0\;\exists y_-,y_+\in B_r(x)\) with \(f(y_-)<f(x)<f(y_+)\).
special_cases_latex: In one dimension, the strict-saddle inertia class is empty because a scalar Hessian cannot be indefinite.
A Morse function has no degenerate critical points, so its critical set is exhausted by the three nondegenerate classes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point in \(K_{\min}^{\mathrm{nd}}\) is an isolated strict local minimum, and every point in \(K_{\max}^{\mathrm{nd}}\) is an isolated strict local maximum.
A point with \(H(x)\succeq0\) and singular Hessian remains in \(K_{\mathrm{deg}}\) until a value or higher-order test classifies it.
boundary_notes: This is a taxonomy, not a Whitney stratification by smooth manifolds.
Constrained and nonsmooth problems require tangent-space Hessians or generalized derivatives and are outside this slot.
No inspected source states this complete four-class object under the title used by the node.

notation.meaning: Critical points unresolved by nonsingular Hessian inertia.

review_flags: Standard ingredients are well known, but a source supporting the exact combined stratification and terminology is missing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolated local extrema and their curvature classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(x^\star\in X\). When curvature classes are invoked, assume that \(x^\star\in\operatorname{int}X\) and \(f\in C^2\) on a neighborhood of \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local classification. Isolation, strictness, and nondegeneracy are distinct properties; the definition records them separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(x^\star\) is a local minimum if \[\exists r>0\; orall x\in X\cap B_r(x^\star),\quad f(x^\star)\le f(x),\] and a strict local minimum if the inequality is strict for all \(x
e x^\star\) in that set. It is an isolated local minimizer if there exists \(r>0\) such that \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X\cap B_r(x^\star)}f(x)=\{x^\star\}.\] Local maximum, strict local maximum, and isolated local maximizer are defined by reversing the inequalities. In the unconstrained \(C^2\) setting, a critical point is a nondegenerate local minimum when \(
abla f(x^\star)=0\) and \(
abla^2f(x^\star)\succ0\), and a nondegenerate local maximum when \(
abla f(x^\star)=0\) and \(
abla^2f(x^\star)\prec0\). An isolated extremum is curvature-degenerate when its Hessian is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimum has no smaller feasible value in some neighborhood, while a strict local minimum has strictly smaller value than every other feasible point in that neighborhood. It is isolated as a minimizer when it is the unique minimizer of the objective restricted to some neighborhood. Maxima use the reversed inequalities. For an interior twice continuously differentiable objective, positive-definite Hessian at a critical point defines a nondegenerate local minimum and negative-definite Hessian defines a nondegenerate local maximum. An isolated extremum whose Hessian is singular is curvature-degenerate. Strictness and isolation are not identified with nondegeneracy.
assumptions_latex: \(x^\star\in X\) and neighborhoods are taken in the Euclidean metric relative to \(X\).
For Hessian classifications, \(x^\star\in\operatorname{int}X\) and \(f\in C^2\) locally.
Nondegeneracy is evaluated only at a critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) receives the local, strict, isolated, and curvature classifications exactly when the corresponding quantified value and Hessian conditions hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Isolation as a local minimizer is equivalent to \(\exists r>0\) such that \(x^\star\) is the unique point attaining \(\min_{X\cap B_r(x^\star)}f\).
A strict local minimum is characterized by \(f(x)>f(x^\star)\) for every distinct feasible \(x\) sufficiently near \(x^\star\).
special_cases_latex: A nondegenerate local minimum or maximum is isolated and strict.
The function \(f(x)=x^4\) has an isolated strict local minimum at zero with singular Hessian, showing that isolation does not imply nondegeneracy.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every isolated local minimizer is a strict local minimizer under the displayed unique-neighborhood-argmin definition.
A positive-semidefinite singular Hessian does not by itself decide whether a critical point is a minimum, maximum, or saddle.
boundary_notes: Some literature uses 'isolated local minimum' to mean only that no other local minimizer lies nearby; this record uses the stronger unique neighborhood argmin convention.
For boundary-constrained extrema, ambient Hessian definiteness is not the appropriate curvature test.

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Local Minima
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is an isolated local minimum when every distinct sufficiently close feasible point has strictly larger objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(x^\star\in X\) with \(f(x^\star)<+\infty\). The point \(x^\star\) is an isolated local minimum of \(f\) on \(X\) if there exists \(r>0\) such that
\[
f(x)>f(x^\star)\qquad
\text{for every }x\in X\text{ with }0<\|x-x^\star\|<r.
\]
Equivalently, within the relative ball \(X\cap B_r(x^\star)\), the point \(x^\star\) is the unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r>0\ \forall x\in X:\ 0<\|x-x^\star\|<r\Rightarrow f(x)>f(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative isolated strict minimum on a finite-dimensional feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Curvature Classification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth critical point, definite Hessian curvature certifies an isolated extremum, indefinite curvature certifies a strict saddle, and singular semidefinite curvature is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x^\star\), with \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\), and write \(H=\nabla^2f(x^\star)\). The eigenvalue signs of \(H\) give verifiable certificates:
\[
H\succ0\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ is a strict isolated local minimum},
\]
\[
H\prec0\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ is a strict isolated local maximum},
\]
\[
\lambda_{\min}(H)<0<\lambda_{\max}(H)\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ is a strict saddle}.
\]
If \(H\) is merely positive or negative semidefinite and singular, second-order curvature alone does not classify \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inertia of \(\nabla^2f(x^\star)\) yields the displayed minimum, maximum, saddle, or inconclusive classification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained second-order classification at a smooth critical point.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Saddles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict saddle is a smooth critical point whose Hessian has a negative eigenvalue, providing a directly detectable direction of negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable at \(x^\star\). The point \(x^\star\) is a strict saddle if
\[
\nabla f(x^\star)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x^\star))<0.
\]
Equivalently, there exist a unit vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) and a constant \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
v^T\nabla^2f(x^\star)v\leq-\mu.
\]
The vector \(v\) is a negative-curvature direction detectable by a second-order test; this definition does not require the Hessian to be nonsingular in all other directions.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice differentiable at \(x^\star\).
\(\nabla^2f(x^\star)\) is interpreted as a symmetric Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x^\star))<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained smooth strict saddle defined by detectable negative curvature.
review_flags: The supplied saddle-point locator does not explicitly identify the modern strict-saddle negative-curvature definition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf and the negative-eigenvalue condition is a common modern strict-saddle convention. Because strict-saddle terminology is not completely uniform and no citation is supplied, an authoritative locator explicitly supporting this convention is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate saddles classified by first nonzero directional order
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f\in C^p(U)\) for an integer \(p\ge3\), and let \(x^\star\in U\) satisfy \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x^\star)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth critical points not detected as saddles by negative Hessian curvature. The classification is directional and finite-order; flat points with no finite nonzero directional jet remain unclassified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a unit direction \(d\in\mathbb S^{n-1}\), define its first nonzero directional order at \(x^\star\) by \[q(d)=\min\{j\in\{3,\ldots,p\}:D^jf(x^\star)[d^j]\ne0\},\] with \(q(d)=\infty\) if the set is empty. The critical point \(x^\star\) is an order-\(q\) one-sided degenerate saddle if some unit \(d\) has \(q(d)=q\) odd. It is an order-\(q\) signed even saddle if \(q\) is even and there are unit directions \(d_+,d_-\) such that all lower directional terms through order \(q-1\) vanish along both directions and \[D^qf(x^\star)[d_+^q]>0>D^qf(x^\star)[d_-^q].\] It is a finite-order beyond-second-order saddle if it belongs to either class for some \(q\ge3\). A degenerate critical point not certified at any available finite order is placed in the flat or unresolved class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a critical point with no negative Hessian direction, higher directional derivatives can still reveal saddle behavior. For each direction, consider the first nonzero derivative order beyond two. An odd first nonzero order gives opposite value changes on the two orientations of that direction and defines a one-sided degenerate saddle. At an even order, saddle behavior requires two directions with first nonzero terms of opposite sign. A point detected in either way is a finite-order beyond-second-order saddle. If all tested directional jets vanish or have no sign pattern of this kind, the point remains flat or unresolved rather than being declared a minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(x^\star\) is critical and \(\nabla^2f(x^\star)\succeq0\), so ordinary negative-curvature classification does not apply.
Directional tensors \(D^jf(x^\star)[d^j]\) are evaluated on unit directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated parity and sign conditions classify \(x^\star\) as a finite-order beyond-second-order saddle; otherwise it remains unresolved at order \(p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For odd \(q(d)\), the leading directional term changes sign when \(d\) is replaced by \(-d\).
The signed even class requires the homogeneous degree-\(q\) directional form to take both positive and negative values on directions for which all lower terms vanish.
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=x^3\), zero is an order-three one-sided degenerate saddle.
For \(f(x,y)=x^4-y^4\), zero is an order-four signed even saddle.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite-order class in this definition has points of both larger and smaller objective value arbitrarily near \(x^\star\).
A positive-semidefinite Hessian does not exclude higher-order saddle behavior.
boundary_notes: The definition does not classify infinitely flat smooth functions or nonsmooth saddles.
Mixed curves not represented by fixed rays can reveal behavior missed by purely directional jets.
No inspected source supports this exact parity-based taxonomy.

notation.meaning: jth derivative tensor evaluated j times on d.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate saddles classified by first nonzero directional order
Degenerate Saddles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate saddle is a critical saddle with a singular Hessian: nearby objective values occur on both sides, but quadratic curvature is insufficient for nondegenerate classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable near \(x^\star\). The point \(x^\star\) is a degenerate saddle if
\[
\nabla f(x^\star)=0,
\qquad
\det\nabla^2f(x^\star)=0,
\]
and every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^\star\) contains points \(x_+,x_-\in U\) satisfying
\[
f(x_+)>f(x^\star)>f(x_-).
\]
Thus \(x^\star\) is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum, while its singular Hessian prevents a nondegenerate Morse classification. Degeneracy alone does not imply the saddle inequalities, so both requirements are essential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is a saddle and \(\det\nabla^2f(x^\star)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Saddles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order saddle has no Hessian-detectable descent in its null directions, but the first nonzero higher-order Taylor form changes sign there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^m\) near a critical point \(x^\star\), where \(m\geq3\), and suppose \(H=\nabla^2f(x^\star)\succeq0\) has nontrivial nullspace \(N\). The point is a higher-order saddle of order \(m\) when the restrictions to \(N\) of the homogeneous Taylor forms of orders \(3,\ldots,m-1\) vanish, while
\[
P_m(v)=\frac{1}{m!}D^mf(x^\star)[v,\ldots,v]
\]
takes both positive and negative values on the unit sphere of \(N\). The sign-changing first nonzero form supplies ascent and descent directions invisible to the Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_m\) assumes both signs on \(\{v\in N:\|v\|=1\}\), so \(x^\star\) has higher-order ascent and descent directions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate saddles classified by the first nonzero Taylor form on the Hessian nullspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Classification Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero gradient and singular Hessian cannot distinguish a minimum, maximum, and higher-order saddle; functions with identical second-order data can have all three behaviors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(m\ge 2\), define \(f_+(t)=t^{2m}\), \(f_-(t)=-t^{2m}\), and \(f_0(t)=t^{2m+1}\) on \(\mathbb R\). At \(t=0\), all three functions satisfy \(f'(0)=f''(0)=0\), so their second-order data coincide. Nevertheless, \(0\) is a strict local minimum of \(f_+\), a strict local maximum of \(f_-\), and neither a local minimum nor a local maximum of \(f_0\). Thus a singular Hessian, even together with stationarity, does not determine the local critical-point type.
assumptions_latex: The classification is unconstrained and local on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(0)=0\) and \(\nabla^2 f(0)=0\) do not determine the local critical-point class.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f\in C^2(U)\), and let \(K=\{x\in U:\nabla f(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth nonisolated critical sets admitting a finite Whitney stratification. This definition separates the geometry of the critical set from normal curvature of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Whitney-stratified critical-set geometry for \(f\) is a finite disjoint decomposition \[K=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha\] into connected embedded \(C^2\) submanifolds satisfying the frontier condition \[S_\alpha\cap\overline{S_\beta}\ne\varnothing\implies S_\alpha\subseteq\overline{S_\beta}\quad\text{and}\quad\dim S_\alpha<\dim S_\beta,\] and Whitney condition (a): whenever \(x_j\in S_\beta\) converges to \(x\in S_\alpha\) and \(T_{x_j}S_\beta\) converges to a subspace \(T\), one has \(T_xS_\alpha\subseteq T\). The geometry is Morse–Bott on a stratum \(S_\alpha\) when \[\ker\nabla^2f(x)=T_xS_\alpha\qquad\text{for every }x\in S_\alpha.\] It is normally minimizing, maximizing, or saddle-type according as the Hessian restricted to the normal space \(N_xS_\alpha\) is positive definite, negative definite, or indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified critical set is a finite disjoint union of connected smooth manifold strata satisfying the frontier condition and Whitney condition (a). The frontier condition controls which lower-dimensional strata may occur in closures of higher-dimensional ones. Whitney condition (a) requires limiting tangent spaces of an incident higher-dimensional stratum to contain the tangent space of the lower-dimensional stratum. A stratum is Morse–Bott when the Hessian kernel equals its tangent space at every point. Normal Hessian definiteness then classifies the stratum as normally minimizing, maximizing, or saddle-type while allowing the critical points to be nonisolated along tangent directions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_\alpha\) is a connected embedded \(C^2\) submanifold and the decomposition is finite.
The frontier and Whitney-(a) quantified conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition defines a Whitney-stratified critical set, with optional Morse–Bott and normal-curvature classifications on its strata.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Morse–Bott condition is equivalent to Hessian nondegeneracy on any complementary normal space together with Hessian vanishing along the stratum tangent space.
Normal saddle type means that the quadratic form \(v\mapsto\langle v,\nabla^2f(x)v\rangle\) takes both signs on \(N_xS_\alpha\).
special_cases_latex: An isolated nondegenerate critical point is a zero-dimensional Morse–Bott stratum.
A smooth manifold of minimizers with positive-definite normal Hessian is a normally minimizing Morse–Bott critical stratum.
immediate_consequences_latex: Critical points may vary continuously within a stratum without being isolated.
At a Morse–Bott point, all Hessian degeneracy is tangent to the critical stratum.
boundary_notes: Whitney condition (b), when required, is stronger and is not included here.
A set-theoretic partition into critical types need not be a Whitney stratification.
No inspected source supplies the exact combined critical-set, Whitney, and Morse–Bott definition.

notation.meaning: Tangent space of a stratum at x.
Orthogonal normal space to the stratum.

review_flags: Authoritative sources for Whitney stratifications and Morse–Bott critical manifolds must be attached before review.
The chosen definition uses Whitney condition (a), not the stronger condition (b).
knowledge_statements.title: Whitney-stratified critical-set geometry
Critical Manifolds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical manifold is an embedded manifold of stationary points; it is Morse–Bott when the Hessian degenerates exactly along tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let \(f\in C^2(X)\). An embedded submanifold \(M\subset X\) is a critical manifold of \(f\) if \(df(x)=0\) for every \(x\in M\). It is a Morse–Bott critical manifold if, additionally, \(M\) is locally equal to the critical set near each of its points and \(\ker \operatorname{Hess}f(x)=T_xM\) for every \(x\in M\). Equivalently, the Hessian is nondegenerate on the normal quotient \(T_xX/T_xM\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\subset\operatorname{Crit}(f)\), with \(\ker\operatorname{Hess}f(x)=T_xM\) in the Morse–Bott case.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded components of a smooth function's critical set, with the Morse–Bott refinement distinguished.

notation.meaning: The set of points where the differential of f vanishes.
Tangent space of M at x.
Riemannian Hessian of f at x.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between a general critical manifold and a Morse–Bott critical manifold is mathematically plausible and fits the definition container, but no inspectable citation supports the precise local-critical-set and Hessian-kernel formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Critical Strata
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular critical set is decomposed into smooth stationary strata whose closures meet only along lower-dimensional strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a smooth manifold \(X\), and set \(C=\operatorname{Crit}(f)\). A singular critical stratification is a locally finite disjoint decomposition \(C=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha\) into connected embedded smooth submanifolds such that whenever \(S_\beta\cap\overline{S_\alpha}\ne\varnothing\), one has \(S_\beta\subseteq\overline{S_\alpha}\) and \(\dim S_\beta<\dim S_\alpha\). A stratum incident to a higher-dimensional stratum through this frontier relation is called a singular critical stratum; the full critical set need not itself be a manifold there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha\) satisfies the stated local-finiteness and frontier conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth pieces used to resolve a nonsmooth or dimension-varying critical set.

notation.meaning: Closure of a stratum in X.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The proposed frontier conditions describe a standard type of stratification, but the definition of a singular critical stratum is convention-dependent and currently unsupported. An authoritative stratification source is required before fixing the terminology and hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratum-Transition Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a transition to a lower stratum, every limiting tangent space of the higher stratum must contain the lower stratum's tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) and \(R\) be smooth strata of a critical set with \(R\subset\overline S\setminus S\), and let \(x_k\in S\) converge to \(x\in R\). Whitney condition \((a)\) at \(x\) requires that, whenever \(T_{x_k}S\) converges in the Grassmannian to a subspace \(\tau\), one has \(T_xR\subseteq\tau\). Consequently, tangent directions intrinsic to the lower-dimensional stratum persist in every limiting tangent space of the incident higher-dimensional stratum, excluding arbitrary tangent-space jumps at the transition.
assumptions_latex: The tangent spaces \(T_{x_k}S\) converge to \(\tau\) in the appropriate Grassmannian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_xR\subseteq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whitney compatibility governing limiting tangent spaces across incident critical strata.

notation.meaning: A limiting tangent space of S at x.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a precise formulation of Whitney condition (a), and the condition kind fits the transition-geometry container, but no citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Benign-Landscape Principles
children.top_down_role: Global properties that connect local criticality to global optimization status.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Benign critical landscape relative to a solution set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space or smooth manifold, let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(f_\star=\inf_M f\), and assume \(X_\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_M f\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-independent smooth landscape property. Benignity is defined relative to an explicitly chosen nonoptimal escape predicate; it does not itself guarantee that a particular algorithm reaches a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an escape predicate \(E:M\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\). The landscape of \(f\) is benign relative to \(E\) when every point \(x\in M\) satisfies at least one of \[x\in X_\star,\qquad \|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|>0,\qquad E(x)=\mathrm{true},\] and every critical point satisfies the sharper dichotomy \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\implies x\in X_\star\ \text{or}\ E(x)=\mathrm{true}.\] It is quantitatively \((\epsilon,\gamma,\delta)\)-benign when \(M\) is covered by \[\{x:\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\ge\epsilon\}\cup\{x:\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\le-\gamma\}\cup\{x:d(x,X_\star)\le\delta\},\] and all local minimizers belong to \(X_\star\). More general versions replace negative curvature by a specified higher-order, nonsmooth, or symmetry-reduced escape certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A landscape is benign relative to an escape predicate if every critical point is either globally optimal or has the declared escape certificate. Away from criticality, a nonzero gradient already supplies first-order movement. A quantitative smooth version covers the entire domain by a large-gradient region, a negative-curvature region, and a neighborhood of the global solution set, while also requiring every local minimum to be global. The definition is relative to the chosen certificate: negative curvature is one option, while higher-order or nonsmooth certificates yield different benignity classes.
assumptions_latex: \(X_\star\ne\varnothing\) and the chosen criticality, gradient, Hessian, and distance notions are defined on \(M\).
The escape predicate \(E\) is expressed by a mathematically checkable quantified condition.
For quantitative smooth benignity, \(f\in C^2(M)\) and \(\epsilon,\gamma,\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The landscape is benign relative to \(E\), or quantitatively \((\epsilon,\gamma,\delta)\)-benign, exactly when the corresponding critical-point dichotomy and global cover hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Relative benignity is \(\operatorname{crit}f\subseteq X_\star\cup\{x:E(x)\}\).
The quantitative cover states that no point simultaneously has gradient norm below \(\epsilon\), Hessian minimum eigenvalue above \(-\gamma\), and distance greater than \(\delta\) from \(X_\star\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(E\equiv\mathrm{false}\) yields the property that every critical point is globally minimizing.
Taking \(E(x)\) to mean \(\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))<0\) yields a strict-saddle benign landscape.
immediate_consequences_latex: The no-spurious-local-minima property is necessary for the quantitative smooth definition used here.
Benignity is invariant under adding a constant to the objective when the same escape predicate is retained.
boundary_notes: A benign landscape does not imply convexity, uniqueness, or algorithmic global convergence.
Symmetry may make \(X_\star\) a manifold rather than a singleton.
No inspected source defines this exact umbrella property.
review_flags: The umbrella term 'benign landscape' has multiple conventions; a source matching this exact relative and quantitative definition is needed.

children.title: No-Spurious-Local-Minima Principle
children.top_down_role: Landscape families in which local minima have the intended global status.

knowledge_statements.title: No-Spurious-Local-Minima Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A landscape has no spurious local minima when every feasible local minimum is globally optimal, without implying uniqueness or algorithmic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\). The landscape has no spurious local minima if every \(x\in F\) for which there exists \(r>0\) satisfying \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for all \(y\in F\cap B_r(x)\) also satisfies \(f(x)=\inf_{y\in F}f(y)\). Equivalently, the set of constrained local minimizers is contained in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in F}f(y)\). The principle concerns objective status only and does not by itself ensure uniqueness, convergence, or absence of nonminimizing stationary points.
assumptions_latex: \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is bounded below if a finite optimal value is intended.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{LocMin}_F(f)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in F}f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality of every locally minimizing point in a specified feasible landscape.

notation.meaning: Open Euclidean ball of radius r centered at x.
Set of local minimizers relative to F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No spurious local minima relative to a target solution set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, assume \(f_\star=\inf_Xf\) is attained, and write \(X_\star=\{x\in X:f(x)=f_\star\}\). Optionally let \(T\subseteq X_\star\) be an intended target set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General metric-space landscape property. It distinguishes global-value correctness from application-specific identifiability relative to a target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a local minimizer when \[\exists r>0\;\forall y\in B_r(x),\qquad f(x)\le f(y).\] It is spurious when it is a local minimizer but \(f(x)>f_\star\). The function \(f\) has no spurious local minima on \(X\) when \[\forall x\in X,\quad\bigl[\exists r>0\;\forall y\in B_r(x),\ f(x)\le f(y)\bigr]\implies f(x)=f_\star.\] Equivalently, every local minimizer belongs to \(X_\star\). Relative to an intended target set \(T\subseteq X_\star\), the landscape has no target-spurious local minima when every local minimizer lies in \(T\); this stronger property separates optimization optimality from identifiability among globally equivalent solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer is spurious if its value is strictly larger than the attained global minimum. The no-spurious-local-minima principle says that every point minimizing the objective in some neighborhood must attain the global optimum value, equivalently that the local-minimizer set is contained in the global-minimizer set. If an application specifies a smaller intended target set within the global solution set, the stronger target-relative version requires every local minimizer to belong to that target set. Thus a point may be globally optimal and nonspurious in the value sense yet fail a target-identifiability requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f\) is proper.
For the target-relative form, \(T\subseteq X_\star\) is specified in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The landscape has no spurious local minima exactly when \(\operatorname{locmin}f\subseteq X_\star\), and has no target-spurious minima exactly when \(\operatorname{locmin}f\subseteq T\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\{x:x\text{ is a local minimizer and }f(x)>f_\star\}=\varnothing\).
Every local minimum value equals \(f_\star\).
special_cases_latex: Every convex function on a convex domain has no spurious local minima.
A nonconvex function may satisfy the property even when it has saddle points, local maxima, or multiple disconnected global-minimizer components.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every strict local minimizer is globally minimizing under the principle.
The principle does not imply that all stationary points are globally minimizing.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns local minima, not all first- or second-order stationary points.
If the infimum is not attained, the formulation through \(X_\star\) must be replaced by a value-only condition.
Target-relative nonspuriousness depends on how symmetries and equivalent representations are encoded.

children.title: Strict-Saddle Landscape Principle
children.top_down_role: Global organization by large-gradient, negative-curvature, and minima-neighborhood regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Saddle Landscape Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point has a large gradient, a direction of uniformly negative curvature, or lies near the local-minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(X_\star\) be its set of local minimizers, and fix \(\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta>0\). A quantitative strict-saddle landscape satisfies, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), at least one of \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge\varepsilon\), \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\le-\gamma\), or \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X_\star)\le\delta\). Hence every point lies in a large-gradient region, a uniformly negative-curvature region, or a prescribed neighborhood of the local-minimizer set. Additional local regularity is required to infer attraction inside the third region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n=G_\varepsilon\cup N_\gamma\cup B_\delta(X_\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative three-region decomposition of a twice-differentiable nonconvex landscape.

notation.meaning: Set where the gradient norm is at least epsilon.
Set where the least Hessian eigenvalue is at most minus gamma.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The three-region coverage statement matches the node's stated role, but quantitative strict-saddle definitions vary, particularly in the regularity required within minima neighborhoods. A source is needed to establish this exact variant and terminology.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), assume \(X_\star=\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), and let \(d(x,X_\star)=\inf_{z\in X_\star}\|x-z\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional smooth landscape property. The definition uses three quantitative regions: large gradient, negative curvature, and a neighborhood of global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constants \(\alpha>0\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(\delta>0\), the function \(f\) has an \((\alpha,\gamma,\delta)\)-strict-saddle landscape when, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), at least one of the following holds: \[(i)\ \|
abla f(x)\|\ge\alpha;\qquad (ii)\ \lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\le-\gamma;\qquad (iii)\ d(x,X_\star)\le\delta.\] In addition, every local minimizer belongs to \(X_\star\), and the minima-neighborhood region is locally attracting in the geometric sense that there exists \(\mu>0\) with \[\langle
abla f(x),x-P_{X_\star}(x)angle\ge\mu d(x,X_\star)^2\] whenever \(d(x,X_\star)\le\delta\) and a nearest-point selection \(P_{X_\star}(x)\) is defined. The qualitative strict-saddle principle is the critical-point condition \[
abla f(x)=0\implies x\in X_\star\ 	ext{or}\ \lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))<0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantitative strict-saddle landscape divides every point into at least one of three regions: the gradient is uniformly large, the Hessian has uniformly negative curvature, or the point lies near the global minimizer set. Every local minimum must be global, and the stated inner-product condition makes the solution neighborhood locally attracting toward a nearest global minimizer. The qualitative version requires only that every critical point be either globally minimizing or possess a strictly negative Hessian eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: For the attraction clause, a nearest-point selection onto \(X_\star\) exists throughout the stated neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three regions cover \(\mathbb R^n\), all local minima are global, and critical points outside \(X_\star\) have negative curvature.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The cover is equivalent to excluding any point satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x)\|<\alpha\), \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))>-\gamma\), and \(d(x,X_\star)>\delta\) simultaneously.
The qualitative form is \(\operatorname{crit}f\subseteq X_\star\cup\{x:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))<0\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(X_\star=\{x^\star\}\) and \(f\) is strongly convex on \(B_\delta(x^\star)\), the attraction inequality holds locally.
For a symmetry orbit of minimizers, the attraction condition is naturally normal to the orbit rather than strongly convex in all directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonoptimal critical point cannot have a positive-semidefinite Hessian under the qualitative principle.
The quantitative property includes the no-spurious-local-minima principle.
boundary_notes: The attraction clause is stronger than some definitions of robust strict saddle and should be sourced explicitly.
Higher-order degenerate saddles are excluded from the qualitative strict-saddle class.
No inspected source states this exact global three-region definition.

children.title: Gradient-Dominance Landscapes
children.top_down_role: Landscape classes with global or regional value-gap control through first-order geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Dominance Landscapes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient dominance bounds objective suboptimality by squared gradient norm, forcing every stationary point in the region to have optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f\) be differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\), and suppose \(f_\star=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)>-\infty\). The function is gradient dominated on \(D\) with constant \(\mu>0\) if \(\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f_\star\bigr)\) for every \(x\in D\). In particular, every stationary point in \(D\) attains value \(f_\star\). This condition does not require convexity and may be imposed globally or only on a designated region.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) with \(x\in D\) implies \(f(x)=f_\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak–Łojasiewicz value-gap control by the squared gradient norm.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and its stationary-point consequence are mathematically precise, but the cited generic gradient-method section does not establish inspectable support for this exact inequality. A specific PL or gradient-dominance locator is required.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f\) be differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(\mathcal F\), assume \(f_\star=\min_{x\in\mathcal F}f(x)\), and let \(p\in[1,2]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable, possibly nonconvex objectives. The degree-p definition includes the degree-two Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition as a normalization-equivalent special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is gradient dominated of degree \(p\) on \(\mathcal F\) with constant \(\tau>0\) when \[f(x)-f_\star\le\tau\|\nabla f(x)\|^p\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal F.\] It is globally gradient dominated when \(\mathcal F=\mathbb R^n\), and regionally gradient dominated when the inequality is asserted only on a declared subset \(\mathcal F\). For \(p=2\), the Polyak–Łojasiewicz normalization with constant \(\mu>0\) is \[\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f_\star)\qquad(x\in\mathcal F),\] which is the same condition with \(\tau=1/(2\mu)\). No convexity or uniqueness of the global minimizer is included in the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is gradient dominated of degree p on a region when its objective gap above the attained global minimum is bounded by a fixed constant times the pth power of the gradient norm at every point in that region. The property is global if the region is all of Euclidean space and regional otherwise. At degree two it is the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition after a reciprocal change of constant. Gradient dominance does not require convexity or a unique minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal F\).
The global minimum value \(f_\star\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_\star\le\tau\|\nabla f(x)\|^p\) holds throughout the declared global or regional domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(p=2\), \(\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge2\mu(f(x)-f_\star)\) with \(\mu=1/(2\tau)\).
The inequality can be written \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge\tau^{-1/p}(f(x)-f_\star)^{1/p}\).
special_cases_latex: A \(\mu\)-strongly convex differentiable function is degree-two gradient dominated with \(\tau=1/(2\mu)\).
A singular positive-semidefinite quadratic can satisfy degree-two gradient dominance despite having a non-singleton minimizer set and lacking strong convexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every stationary point in \(\mathcal F\) is globally minimizing whenever the dominance inequality holds there.
Regional dominance controls objective values only for points inside the declared region.
boundary_notes: Gradient dominance does not imply convexity, Hessian positivity, uniqueness, or an error bound in distance without additional assumptions.
The gradient must be replaced by an appropriate slope or subgradient for nonsmooth objectives.

children.title: Local Attraction Geometry
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood geometry supporting stable local refinement.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local attraction geometry around a minimizer set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^1(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(X_\star\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}f\) be nonempty and closed, and suppose the metric projection \(P_{X_\star}\) is single-valued on the tube \(U_\delta=\{x:d(x,X_\star)<\delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local geometry around a possibly nonisolated minimizer set. The definition concerns continuous-time gradient orientation and local error control, not the global landscape.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((f,X_\star)\) has \((\mu,c,\delta)\)-local attraction geometry when \(\mu,c,\delta>0\) and, for every \(x\in U_\delta\), \[\langle\nabla f(x),x-P_{X_\star}(x)\rangle\ge\mu d(x,X_\star)^2\] and \[f(x)-f_\star\ge c\,d(x,X_\star)^2.\] It has two-sided quadratic growth when there is also \(C<\infty\) such that \[f(x)-f_\star\le C\,d(x,X_\star)^2\qquad(x\in U_\delta).\] For an isolated minimizer \(X_\star=\{x^\star\}\), the attraction inequality becomes \(\langle\nabla f(x),x-x^\star\rangle\ge\mu\|x-x^\star\|^2\). For a smooth minimizer manifold, the inequalities measure only normal displacement through the nearest-point projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local attraction geometry around a closed minimizer set requires a tubular neighborhood with a unique nearest-point projection. Inside that neighborhood, the gradient must have a uniformly positive component along the displacement away from the nearest minimizer, and the objective gap must grow at least quadratically with distance to the minimizer set. An optional upper quadratic bound gives two-sided quadratic growth. For an isolated minimizer this reduces to a radial gradient inequality. For a smooth manifold of minimizers, it measures normal rather than tangential displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1(\mathbb R^n)\), \(X_\star\ne\varnothing\) is closed, and \(f=f_\star\) on \(X_\star\).
\(\mu,c,\delta>0\), and \(C>0\) when two-sided growth is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The gradient orientation and quadratic-growth inequalities hold uniformly throughout the declared attraction neighborhood.

Local Growth Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the solution set, objective suboptimality grows at least quadratically with distance from that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(X_\star\subseteq F\) be a nonempty local solution set on which \(f\) has the constant value \(f_\star\), and let \(U\) be a neighborhood of \(X_\star\). Local quadratic growth holds on \(U\) with modulus \(\alpha>0\) if \(f(x)-f_\star\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X_\star)^2\) for every \(x\in F\cap U\). It quantitatively isolates the solution set in objective value while allowing multiple or nonisolated minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_\star\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X_\star)^2\) for all \(x\in F\cap U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Attraction-Basin Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attraction basin contains exactly the initial points whose iterates approach the designated invariant solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(T:X\to X\) be an iteration map, and let \(A\subseteq X\) be nonempty and invariant, meaning \(T(A)\subseteq A\). The attraction basin of \(A\) is \(\mathcal B_T(A)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(T^k(x),A)\to0\text{ as }k\to\infty\}\). If convergence to individual points is intended, the stronger pointwise basin is \(\{x\in X:T^k(x)\to a\text{ for some }a\in A\}\). The basin is algorithm-dependent even when \(A\) is determined by the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal B_T(A)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{dist}(T^k(x),A)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initial points whose iterates converge to a designated invariant solution set.

notation.meaning: Attraction basin of A under T.

knowledge_statements.title: Basin-Boundary Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For invertible dynamics with invariant open basins, basin boundaries are invariant separatrices whose every neighborhood meets competing basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space, let \(T:X\to X\) be a homeomorphism, and let \(A_1,A_2\subseteq X\) be disjoint invariant attractors with disjoint open basins \(B_1\) and \(B_2\). If each basin is fully invariant, \(T(B_i)=B_i\), then its boundary is fully invariant: \(T(\partial B_i)=\partial B_i\). Hence a common boundary \(\Sigma=\partial B_1\cap\partial B_2\), when nonempty, satisfies \(T(\Sigma)=\Sigma\) and acts as a separatrix: every neighborhood of each \(x\in\Sigma\) meets both basins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\partial B_i)=\partial B_i\) and \(T(\Sigma)=\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant separatrices between attraction basins under invertible dynamics.

notation.meaning: Attraction basin of the invariant attractor A_i.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f\in C^2(D)\), let \(X_\star\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_D f\) be nonempty, and fix positive thresholds \(\alpha,\gamma,\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth landscape decomposition. Regions may overlap; the certificate consists of their coverage and the quantified mechanism valid on each region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the large-gradient, negative-curvature, and solution-neighborhood regions by \[R_G=\{x\in D:\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge\alpha\},\] \[R_C=\{x\in D:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\le-\gamma\},\] \[R_S=\{x\in D:d(x,X_\star)\le\delta\}.\] A three-region landscape certificate is the assertion \[D=R_G\cup R_C\cup R_S\] together with a declared local refinement predicate \(A_S(x)\) satisfying \(A_S(x)=\mathrm{true}\) for all \(x\in R_S\). A general regional landscape certificate is a finite family \(\{(R_i,C_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) such that \[D=\bigcup_{i=1}^N R_i\qquad\text{and}\qquad \forall i\;\forall x\in R_i,\ C_i(x)=\mathrm{true},\] where each \(C_i\) is a quantified optimization mechanism, such as gradient lower bounds, curvature bounds, error bounds, local attraction, or value-gap control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regional landscape certificate partitions or covers the domain by finitely many regions and attaches a quantified optimization mechanism to each one. The standard smooth three-region form uses a large-gradient region, a uniformly negative-curvature region, and a neighborhood of the global minimizer set. The certificate is valid when these regions cover the domain and the declared local refinement predicate holds throughout the solution neighborhood. Regions may overlap; points in an overlap must satisfy every predicate asserted there. The general form allows other mechanisms such as error bounds or value-gap control.
assumptions_latex: Every regional predicate \(C_i\) is stated with explicit constants and quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regional family is a valid certificate exactly when it covers \(D\) and every attached predicate holds on its entire declared region.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The three-region cover excludes the residual set \(\{x:\|\nabla f(x)\|<\alpha,\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))>-\gamma,\ d(x,X_\star)>\delta\}\).
A disjoint regional certificate can be obtained from an overlapping finite cover by assigning overlap points according to a fixed priority rule, while retaining valid predicates.
special_cases_latex: A gradient-dominated region may use \(f(x)-f_\star\le\tau\|\nabla f(x)\|^p\) as its predicate.
A minimizer tube may use quadratic growth and inward gradient orientation as its predicate.
immediate_consequences_latex: A valid cover leaves no point without at least one declared optimization mechanism.
Uniform constants make the regional statement quantitative rather than merely taxonomic.
boundary_notes: A plotted or heuristic partition is not a certificate without universally quantified predicates.
Coverage alone does not show that a particular algorithm transitions favorably between regions.
