knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large-gradient region at a fixed threshold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty analysis domain, let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\supseteq\Omega\), and equip \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, deterministic, unconstrained first-order geometry on the prescribed domain \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a threshold \(\eta>0\), the \(\eta\)-large-gradient region of \(f\) in \(\Omega\) is
\[
\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega):=\{x\in\Omega:\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\geq\eta\}.
\]
Its strict version is \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}^{>}(f;\Omega):=\{x\in\Omega:\|\nabla f(x)\|_2>\eta\}\). Membership certifies quantitative first-order noncriticality: every \(x\in\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)\) has first-order stationarity residual at least \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a continuously differentiable objective on a neighborhood of an analysis domain, the large-gradient region at threshold \(\eta>0\) consists exactly of points in the domain whose Euclidean gradient norm is at least \(\eta\). A strict-threshold version replaces the weak inequality by a strict inequality. Thus membership records a quantitative failure of first-order stationarity, rather than merely asserting that the gradient is nonzero.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and \(f\in C^1(U)\) for an open neighborhood \(U\supseteq\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\geq\eta\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With the first-order residual \(r_1(x):=\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\), one has \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:r_1(x)\geq\eta\}\).
Its complement relative to \(\Omega\) is \(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:\|\nabla f(x)\|_2<\eta\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=1\), \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:|f'(x)|\geq\eta\}\).
If \(\eta_2\geq\eta_1>0\), then \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta_2}(f;\Omega)\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{\eta_1}(f;\Omega)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No first-order stationary point \(x\) with \(\nabla f(x)=0\) belongs to \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)\) when \(\eta>0\).
If \(\nabla f\) is continuous and \(\Omega\) is closed, then \(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(f;\Omega)\) is closed.
boundary_notes: For constrained optimization, the appropriate residual is generally a projected gradient, gradient mapping, or stationarity measure rather than \(\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\).
This definition does not by itself assert a descent rate, an algorithmic step, or global coverage of \(\Omega\).

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Regions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit vector with Hessian curvature at most minus gamma certifies negative curvature and rules out local minimality at stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(D)\) on an open set \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). The negative-curvature region is \(N_\gamma=\{x\in D:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\le-\gamma\}\). Membership is certified by a unit vector \(v\) satisfying \(v^\top\nabla^2f(x)v\le-\gamma\). At a stationary point \(x\in N_\gamma\), the second-order necessary condition for a local minimum fails, so \(x\) cannot be a local minimizer. Away from stationarity, the certificate records curvature rather than guaranteeing that both signs of a finite step decrease the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and \(x\in N_\gamma\) imply that \(x\) is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order certificate providing a direction of strict descending curvature.

notation.meaning: Region where the least Hessian eigenvalue is at most minus gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-curvature region at a fixed margin
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood \(U\supseteq\Omega\), and let \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\) denote the smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, deterministic second-order geometry measured by the Euclidean Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a curvature margin \(\gamma>0\), the \(\gamma\)-negative-curvature region of \(f\) in \(\Omega\) is
\[
\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega):=\{x\in\Omega:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x))\leq-\gamma\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(x\in\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)\) precisely when there exists a unit vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v\leq-\gamma\). The vector supplies a direction of descending curvature with a uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable objective and a positive margin \(\gamma\), the negative-curvature region consists of points where the smallest Hessian eigenvalue is no greater than \(-\gamma\). Equivalently, at every point in the region there is a unit direction whose second directional derivative is at most \(-\gamma\). The definition is quantitative: merely having a negative eigenvalue is insufficient unless its magnitude reaches the specified margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\leq-\gamma\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)\) if and only if \(\min_{\|v\|_2=1}v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v\leq-\gamma\).
The relative complement is \(\{x\in\Omega:\nabla^2f(x)\succ-\gamma I\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=1\), \(\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)=\{x\in\Omega:f''(x)\leq-\gamma\}\).
If \(\gamma_2\geq\gamma_1>0\), then \(\mathcal{N}_{\gamma_2}(f;\Omega)\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{\gamma_1}(f;\Omega)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A point in \(\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)\) cannot satisfy the second-order necessary condition \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\).
If \(\nabla^2f\) is continuous and \(\Omega\) is closed, then \(\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}(f;\Omega)\) is closed.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require \(\nabla f(x)=0\); negative curvature can occur away from critical points.
For constrained or Riemannian problems, curvature must be restricted to feasible or tangent directions and may require a Lagrangian or Riemannian Hessian.

children.title: Solution-Basin Regions

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Basin Regions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution basin is a neighborhood where objective growth and a stationarity error bound both control distance to the designated solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(S\subseteq\operatorname{argmin} f\) be nonempty and closed. A neighborhood \(B\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is a solution-basin region for \(S\) if constants \(\mu,c>0\) exist such that, for every \(x\in B\), \[ f(x)-\inf f\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2, \qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq c\,\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)). \] Thus objective growth and stationarity residual jointly identify proximity to \(S\) throughout \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) satisfies uniform quadratic growth and a subdifferential error bound relative to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local region certified by quadratic growth and an error bound relative to a solution set.

notation.meaning: limiting subdifferential of f at x
Euclidean distance from x to S

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable on \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(S\subseteq\Omega\) be a nonempty closed solution set on which \(f\) has the common value \(f_\star\), and define \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S):=\inf_{s\in S}\|x-s\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local smooth basin certificate around a possibly non-singleton solution set; identifiability is measured modulo the set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constants \(r>0\), \(\mu>0\), and \(\kappa>0\), the certified solution-basin region is
\[
\mathcal{B}_{r,\mu,\kappa}(f,S):=\left\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<r,\ f(x)-f_\star\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2,\ \|\nabla f(x)\|_2\geq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\right\}.
\]
Thus the basin combines a neighborhood condition, quadratic growth away from the solution set, and a first-order error bound that excludes non-solution stationary points within the certified portion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic-growth solution basin around a closed solution set \(S\) is the portion of a radius-\(r\) neighborhood where the objective gap is at least \(\mu/2\) times squared distance to \(S\), and the gradient norm is at least \(\kappa\) times that distance. The solution set may contain several equivalent parameters, so recovery means approaching \(S\), not necessarily a distinguished representative.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\Omega\) is nonempty and closed, and \(f(s)=f_\star\) for every \(s\in S\).
\(f\) is differentiable at every point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{B}_{r,\mu,\kappa}(f,S)\) is the set of points satisfying the stated neighborhood, quadratic-growth, and gradient-error-bound inequalities.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The gradient condition is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa^{-1}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\).
If the two inequalities hold throughout \(\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<r\}\), then that entire neighborhood equals \(\mathcal{B}_{r,\mu,\kappa}(f,S)\).
special_cases_latex: When \(S=\{x_\star\}\), distance to the solution set becomes \(\|x-x_\star\|_2\).
For a strongly convex \(f\) with unique minimizer \(x_\star\), suitable positive \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\) can certify the whole convex domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(x\in\mathcal{B}_{r,\mu,\kappa}(f,S)\) and \(\nabla f(x)=0\), then \(x\in S\).
Every point in the basin satisfies \(f(x)\geq f_\star\), with strict inequality whenever \(x\notin S\).

The definition alone does not guarantee that a particular algorithm enters or remains in the basin.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage gap of a regional certificate family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be an analysis domain and let \(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{N},\mathcal{B}\subseteq\Omega\) denote, respectively, chosen large-gradient, negative-curvature, and solution-basin certificate regions with fixed margins.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic coverage for a fixed objective, domain, and fixed certificate parameters; no probabilistic or asymptotic quantifier is implicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The regional certificate coverage gap associated with \((\mathcal{G},\mathcal{N},\mathcal{B})\) is
\[
\mathcal{U}(\Omega;\mathcal{G},\mathcal{N},\mathcal{B}):=\Omega\setminus(\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{N}\cup\mathcal{B}).
\]
Equivalently, \(x\in\mathcal{U}\) exactly when \(x\in\Omega\) but none of the three selected regional certificates holds at \(x\). The decomposition is complete on \(\Omega\) precisely when \(\mathcal{U}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed regional certificates, their coverage gap is the part of the analysis domain lying in none of the large-gradient, negative-curvature, or solution-basin regions. A point belongs to the gap exactly when all three certificates fail there. The standard regional decomposition covers the entire domain exactly when this gap is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{N},\mathcal{B}\) are specified subsets of the same domain \(\Omega\).
All thresholds and margins used to construct the three certificate regions are fixed before the complement is taken.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{U}=\Omega\setminus(\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{N}\cup\mathcal{B})\), and complete coverage is equivalent to \(\mathcal{U}=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathcal{U}=(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{G})\cap(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{N})\cap(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{B})\).
\(\mathcal{U}=\varnothing\) if and only if \(\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{N}\cup\mathcal{B}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mathcal{B}=\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal{U}=\Omega\setminus(\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{N})\).
If any one certificate region equals \(\Omega\), the coverage gap is empty.
immediate_consequences_latex: Enlarging any certificate region while holding the others fixed can only shrink \(\mathcal{U}\).
A nonempty \(\mathcal{U}\) identifies points for which the stated three-way certificate system makes no regional classification.
boundary_notes: An empty gap is a coverage statement, not a claim that the regions are disjoint.
The gap depends on certificate margins; changing a gradient, curvature, or basin threshold generally changes \(\mathcal{U}\).

Transition Regions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition region contains uncertified points lying within the prescribed width of at least one certified regime, representing ambiguity near certificate thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq D\) be regions on which distinct landscape certificates hold, and set \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\). Given widths \(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_m>0\), define the transition region by \[T=\left\{x\in D\setminus C:\text{there exists }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\text{ such that }\operatorname{dist}(x,C_i)\leq\delta_i\right\}.\] Points in \(T\) satisfy none of the selected regional certificates but lie within the prescribed width of at least one certified region; membership therefore records threshold-induced ambiguity rather than adverse objective geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq D\) are the selected certified regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\subseteq D\setminus C\) consists precisely of points outside all selected certified regions that lie within width \(\delta_i\) of at least one \(C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points lying between certified landscape regimes because certificate thresholds are not yet decisive.

transition width associated with certified region i

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Regions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uncertified region is the complement of all selected certificate regions; nonclassification alone implies no particular optimization geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be an analysis domain and let \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) be the predicates defining the selected regional landscape certificates. For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(C_i=\{x\in D:P_i(x)\}\). The uncertified region associated with this certificate family is \[ U=D\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i=\{x\in D:P_i(x)\text{ is false for every }i\}. \] Membership in \(U\) means only that the chosen certificate family does not classify the point; it does not imply stationarity, local optimality, saddle structure, or failure of convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=D\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\), with no additional geometric conclusion from membership alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Coverage Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate-coverage gap is the nonempty remainder after all certified regions are removed; any point in it witnesses incomplete classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be an analysis domain and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq D\) be the regions certified by a prescribed finite certificate family. Its coverage gap is \[ G=D\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i. \] The family has complete coverage exactly when \(G=\varnothing\). If \(G\neq\varnothing\), any \(x\in G\) is a verifiable witness that no certificate in the family establishes its advertised conclusion at \(x\). This is a boundary of the certificate system, not necessarily a pathological feature of the objective.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq D\) is exactly the validity region of certificate i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete coverage is equivalent to \(G=\varnothing\); any \(x\in G\) certifies incomplete coverage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Identifiability geometry induced by an invariant group action
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a parameter space \(\Theta\) by \((g,\theta)\mapsto g\cdot\theta\), let \(\Phi:\Theta\to\mathcal{X}\) be a representation map, and let \(f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\) be an objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic parameter nonidentifiability generated by an exact group symmetry; both discrete and continuous groups are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The parameterization has symmetry-induced identifiability geometry \((\Theta,G,\Phi,f)\) when
\[
\Phi(g\cdot\theta)=\Phi(\theta)\quad\text{and}\quad f(g\cdot\theta)=f(\theta)
\]
for every \(g\in G\) and \(\theta\in\Theta\). The identifiable object associated with \(\theta\) is then its orbit
\[
G\cdot\theta:=\{g\cdot\theta:g\in G\},
\]
and parameters are equivalent when \(\theta\sim_G\theta'\) if and only if \(\theta'=g\cdot\theta\) for some \(g\in G\). Recovery and local geometry are measured relative to an orbit or the quotient \(\Theta/G\), rather than to an individual representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized model has symmetry-induced identifiability geometry when a group acts on its parameter space without changing either the represented object or the objective. Every parameter is then identifiable only through its group orbit. Two parameters are equivalent exactly when a group element maps one to the other, and recovery should be formulated as recovery of an orbit or quotient point rather than of a chosen representative.
assumptions_latex: The representation and objective are invariant under the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identifiable parameter object is \([\theta]=G\cdot\theta\in\Theta/G\), with \(\theta\sim_G\theta'\) exactly when both parameters lie on the same orbit.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The map \(\Phi\) factors through the orbit projection \(\pi:\Theta\to\Theta/G\): there exists \(\bar\Phi\) with \(\Phi=\bar\Phi\circ\pi\).
The invariant objective factors as \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\) for a function \(\bar f:\Theta/G\to\mathbb{R}\).
special_cases_latex: A finite permutation or sign group produces finite equivalence classes.
A positive-dimensional Lie-group action produces continuous orbit directions and may create Hessian null directions at critical points.
immediate_consequences_latex: A unique parameter-level minimizer cannot be expected when a nontrivial orbit of minimizers is present.
An orbit-aware error may be written as \(\operatorname{dist}_G(\theta,\theta_\star):=\inf_{g\in G}\|\theta-g\cdot\theta_\star\|\) when a compatible norm is available.
boundary_notes: The definition addresses exact invariance; approximate symmetries require perturbation tolerances.
Different orbits may represent the same object if the group does not capture all parameter redundancy.

notation.meaning: Orbit of a parameter under the group action.
Equivalence relation induced by the action.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Symmetries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete symmetry is a finite group action preserving the objective; parameters are identifiable only up to their finite symmetry orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on a parameter space \(X\) by \((g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The action is a discrete symmetry of \(f\) when \[ f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }g\in G\text{ and }x\in X. \] Parameters \(x,y\in X\) are symmetry-equivalent when \(y=g\cdot x\) for some \(g\in G\). Their orbit \(G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}\) is finite, so identifiability can hold only modulo this orbit unless an orbit representative is selected.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite group acting on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective values are constant on each finite orbit \(G\cdot x\), producing discrete parameter equivalence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite parameter transformations that preserve the objective and induce discrete equivalence classes.

notation.meaning: orbit of x under the finite group action

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete symmetry of a parameterized objective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a topological parameter space, let \(G\) be a group acting on \(\Theta\), and let \(f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\Phi:\Theta\to\mathcal{X}\) denote an objective and its represented object.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite or discrete parameter equivalences, including permutations and sign changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A discrete symmetry of \((\Phi,f)\) is an action of a discrete group \(G\) on \(\Theta\) such that
\[
\Phi(g\cdot\theta)=\Phi(\theta),\qquad f(g\cdot\theta)=f(\theta)
\]
for all \(g\in G\) and \(\theta\in\Theta\). If \(G\) is finite, every orbit \(G\cdot\theta\) is finite, with cardinality \(|G\cdot\theta|=|G|/|G_\theta|\), where \(G_\theta:=\{g\in G:g\cdot\theta=\theta\}\) is the stabilizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete symmetry is a discrete group action on parameter space that preserves both the represented object and the objective. For a finite symmetry group, each parameter has finitely many equivalent representatives. The number of representatives in an orbit equals the group size divided by the size of the parameter's stabilizer, so parameters fixed by nonidentity symmetries have smaller orbits.
assumptions_latex: Both \(\Phi\) and \(f\) are invariant under the action.
The orbit-cardinality formula is asserted only when \(G\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent parameters are precisely members of the discrete orbit \(G\cdot\theta\); for finite \(G\), \(|G\cdot\theta|=|G|/|G_\theta|\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(g\in G\), the transformation \(T_g(\theta):=g\cdot\theta\) satisfies \(\Phi\circ T_g=\Phi\) and \(f\circ T_g=f\).
The objective descends to a function on the orbit space \(\Theta/G\).
special_cases_latex: For component permutation, \(G\) may be a symmetric group \(S_r\) acting by column permutations.
For paired-factor sign ambiguity, \(G\) may contain diagonal sign matrices \(D\) with \(D^2=I\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\theta_\star\) is a minimizer, every \(g\cdot\theta_\star\) is a minimizer with the same objective value.
A parameter can be locally isolated despite a nontrivial finite orbit, provided distinct orbit representatives are separated.
boundary_notes: A countably infinite discrete group may have infinite orbits, so finite-orbit conclusions require finite \(G\).
Continuous scaling, rotational, and gauge symmetries are excluded from this definition.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The invariant discrete action and orbit-stabilizer description are standard group-action definitions.
No inspected source locator supports the exact optimization-specific formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete symmetry of a parameterized objective

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Group Symmetries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous symmetry is a smooth positive-dimensional group action preserving the objective, making all infinitesimal orbit directions objective-flat.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a positive-dimensional Lie group \(G\) act smoothly on a smooth manifold \(X\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. The action is a continuous symmetry of \(f\) if \[ f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }g\in G\text{ and }x\in X. \] For every \(\xi\) in the Lie algebra of \(G\), the infinitesimal orbit direction \(\xi_X(x)\) satisfies \(Df(x)[\xi_X(x)]=0\). Hence the objective is constant along each orbit, and ordinary parameter identifiability fails in every nonzero orbit direction.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a positive-dimensional Lie group acting smoothly on \(X\).
\(f\) is differentiable and invariant under the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(x)[\xi_X(x)]=0\) for every infinitesimal orbit direction \(\xi_X(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lie-group actions generating continuous families of objective-equivalent parameters.

notation.meaning: infinitesimal action vector induced by Lie-algebra element xi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Lie-group symmetry of a smooth landscape
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a smooth manifold, let \(G\) be a Lie group, and let \(a:G\times\Theta\to\Theta\), \(a(g,\theta)=g\cdot\theta\), be a smooth group action. Let \(f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\) be smooth.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact smooth symmetries generated by positive-dimensional Lie groups; examples include rotations, scalings, and gauge transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The action \(a\) is a continuous group symmetry of the landscape \(f\) when
\[
f(g\cdot\theta)=f(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }(g,\theta)\in G\times\Theta.
\]
For \(\xi\) in the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\), define the infinitesimal orbit direction
\[
\xi_\Theta(\theta):=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\exp(t\xi)\cdot\theta.
\]
Invariance means \(Df(\theta)[\xi_\Theta(\theta)]=0\) for every \(\xi\in\mathfrak g\). The orbit tangent space is \(T_\theta(G\cdot\theta)=\{\xi_\Theta(\theta):\xi\in\mathfrak g\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous symmetry of a smooth objective is a smooth Lie-group action that leaves the objective unchanged. Each Lie-algebra element generates a tangent direction along the parameter orbit, and the directional derivative of the objective vanishes in every such direction. The span of these infinitesimal directions is the tangent space to the symmetry orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a Lie group acting smoothly on the smooth manifold \(\Theta\).
The objective \(f\) is smooth and invariant under the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is constant on every orbit, and \(Df(\theta)[v]=0\) for all \(v\in T_\theta(G\cdot\theta)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\theta\), the orbit map \(a_\theta:G\to\Theta\) satisfies \(f\circ a_\theta\equiv f(\theta)\).
The differential \(Df(\theta)\) annihilates the image of the infinitesimal action \(\mathfrak g\to T_\theta\Theta\).
special_cases_latex: Orthogonal symmetry uses \(G=O(r)\) or \(SO(r)\).
Scaling symmetry may use \(G=\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) acting by \(c\cdot(U,V)=(cU,c^{-1}V)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive-dimensional orbit contains infinitely many parameter representatives with the same objective value.
At a critical point, sufficiently smooth invariant landscapes commonly have Hessian degeneracy along regular orbit directions; the definition itself only asserts first-order annihilation.
boundary_notes: A continuous action need not be free or proper; without these properties the orbit space may fail to be a smooth manifold.
Noncompact scaling groups can generate unbounded parameter orbits even though the represented object remains fixed.

notation.meaning: Lie algebra of the symmetry group.
Tangent space to the group orbit.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Smooth invariant Lie-group actions and their infinitesimal generators are standard differential-geometric definitions.
A precise source for this optimization-landscape specialization was not inspected.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Landscapes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant objective factors uniquely through the orbit space. If a group acts smoothly, freely, and properly on a smooth manifold, that orbit space has a smooth quotient-manifold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a set \(X\), let \(\pi:X\to X/G\) send each point to its orbit, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be \(G\)-invariant. Then there is a unique function \(\bar f:X/G\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \[\bar f([x])=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X,\qquad f=\bar f\circ\pi.\] The quotient objective is well defined because all representatives of \([x]\) have the same value. If, additionally, \(X\) is a smooth manifold and \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, and properly on \(X\), then \(X/G\) carries the corresponding smooth quotient-manifold structure.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(X\), and \(f\) is constant on every orbit.
For the manifold conclusion, \(X\) is a smooth manifold and the action is smooth, free, and proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique quotient objective \(\bar f\) satisfying \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\); under the additional smooth, free, and proper action hypotheses, \(X/G\) is a smooth quotient manifold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An invariant objective represented on equivalence classes after symmetry redundancy is removed.

notation.meaning: canonical projection from X to the orbit space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invariant functions factor uniquely through orbit spaces and smooth free proper actions yield smooth quotients

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Landscape induced on a symmetry quotient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a set or smooth manifold \(\Theta\), let \(\pi:\Theta\to\Theta/G\) be the orbit projection \(\pi(\theta)=[\theta]\), and let \(f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(G\)-invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact removal of parameter redundancy by orbit identification; smooth differential geometry requires a free and proper Lie-group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quotient landscape induced by \(f\) is the function
\[
\bar f:\Theta/G\to\mathbb{R},\qquad \bar f([\theta]):=f(\theta).
\]
It is well defined because \(f(g\cdot\theta)=f(\theta)\) for all \(g\in G\). Equivalently, \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\). If \(\Theta\) is a smooth manifold and the Lie-group action is smooth, free, and proper, then \(\Theta/G\) is taken with its quotient-manifold structure, so the landscape can be analyzed without vertical orbit directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant objective induces a quotient landscape by assigning to each orbit the common objective value of its representatives. This assignment is well defined precisely because the objective is constant along every orbit, and the original objective factors through the orbit projection. Under a smooth, free, and proper Lie-group action, the orbit space is a quotient manifold and removes the redundant orbit directions from the parameter geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(\Theta\) and \(f(g\cdot\theta)=f(\theta)\) for all \(g\) and \(\theta\).
For the quotient-manifold interpretation, \(\Theta\) is smooth and the Lie-group action is smooth, free, and proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique function \(\bar f\) on \(\Theta/G\) satisfying \(\bar f([\theta])=f(\theta)\) and \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\bar f\circ\pi=f\).
For any two parameters \(\theta,\theta'\), \([\theta]=[\theta']\) implies \(f(\theta)=f(\theta')\).
special_cases_latex: For a finite group, \(\Theta/G\) identifies finitely many symmetry-related representatives and may have singular points at nontrivial stabilizers.
For a free orthogonal action on a factor manifold, horizontal tangent vectors represent tangent directions in the quotient.
immediate_consequences_latex: Minimizers of \(\bar f\) correspond to minimizing orbits of \(f\).
Orbit-equivalent critical representatives describe one quotient-level critical object when the differential structure is regular.
boundary_notes: If the action is not free, the quotient may be an orbifold or stratified space rather than a manifold.
The quotient construction removes only redundancies represented by the specified group.

notation.meaning: Projection from parameter space to orbit space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: An invariant function descending through an orbit projection is the standard quotient-landscape construction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orbit normalization by an invariant representative selector
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a parameter space \(\Theta\), let \(D\subseteq\Theta\) be a \(G\)-invariant domain, and let \(C\subseteq D\) be a prescribed normalized cross-section or gauge set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic normalization of redundant parameters, particularly for noncompact or asymmetric orbits; global uniqueness is optional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An orbit-normalization mechanism on \(D\) is a map \(N:D\to C\) satisfying
\[
N(\theta)\in G\cdot\theta,
\qquad
N(g\cdot\theta)=N(\theta)
\]
for every \(\theta\in D\) and every \(g\in G\) with \(g\cdot\theta\in D\). It is a unique normalization when each orbit in \(D\) meets \(C\) in exactly one point. It is orbit-controlling when normalized representatives lie in a bounded or compact set \(K\subseteq C\), or satisfy a coercive gauge bound \(q(N(\theta))\leq M\) on the family under study.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orbit-normalization mechanism selects a representative from each symmetry orbit and makes the same selection for every representative of that orbit. A normalization is unique if the chosen cross-section intersects each relevant orbit exactly once. It controls noncompact orbits when the selected representatives remain in a bounded or compact set, or obey a uniform bound for a coercive gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(\Theta\), and \(D\) is invariant under the relevant group transformations.
\(C\subseteq D\) is the admissible set of normalized representatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\) factors through \(D/G\) and selects an orbit-equivalent representative in \(C\); uniqueness holds when \(|C\cap(G\cdot\theta)|=1\) for every \(\theta\in D\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a section \(s:D/G\to C\) such that \(N=s\circ\pi\), where \(\pi:D\to D/G\).
Unique normalization is equivalent to the restriction \(\pi|_C:C\to D/G\) being bijective.
special_cases_latex: For scaling \((U,V)\mapsto(cU,c^{-1}V)\), a balancing rule may impose \(\|U\|_F=\|V\|_F\).
For sign symmetry, a convention may choose the first nonzero coordinate to be positive.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any invariant objective satisfies \(f(N(\theta))=f(\theta)\).
A bounded normalized representative prevents divergence caused solely by motion along a noncompact symmetry orbit.
boundary_notes: A global continuous selector need not exist, even when every orbit has normalized representatives.
Regularization that changes objective values along an orbit is an orbit-breaking mechanism, not an invariant selector of the form defined here.

notation.meaning: Coercive gauge used to quantify orbit control.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: An orbit-invariant representative selector is a standard abstract model of gauge fixing.
The node also mentions modeling mechanisms that may break symmetry; a source is needed to determine whether those should be included in the canonical definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit normalization by an invariant representative selector
Balancing Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancing selects factor representatives with equal Gram matrices, controlling reciprocal scaling while preserving the represented matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a factorization \(X=UV^{\mathsf T}\) with \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), the transformation \((U,V)\mapsto(UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})\) preserves \(X\) for every invertible \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\). A representative is balanced when \[ U^{\mathsf T}U=V^{\mathsf T}V. \] Equivalently, it minimizes \(\|UR\|_F^2+\|VR^{-\mathsf T}\|_F^2\) over its invertible gauge orbit whenever such a minimizer exists. Balancing removes reciprocal scaling disparity without changing the represented matrix or any objective depending only on \(UV^{\mathsf T}\).
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) have the same column dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(U^{\mathsf T}U=V^{\mathsf T}V\) normalizes reciprocal factor scaling while leaving \(UV^{\mathsf T}\) invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit normalization by equalizing scale-dependent magnitudes in a factorized representation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The balancing condition and gauge invariance fit the container, but the asserted equivalence with global minimization over the full invertible gauge orbit is nontrivial and lacks an authoritative source specifying the necessary existence and rank conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Selection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge selection is a normalization slice meeting every relevant symmetry orbit exactly once. A local condition gives a local gauge, while multiple intersections leave residual ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a parameter space \(X\), and let \(N:X\to Y\) be a normalization map with prescribed value \(y_0\in Y\). Define the normalization slice \(\Sigma=\{x\in X:N(x)=y_0\}\). The slice is a gauge selection on a set \(D\subseteq X\) if \[\left|\Sigma\cap(G\cdot x)\right|=1\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.\] Existence of the intersection makes the normalization attainable, while uniqueness removes orbit ambiguity on \(D\). If the condition holds only on a neighborhood, \(\Sigma\) is a local gauge; multiple intersections leave residual gauge ambiguity.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq X\) is the set of parameters whose orbits are to be normalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma\) selects one representative of each orbit through \(D\) exactly when \(\left|\Sigma\cap(G\cdot x)\right|=1\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of one representative per symmetry orbit by a normalization predicate.

notation.meaning: set on which orbit representatives are to be selected

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a gauge slice selects orbit representatives through existence and uniqueness of intersection

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact-Orbit Control
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noncompact-orbit control ensures that normalized representatives of compact families of represented objects remain bounded instead of diverging along symmetry orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a noncompact group \(G\) act on a normed parameter space \(X\), and let \(\rho:X\to Z\) be constant on each orbit. A normalization set \(\Sigma\subseteq X\) controls noncompact orbits over \(K\subseteq Z\) if \[ \Sigma\cap\rho^{-1}(K)\text{ is bounded whenever }K\text{ is compact}. \] If \(\Sigma\) meets every relevant orbit, then any sequence of represented objects \(\rho(x_k)\) contained in a compact set admits normalized representatives \(\hat x_k\in(G\cdot x_k)\cap\Sigma\) that cannot escape to infinity. This condition suppresses divergence caused solely by noncompact symmetry transformations.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is noncompact and acts on the normed space \(X\).
\(\rho\) is orbit-invariant and \(\Sigma\) meets every relevant orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compact represented families have bounded normalized representatives in \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A coercive normalization preventing bounded represented objects from having divergent parameter representatives.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: properness over compact represented sets is a standard boundedness formulation for normalized representatives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy datum for structured optimization representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be an ambient object space, let \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) be a structured feasible set, and let \(F:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}\) be an objective on represented objects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal comparison framework for alternative exact or relaxed representations of the same structured object class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A structured representation is a tuple
\[
\mathfrak R=(P,\Phi,G,\mathcal C),
\]
where \(P\) is a parameter domain, \(\Phi:P\to\mathcal{X}\) is a representation map, \(G\) is a group acting on \(P\) with \(\Phi(g\cdot p)=\Phi(p)\), and \(\mathcal C:=\Phi(P)\) is the represented class. It is exact for \(\mathcal S\) when \(\mathcal C=\mathcal S\), and relaxed when \(\mathcal S\subsetneq\mathcal C\). Its induced objective is \(f_{	iny\mathfrak R}:=F\circ\Phi\) whenever \(F\) is defined on \(\mathcal C\). A representation taxonomy classifies \(\mathfrak R\) by the geometry of \(P\), the redundancy group \(G\), and whether \(\mathcal C\) is exact or relaxed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured representation consists of a parameter domain, a map from parameters to ambient objects, a group describing explicit parameter redundancy, and the image class produced by the map. It is exact when its image is exactly the target structured set and relaxed when the image strictly contains that set. The represented objective is obtained by composing the object-level objective with the representation map. The taxonomy distinguishes representations through parameter geometry, redundancy, and exactness.
assumptions_latex: The representation is invariant under \(G\): \(\Phi(g\cdot p)=\Phi(p)\).
The object-level objective is defined on the represented image when \(F\circ\Phi\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak R=(P,\Phi,G,\Phi(P))\) records the domain geometry, representation map, symmetry redundancy, and exact-versus-relaxed image relation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An exact representation is a surjection \(\Phi:P\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal S\).
If the fibers of \(\Phi\) equal the \(G\)-orbits, then \(P/G\) is in bijection with \(\mathcal C\).
special_cases_latex: Euclidean factorization uses an open or full Euclidean factor domain.
Embedded-manifold and quotient representations place smooth geometry directly on \(P\) or \(P/G\).
Lifted convex representations use a convex parameter or image set and may be relaxations.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different representations of the same \(\mathcal S\) can induce different critical-point and curvature geometry.
A noninjective \(\Phi\) creates representational nonidentifiability unless its fibers are explicitly quotiented or normalized.
boundary_notes: This is a taxonomy datum, not a theorem asserting equivalence of algorithms across representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Factorized Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unconstrained factors represent every matrix of rank at most r, but invertible changes of factor coordinates create redundant equivalent parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(m,n,r\geq1\), define \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) by \[ \Phi(U,V)=UV^{\mathsf T}. \] Its image is exactly \(\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\}\). For every invertible \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\), \(\Phi(UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})=\Phi(U,V)\), so the Euclidean coordinates are redundant. An objective \(F\) on matrices induces the unconstrained factor objective \(f(U,V)=F(UV^{\mathsf T})\), which is invariant under this gauge action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{im}\Phi=\{X:\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\}\), and \(\Phi\) is invariant under \((U,V)\mapsto(UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A low-rank matrix represented by unconstrained Euclidean factors with explicit gauge redundancy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean factorization of a rank-constrained matrix
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix integers \(m,n,r\geq1\). Let \(\mathcal{M}_{\leq r}:=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\}\) and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}\) be an object-level objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained rectangular factors in Euclidean coordinates, with explicit change-of-basis redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Euclidean factorized representation of \(\mathcal{M}_{\leq r}\) is
\[
P:=\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times r},
\qquad
\Phi(U,V):=UV^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
f(U,V):=F(UV^{\mathsf T}).
\]
The map is surjective onto \(\mathcal{M}_{\leq r}\). For every \(R\in GL(r)\),
\[
\Phi(UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})=UV^{\mathsf T},
\]
so the factor coordinates are redundant. When both factors have full column rank, this \(GL(r)\) action describes the usual change-of-basis equivalence within the rank-\(r\) stratum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix of rank at most \(r\) is represented by two unconstrained Euclidean factors \(U\) and \(V\) through the product \(UV^{\mathsf T}\). An object-level objective becomes a generally nonconvex factor objective by composition with this product map. Invertible changes of latent basis, sending \(U\) to \(UR\) and \(V\) to \(VR^{-\mathsf T}\), leave the represented matrix unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\), \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), and \(F\) is defined on all represented matrices.
For the stated group equivalence, \(R\in GL(r)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(P)=\mathcal{M}_{\leq r}\), and \((U,V)\) and \((UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})\) represent the same matrix for every \(R\in GL(r)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The rank constraint \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\) is enforced automatically by writing \(X=UV^{\mathsf T}\).
The factor objective is the pullback \(f=F\circ\Phi\).
special_cases_latex: For positive-semidefinite structure, a tied factorization uses \(X=UU^{\mathsf T}\) and orthogonal redundancy \(U\mapsto UQ\).
For \(r=1\), the scaling symmetry is \((u,v)\mapsto(cu,c^{-1}v)\) for \(c\neq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(F\) in \(X\) does not generally imply convexity of \(f\) in \((U,V)\).
A unique represented matrix can correspond to infinitely many factor pairs.
boundary_notes: At rank-deficient factor pairs, fibers can be larger and the group action can be nonfree.
Additional factor constraints or regularizers define different representations and may break the full \(GL(r)\) symmetry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedded-manifold representation of a structured set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq E\) be a smooth embedded submanifold, let \(i:\mathcal{M}\hookrightarrow E\) be inclusion, and let \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be smooth on an open neighborhood \(U\supseteq\mathcal{M}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct smooth constrained optimization on a regular embedded manifold, without introducing redundant ambient factor coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The embedded-manifold representation of the structured optimization problem is the pair
\[
(\mathcal{M},f),\qquad f:=F|_{\mathcal{M}}=F\circ i.
\]
At each \(x\in\mathcal{M}\), feasible first-order directions form the tangent space \(T_x\mathcal{M}\subseteq E\), and the Riemannian gradient for the induced metric is
\[
\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_{T_x\mathcal{M}}\nabla F(x),
\]
where \(P_{T_x\mathcal{M}}\) is the orthogonal projector onto the tangent space. The representation is direct because each feasible point is itself the represented object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded-manifold representation treats a smooth structured subset of a Euclidean space as the optimization domain itself. The objective is the restriction of an ambient smooth function to that manifold. Feasible first-order directions are tangent vectors, and under the metric inherited from the ambient space the Riemannian gradient is the orthogonal projection of the ambient gradient onto the tangent space.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq E\) is a smooth embedded submanifold.
\(F\) is smooth on an open neighborhood of \(\mathcal{M}\).
The Riemannian metric is induced by the Euclidean inner product on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The represented objective is \(f=F|_{\mathcal{M}}\), with \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_{T_x\mathcal{M}}\nabla F(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The representation map is the injective inclusion \(i:\mathcal{M}\hookrightarrow E\).
First-order criticality is \(P_{T_x\mathcal{M}}\nabla F(x)=0\), equivalently \(\nabla F(x)\in(T_x\mathcal{M})^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: The sphere, Stiefel manifold, and fixed-rank matrix manifold are standard embedded-manifold domains.
For an open set \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq E\), the tangent projector is the identity and the representation reduces to ordinary unconstrained optimization.
immediate_consequences_latex: No parameter symmetry is introduced by the inclusion map itself.
Ambient and intrinsic gradients differ whenever the ambient gradient has a nonzero normal component.
boundary_notes: Sets with singularities, boundaries, or varying dimension are not globally smooth embedded manifolds.
A quotient representation may describe the same objects using redundant factors and is geometrically distinct from direct embedding.

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the manifold at \(x\).
Inclusion of the manifold into its ambient space.

Embedded Fixed-Rank Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrices of exactly rank r form a smooth embedded manifold with dimension r(m+n-r), allowing direct rank-constrained optimization in matrix coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(1\leq r<\min\{m,n\}\), let \[ \mathcal{M}_r=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}. \] Then \(\mathcal{M}_r\) is a smooth embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\). If \(X=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) is a compact singular-value decomposition with orthonormal \(U,V\), its tangent space is \[ T_X\mathcal{M}_r=\{UA^{\mathsf T}+BV^{\mathsf T}:A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r},\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\}. \] Thus optimization variables are matrices themselves, while rank is enforced by manifold membership rather than redundant factor coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{M}_r\) is an embedded manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\) with the displayed tangent-space representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold-Constrained Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth constrained problem on an embedded manifold is the restriction of an ambient objective; stationarity means that the ambient gradient has zero tangent component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^p\) be a smooth embedded manifold and let \(F:U\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood \(U\supset\mathcal M\). The manifold-constrained problem is represented by \[\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x),\qquad f=F|_{\mathcal M}.\] With the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product and orthogonal tangent projector \(P_x:\mathbb R^p\to T_x\mathcal M\), its first-order stationarity condition is \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla F(x)=0.\] Thus feasibility is encoded by membership in \(\mathcal M\), while the intrinsic gradient is the tangent component of the ambient gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^p\) is a smooth embedded manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal M\) is first-order stationary exactly when \(P_x\nabla F(x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Factor Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant factor objective descends uniquely to the quotient, where equivalent factors become one point and minimizing factor orbits correspond to quotient minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly, freely, and properly on a smooth factor space \(\mathcal P\), and let \(\pi:\mathcal P\to\mathcal P/G\) map each factor to its orbit. If \(F:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R\) is invariant, meaning \(F(pg)=F(p)\) for every admissible \(p\) and \(g\), then there is a unique function \(f:\mathcal P/G\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(F=f\circ\pi\). Hence \[\inf_{p\in\mathcal P}F(p)=\inf_{[p]\in\mathcal P/G}f([p]),\] and minimizers correspond by orbit: \(p\) is minimizing exactly when its equivalence class \([p]\) is minimizing.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, and properly on \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(f\) with \(F=f\circ\pi\), and optimization of \(F\) is equivalent to optimization of \(f\) over \(\mathcal P/G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant factor coordinates represented modulo a free proper group action.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factor representation modulo a continuous equivalence group
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a smooth factor manifold, let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly, freely, and properly on \(P\), and let \(\Phi:P\to\mathcal{S}\) be a smooth representation map constant on \(G\)-orbits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth factor coordinates whose exact continuous redundancy is removed by passing to a quotient manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quotient factor representation is the induced map
\[
\bar\Phi:P/G\to\mathcal{S},
\qquad
\bar\Phi([p]):=\Phi(p),
\]
where \([p]=G\cdot p\). It is exact when \(\bar\Phi\) is bijective onto \(\mathcal{S}\), equivalently when
\[
\Phi(p)=\Phi(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q=g\cdot p\text{ for some }g\in G.
\]
For an object-level objective \(F:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}\), the quotient factor objective is \(\bar f:=F\circ\bar\Phi\) on \(P/G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient factor representation identifies factor tuples related by a continuous symmetry group and treats each orbit as one parameter. The representation map descends from factor space to the quotient because it is constant along orbits. The representation is exact when two factor tuples represent the same object exactly when they belong to the same orbit. An object-level objective then induces an objective directly on the quotient.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a smooth manifold and \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, and properly on \(P\).
\(\Phi(g\cdot p)=\Phi(p)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(p\in P\).
For exactness, every fiber of \(\Phi\) is one \(G\)-orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar\Phi([p])=\Phi(p)\) is well defined on \(P/G\), and exactness is equivalent to equality of the fibers of \(\Phi\) with the group orbits.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\Phi=\bar\Phi\circ\pi\), where \(\pi:P\to P/G\) is the orbit projection.
An exact quotient factor representation gives a bijection \(P/G\cong\mathcal{S}\).
special_cases_latex: For full-rank rectangular factors, \(GL(r)\) may act by \((U,V)\mapsto(UR,VR^{-\mathsf T})\).
For positive-semidefinite factors, \(O(r)\) acts by \(U\mapsto UQ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Orbit directions are not distinct tangent directions in the quotient parameterization.
Critical points of the quotient objective represent critical orbits rather than individual factor tuples.
boundary_notes: Rank-deficient strata can violate freeness and require a stratified quotient.
If the chosen group does not account for every fiber of \(\Phi\), the quotient remains nonidentifiable.

notation.meaning: Quotient of factor space by continuous equivalence.
Representation map induced on the quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Convex Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex relaxation over a lifted set gives a lower bound; a lifted optimum lying in the original image certifies exactness and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a nonconvex feasible set, \(\Phi:Z\to E\) a lifting map into a finite-dimensional vector space, and \(K\subset E\) a convex set containing \(\Phi(Z)\). Suppose \(L:K\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex and \(L(\Phi(z))=f(z)\) for every \(z\in Z\). The lifted convex comparator is \[v_{\mathrm{lift}}=\inf_{X\in K}L(X)\leq \inf_{z\in Z}f(z)=v_{\mathrm{orig}}.\] If a lifted minimizer \(X_\star\) belongs to \(\Phi(Z)\), then every \(z_\star\) satisfying \(\Phi(z_\star)=X_\star\) is globally optimal and \(v_{\mathrm{lift}}=v_{\mathrm{orig}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{lift}}\leq v_{\mathrm{orig}}\), with equality and recovery when a lifted minimizer lies in \(\Phi(Z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex lifting used as a lower-bound comparator and exactness certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex lift and convex relaxation of a structured problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) be a structured feasible set in a finite-dimensional vector space, let \(F:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(L:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}\) be linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-dimensional convex representations used either exactly or as relaxations and comparators for a nonconvex structured problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A lifted convex representation of \(\mathcal{S}\) is a nonempty convex set \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\) together with a linear map \(L\) such that
\[
L(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{S}.
\]
It is an exact convex lift when equality holds. A lifted convex relaxation replaces equality by
\[
\mathcal{S}\subseteq L(\mathcal{C}),
\]
and optimizes a convex function \(\widetilde F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}\) chosen to agree with or bound the original objective on lifted representatives of \(\mathcal{S}\). The relaxation is tight for a given instance when an optimal \(Y_\star\in\mathcal C\) projects to a feasible \(X_\star=L(Y_\star)\in\mathcal S\) with the original optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted convex representation places the problem in a higher-dimensional vector space, uses a convex feasible set there, and recovers structured objects through a linear projection. The lift is exact when the projection of the convex set equals the original structured set. A convex relaxation only requires the projection to contain the original set. It is tight for an instance when a lifted optimum projects to an original feasible optimum with the same value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is nonempty and convex, and \(L\) is linear.
For a convex optimization formulation, \(\widetilde F\) is convex on \(\mathcal C\).
Tightness is relative to a specified original objective and problem instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness means \(L(\mathcal C)=\mathcal S\); relaxation means \(\mathcal S\subseteq L(\mathcal C)\); instancewise tightness requires a value-preserving projected optimum in \(\mathcal S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: An exact lift represents every \(X\in\mathcal S\) by at least one \(Y\in\mathcal C\) and represents no projected object outside \(\mathcal S\).
A relaxation enlarges the projected feasible class from \(\mathcal S\) to \(L(\mathcal C)\).
special_cases_latex: Semidefinite lifting uses a positive-semidefinite matrix variable \(Y\succeq0\) with affine constraints.
Convex-hull lifting takes a convex set whose projection equals or contains \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal S)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A relaxation can provide a comparator or bound even when it is not tight.
Exact lifting preserves the feasible object class but may substantially increase dimension.
boundary_notes: Many nonconvex structured sets cannot be the linear image of a convex set, so exact convex lifting is a restrictive property.
Factorization of a positive-semidefinite variable is not itself a convex lift because the factor domain produces a nonconvex parameterized objective.

notation.meaning: Convex feasible set in the lifted space.
Linear projection to the original object space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Linear images of convex feasible sets and their relaxations are standard lift formulations.

children.title: Population-to-Empirical Landscape Transfer
children.top_down_role: The statistical route from idealized expected geometry to finite-data objectives.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(F:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be a twice differentiable population objective, and let \(F_n:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be a twice differentiable empirical objective based on \(n\) observations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample, smooth, uniform transfer of objective values, gradients, and Hessians over a fixed analysis domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For tolerances \(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\geq0\), the population-to-empirical landscape transfer event is
\[
\mathcal E_n(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2;\Omega):=\left\{
\sup_{x\in\Omega}|F_n(x)-F(x)|\leq\varepsilon_0,
\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\|\nabla F_n(x)-\nabla F(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon_1,
\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\|\nabla^2F_n(x)-\nabla^2F(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\varepsilon_2
\right\}.
\]
A landscape certificate transfers at these tolerances when its defining inequalities remain valid for \(F_n\) after reducing their value, gradient, or curvature margins by the corresponding perturbation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Population-to-empirical landscape transfer is recorded by a uniform event controlling the discrepancy between population and empirical objectives at value, gradient, and Hessian levels throughout an analysis domain. A population certificate transfers when its defining inequalities survive these perturbations with appropriately reduced margins. The definition separates the three derivative levels because different landscape claims require different forms of uniform control.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(F_n\) are twice differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\Omega\).
The Hessian discrepancy is measured in operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_n\) is the simultaneous uniform \(C^0\), gradient, and Hessian approximation event on \(\Omega\), and transfer means preservation of certificate inequalities after tolerance-dependent margin degradation.
equivalent_formulations_latex:
The event is \(\{\|F_n-F\|_{\infty,\Omega}\leq\varepsilon_0,\ \|
abla F_n-
abla F\|_{\infty,\Omega}\leq\varepsilon_1,\ \|
abla^2F_n-
abla^2F\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op},\Omega}\leq\varepsilon_2\}\).
Any subset of the three inequalities defines the corresponding lower-order transfer event.
special_cases_latex: First-order landscape transfer uses only the gradient bound \(\varepsilon_1\).
Strict-saddle transfer typically requires both gradient and Hessian controls.
Value-only uniform convergence uses only \(\varepsilon_0\) and does not control critical-point geometry.
immediate_consequences_latex: A population gradient margin larger than \(\varepsilon_1\) remains positive empirically.
A population negative-curvature margin larger than \(\varepsilon_2\) remains negative after empirical perturbation.
boundary_notes: The definition does not supply a probability bound for \(\mathcal E_n\); such a bound depends on the sampling model and function class.
Uniform derivative control may be unnecessarily strong for localized or trajectory-dependent transfer results.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Uniform value, gradient, and Hessian deviations are standard sufficient data for smooth landscape transfer.
A source is needed for the exact named event and the intended certificate-transfer convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Population Landscape Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The population landscape is expected loss over the data distribution, while the empirical landscape replaces the expectation by a finite sample average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) be a random observation with distribution \(P\), let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be the parameter domain, and let \(\ell:D\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable. The population landscape is the deterministic extended-real function \[L(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[\ell(x;\xi)],\qquad x\in D,\] at every point where the expectation is well defined. For independent observations \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\), its empirical counterpart is \[L_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x;\xi_i).\] Derivative-level comparisons require separate integrability and differentiation-under-expectation conditions; they are not part of the definition.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x;\xi)\) is measurable in \(\xi\) for each \(x\in D\).
The displayed expectation exists as an extended-real value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x)=\mathbb E[\ell(x;\xi)]\) is the population comparator for \(L_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x;\xi_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-risk landscape serving as the deterministic comparator for empirical geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Population objective and its deterministic landscape
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a parameter domain, and let \(\ell:\Theta\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb{R}\) be a measurable loss.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized deterministic geometry obtained by averaging a random loss under the data-generating distribution before finite-sample fluctuations are introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The population landscape model generated by \((P,\ell,\Theta)\) is the extended-real function
\[
F(\theta):=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}[\ell(\theta;Z)],
\qquad
\theta\in\operatorname{dom}F:=\{\theta\in\Theta:\mathbb E|\ell(\theta;Z)|<\infty\}.
\]
When differentiation can be interchanged with expectation, its first- and second-order landscape fields are
\[
\nabla F(\theta)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta;Z)],
\qquad
\nabla^2F(\theta)=\mathbb E[\nabla^2_{\theta\theta}\ell(\theta;Z)].
\]
Critical points, curvature regions, and solution basins of the population model are defined from this deterministic function \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A population landscape is the expected loss under the data-generating distribution, defined at parameters where the loss is integrable. When valid differentiation-under-expectation conditions hold, the population gradient and Hessian are the expectations of the sample-loss gradient and Hessian. The resulting objective is deterministic even though it is defined from a random observation, and its critical points, curvature, and solution basins describe the idealized geometry before sampling noise.
assumptions_latex: For every \(\theta\in\operatorname{dom}F\), the map \(z\mapsto\ell(\theta;z)\) is measurable and integrable.
The displayed derivative identities require differentiability in \(\theta\) and valid interchange of differentiation and expectation, such as suitable local domination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The population objective is \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}[\ell(\theta;Z)]\) on its integrability domain, with derivative fields given by expected sample derivatives whenever interchange is valid.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\) is the risk functional associated with loss \(\ell\) and distribution \(P\).
For independent observations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), the empirical counterpart is \(F_n(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta;Z_i)\).
special_cases_latex: For squared loss, \(F\) is the mean squared prediction error.
If \(P\) has finite support, the population objective is a finite probability-weighted sum of losses.
immediate_consequences_latex: The population landscape depends on the full distribution \(P\), not on a realized sample.
If the derivative identities hold, population stationary points satisfy \(\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta;Z)]=0\).
boundary_notes: Existence of \(F\) does not by itself justify exchanging derivatives and expectation.
Misspecified or contaminated distributions define different population landscapes; no finite-sample approximation guarantee is part of this definition.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Expected risk and derivative-under-expectation identities are standard population-model definitions.

children.title: Derivative-Level Transfer Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Derivative-level approximation families used to preserve landscape regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(R\subseteq U\), and let \(F,F_n:U\to\mathbb R\) be respectively a reference objective and an empirical or approximate objective. For an integer \(p\geq 0\), assume both functions are \(p\)-times continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(R\). Derivative tensors are equipped with their induced Euclidean operator norms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns deterministic uniform derivative discrepancies on a specified region. In statistical applications the inequalities may hold on a high-probability event, but no sampling theorem is asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\leq j\leq p\), define the level-\(j\) transfer error by \[\Delta_j(F_n,F;R):=\sup_{x\in R}\|D^jF_n(x)-D^jF(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}},\] where \(D^0F=F\) and the norm at level zero is absolute value. Given tolerances \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_p)\in[0,\infty]^{p+1}\), the pair \((F_n,F)\) has an \((R,p,\varepsilon)\) derivative-level transfer certificate when \(\Delta_j(F_n,F;R)\leq\varepsilon_j\) for every \(j=0,ldots,p\). The ordered family of these conditions is the derivative-level transfer hierarchy: level zero controls objective values, level one controls gradients, and level two controls Hessians and directional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative-level transfer hierarchy compares a reference objective with an empirical or approximate objective uniformly over a region. Its level-j error is the supremum over that region of the operator norm of the difference between their jth derivatives. A certificate through order p requires every error from order zero through order p to lie below its assigned tolerance. Thus value, gradient, and Hessian transfer are separate nested requirements rather than interchangeable notions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(F_n,F)\in\mathcal T_p(R;\varepsilon)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall j\in\{0,\ldots,p\},\ \sup_{x\in R}\|D^jF_n(x)-D^jF(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\varepsilon_j.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(R\) is compact and coordinates are fixed, tensor-norm equivalence gives an equivalent componentwise formulation using uniform bounds on all partial derivatives \(\partial^\alpha(F_n-F)\) with \(|\alpha|\leq p\), after dimension-dependent adjustment of tolerances.
For \(p=1\), the hierarchy is precisely simultaneous uniform convergence of values and gradients on \(R\); for \(p=2\), it additionally requires uniform Hessian convergence.
special_cases_latex: The homogeneous tolerance convention sets \(\varepsilon_j=\varepsilon\) for every \(j\leq p\).
The exact-transfer case is \(\varepsilon_j=0\) for every \(j\), meaning the two functions and all derivatives through order \(p\) coincide on \(R\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(q\leq p\), an \((R,p,\varepsilon)\) certificate restricts to an order-\(q\) certificate with tolerances \((\varepsilon_0,ldots,varepsilon_q)\).
For every \(x\in R\) and unit vector \(v\), level-two transfer yields \(|v^\top(\nabla^2F_n(x)-\nabla^2F(x))v|\leq\varepsilon_2\).
boundary_notes: Value transfer alone does not imply gradient or Hessian transfer without additional regularity assumptions.
The definition does not by itself state which critical-point strata, basins, or minimizers are preserved; those require margins comparing the derivative errors with the reference landscape geometry.
No authoritative source in the supplied materials was located for this exact synthesized hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Level Population-to-Empirical Transfer Hierarchy
Uniform Value Transfer
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For real-valued objectives with finite infima, uniform objective error bounds transfer optimal values and approximate global minimizers, with a two-error loss, but do not control stationary-point geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L,L_n:D\to\mathbb R\) be functions on a nonempty domain \(D\), and suppose that \(\inf_{x\in D}L(x)\) and \(\inf_{x\in D}L_n(x)\) are finite. Uniform value transfer at tolerance \(\varepsilon_0\geq0\) is the condition \[\sup_{x\in D}|L_n(x)-L(x)|\leq\varepsilon_0.\] It implies \[\left|\inf_{x\in D}L_n(x)-\inf_{x\in D}L(x)\right|\leq\varepsilon_0.\] Moreover, if \(\widehat x\in D\) satisfies \(L_n(\widehat x)\leq\inf_D L_n+\eta\) for some \(\eta\geq0\), then \[L(\widehat x)\leq\inf_D L+2\varepsilon_0+\eta.\] Thus uniform value control transfers approximate global optimality, but by itself gives no gradient or curvature information.
assumptions_latex: The infima \(\inf_D L\) and \(\inf_D L_n\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\inf_D L_n-\inf_D L|\leq\varepsilon_0\), and every empirical \(\eta\)-minimizer is a population \((2\varepsilon_0+\eta)\)-minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zeroth-order uniform approximation and its optimal-value consequences.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary uniform approximation bound for finite optimal values and approximate minimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and let \(L,L_n\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(D\). Uniform curvature transfer at tolerance \(\varepsilon_2\geq0\) is \[\sup_{x\in D}\|

children.title: Statistical Landscape Regime Family

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Statistical Landscape Regime Family Induced by Geometric Margins
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be a population objective and let \(F_n\) be a random empirical objective based on sample size \(n\). Let \(R_1,ldots,R_K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be prescribed landscape regions, and let \(m_{k,j}>0\) denote reference margins for derivative orders \(j\in J_k\subseteq\{0,1,2\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The regime family is relative to specified regions, derivative orders, confidence level, and reference margins. It classifies statistical indices; it does not assert that any particular model satisfies the required probability bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and define random transfer errors \[\Delta_{k,j}(n):=\sup_{x\in R_k}\|D^jF_n(x)-D^jF(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}.\] For each index set \(I\subseteq\{(k,j):1\leq k\leq K,\ j\in J_k\}\), the statistical landscape regime \(\mathfrak R_I(\delta)\) is the set of sample sizes \(n\) for which \[\mathbb P\!\left(\Delta_{k,j}(n)<m_{k,j}\ \text{exactly for the indexed certificates }(k,j)\in I\right)\geq1-\delta.\] A statistical landscape regime family is the collection of nonempty cells \(\{\mathfrak R_I(\delta)\}_I\). Crossing a regime boundary means that the collection of derivative-versus-margin certificates guaranteed at confidence \(1-\delta\) changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A statistical landscape regime family partitions sample-size or noise indices according to which regional derivative-transfer errors are smaller than their corresponding population landscape margins with a prescribed probability. Each cell therefore records a distinct collection of certified geometric features. The definition is relative: changing a region, derivative order, margin, or confidence level changes the regime family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[n\in\mathfrak R_I(\delta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathbb P\bigl(\{(k,j):\Delta_{k,j}(n)<m_{k,j}\}=I\bigr)\geq1-\delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A coarser nested regime family may be defined by cumulative cells \(\mathfrak R_{\supseteq I}(\delta):=\{n:\mathbb P(\Delta_{k,j}(n)<m_{k,j}\ \forall(k,j)\in I)\geq1-\delta\}\).

If deterministic upper bounds \(b_{k,j}(n,delta)\) satisfy \(\Delta_{k,j}(n)\leq b_{k,j}(n,delta)\) simultaneously with probability at least \(1-\delta\), the sufficient regime label is determined by the comparisons \(b_{k,j}(n,delta)<m_{k,j}\).
special_cases_latex: With one region and only \(j=1\), there are gradient-transfer and non-gradient-transfer regimes.
With \(j\in\{1,2\}\), separate cells distinguish first-order transfer from joint gradient-and-curvature transfer.
immediate_consequences_latex: If every bound \(b_{k,j}(n,delta)\) is nonincreasing in \(n\), the cumulative regime sets \(\mathfrak R_{\supseteq I}(\delta)\) are upward closed in sample size.
Margins equal to zero cannot be certified by a strict positive-error comparison and must be handled by exact identities or a different regime convention.
boundary_notes: This is not a universal sample-complexity theorem and assigns no numerical transition thresholds without model-specific concentration results.
Different nonnested certificates can yield incomparable regimes rather than a single weak-to-strong ordering.
No supplied source was found that states this exact regime-family construction.

notation.meaning: Positive population geometric margin for region k and derivative order j.
