knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), with gradient \(g(\bar x):=\nabla f(\bar x)\) and Hessian \(H(\bar x):=\nabla^2f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization. “Saddle” is used in the broad optimization sense of a stationary point that is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stationary point \(\bar x\) is a \emph{curvature-invisible saddle} if \[g(\bar x)=0,\qquad H(\bar x)\succeq0,\qquad \bar x\notin\operatorname{locmin}f.\] Equivalently, every quadratic directional curvature is nonnegative, \(v^{\mathsf T}H(\bar x)v\ge0\) for all \(v\), while every neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) contains a point \(y\) with \(f(y)<f(\bar x)\). The class is curvature-invisible because the usual certificate \(\lambda_{\min}(H(\bar x))<0\) is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature-invisible saddle is stationary and has no negative Hessian eigenvalue, but it is not a local minimum because lower objective values occur arbitrarily close to it.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(C^2\) near the point, so the classical Hessian is defined.
Local minimality and nearby descent are evaluated in the full Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\nabla f(\bar x)=0,\quad\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(\bar x))\ge0,\quad\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists y:\|y-\bar x\|<\varepsilon,\ f(y)<f(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The point is second-order stationary but fails the defining neighborhood inequality for local minimality.
special_cases_latex: If \(H(\bar x)=0\) and the first nonzero directional Taylor term permits descent, then \(\bar x\) belongs to this class.
A stationary inflection point in one dimension with zero second derivative and lower values on one side is curvature-invisible.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any escape rule triggered only by a negative Hessian eigenvalue has no trigger at \(\bar x\).
boundary_notes: A strict saddle with \(\lambda_{\min}(H(\bar x))<0\) is excluded.
A flat local minimum with singular positive-semidefinite Hessian is excluded because it is locally minimizing.

notation.meaning: The Hessian of the objective at the stationary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Saddle Obstructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family x²−y²ᵐ hides its descending direction from every derivative order below 2m, making gradient and Hessian classification insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any integer \(m\ge2\), define \(f_m(x,y)=x^2-y^{2m}\). At the origin, \(
abla f_m(0,0)=0\) and \(
abla^2f_m(0,0)=\operatorname{diag}(2,0)\succeq0\), so first- and second-order information is compatible with local minimality. More strongly, all derivatives of the restriction \(t\mapsto f_m(0,t)\) of orders below \(2m\) vanish at \(t=0\), whereas its derivative of order \(2m\) is negative. Since \(f_m(0,t)=-t^{2m}<0=f_m(0,0)\) for \(t
e0\), the origin is a saddle whose descending geometry first appears at order \(2m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The origin is a saddle, but its descending restriction is undetectable by derivatives of order less than \(2m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polynomial family postpones detectable descent to an arbitrarily high even derivative order.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p\ge3\), let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(C^p\) near a stationary point \(\bar x\), and denote its symmetric \(j\)-th derivative tensor by \(D^jf(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization. This slot defines a directional subclass whose descent geometry first becomes visible beyond second order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pair \(( ar x,v)\), with \(v
e0\), is a \emph{higher-order saddle obstruction of order \(r\)} for some \(3\le r\le p\) if \[
abla f( ar x)=0,\qquad 
abla^2f( ar x)\succeq0,\] \[D^jf( ar x)[v^j]=0\quad(1\le j<r),\qquad D^rf( ar x)[v^r]<0.\] The point \( ar x\) has a higher-order saddle obstruction if such \(v\) and \(r\) exist. Gradient and Hessian data provide no descent certificate along \(v\), while the first nonzero directional term does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order saddle obstruction occurs when a stationary point has no negative Hessian curvature, all lower directional derivatives vanish along some direction, and the first nonzero derivative of order at least three is negative.
assumptions_latex: The required derivatives through order \(r\) exist and are continuous near \(\bar x\).
The tensor evaluation \(D^jf(\bar x)[v^j]\) means that \(v\) is inserted into all \(j\) tensor arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists v\ne0,\ \exists r\in\{3,\ldots,p\}:\ D^jf(\bar x)[v^j]=0\ (j<r),\quad D^rf(\bar x)[v^r]<0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\phi(t):=f(\bar x+tv)\), the condition is \(\phi^{(j)}(0)=0\) for \(j<r\) and \(\phi^{(r)}(0)<0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(r\) is odd and the first nonzero term is nonzero, one of the two orientations \(v\) or \(-v\) gives a negative tensor value.
When \(r\) is even, the negative value supplies descent for both sufficiently small signs of the scalar displacement along \(v\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A method whose saddle certificate is restricted to nonzero gradient or negative Hessian curvature cannot certify this directional descent at \(\bar x\).
boundary_notes: This definition does not cover nonanalytic flat saddles for which every finite-order directional derivative vanishes.
A nonzero third- or higher-order derivative does not constitute an obstruction unless its directional sign supplies descent.

notation.meaning: The j-th directional derivative tensor evaluated repeatedly on the direction.

children.top_down_role: Dynamical failures not captured by a static minima-versus-saddle taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Non-Minimizing Invariant Regime of an Optimization Dynamics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space, let \(T:X\to X\) be an iteration map, let \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have solution set \(S:=\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time dynamics. The definition describes recurrent or limiting behavior and is distinct from the static classification of any single critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty closed set \(L\subseteq X\) is a \emph{non-minimizing dynamical regime} for \((T,f)\) if \[T(L)\subseteq L,\qquad L\cap S=\varnothing,\] and there exists a bounded orbit \((x_k)\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,L)\to0,\qquad\omega(x_0)\subseteq L,\qquad\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)>\inf_X f.\] Here \(\omega(x_0)\) is the set of subsequential limits of the orbit. The regime may be a fixed point, periodic orbit, invariant continuum, or more complicated compact limit set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-minimizing dynamical regime is an invariant set, disjoint from the global solution set, that attracts or contains the limit behavior of a bounded algorithmic orbit whose objective values stay globally suboptimal.
assumptions_latex: The orbit is well-defined for every nonnegative integer and has at least one cluster point.
Distance to a set is computed using the metric on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\omega(x_0)\ne\varnothing,\quad\omega(x_0)\subseteq L\subseteq X\setminus S,\quad\liminf_k f(x_k)>\inf_X f.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(L\) is compact and \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,L)\to0\), every cluster point of the orbit lies in \(L\); the explicit \(\omega\)-limit inclusion records this terminal-set interpretation.
special_cases_latex: A nonglobal fixed point \(\bar x=T(\bar x)\) forms the singleton regime \(L=\{\bar x\}\).
A suboptimal periodic cycle \(L=\{z_0,\ldots,z_{q-1}\}\) with \(T(z_i)=z_{i+1\bmod q}\) is a nonstationary regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convergence analyses proving only boundedness or approach to an invariant set do not imply minimization when such a regime is reachable.
boundary_notes: Transient visits near saddles are excluded unless the asymptotic orbit approaches an invariant suboptimal set.
An invariant set containing at least one minimizer is not covered by this disjointness-based definition.

notation.meaning: The omega-limit set of the orbit starting at the initial point.

review_flags: No inspected optimization source was found that defines the node title by this exact invariant-set criterion.
The selected dynamical-systems convention and its optimization-specific value condition require authoritative support.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Minimizing Invariant Regime of an Optimization Dynamics
Non-Minimizing Attractors
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractive iteration can converge globally to a fixed point that is neither stationary nor minimizing for the stated objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the objective be \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\) and let an iterative method use the update map \(T(x)=x/2\). The point \(x_*=0\) is a globally attracting fixed point because \(T^k(x_0)=2^{-k}x_0\to0\) for every \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\). Nevertheless, \(x_*=0\) is not a critical point or minimizer of \(f\): one has \(f'(0)=-2\ne0\) and \(f(0)=1>0=f(1)\). Thus dynamical attraction alone does not certify minimizing geometry; a descent, residual, or stationarity relation linking \(T\) to \(f\) is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to0\) for every initialization, but \(0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}f\) and \(f'(0)\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A contractive update converges to an attracting fixed point unrelated to objective minimization.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The elementary counterexample is correct and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but it has no evidence record. A source is required for the dynamical-attractor terminology and the claimed boundary between attraction and objective minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Minimizing Cycles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable period-two orbit can attract iterates while both cycle points have objective values strictly above the global infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable and suppose distinct points \(a,b\) satisfy \(T(a)=b\), \(T(b)=a\), and \(\rho(DT(b)DT(a))<1\). Then \(\{a,b\}\) is a locally attracting period-two orbit of the iteration \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\). If an objective \(f\) additionally satisfies \(\min\{f(a),f(b)\}>\inf_x f(x)\), the attracting cycle is non-minimizing. Iterates initialized in its basin do not converge to a minimizer, even though their distance to the invariant cycle tends to zero. Excluding this regime requires an algorithmic condition, such as sufficient descent, that rules out nonconstant periodic orbits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{a,b\}\) is a locally attracting, non-minimizing period-two orbit.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A locally attracting periodic orbit may lie strictly above the objective infimum.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The spectral-radius condition is a substantive local stability theorem for the second iterate, not merely an arithmetic example. Although the formulation appears appropriate for the leaf, no source is supplied to validate the precise differentiability and stability hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Static-Taxonomy Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same strict minimizer is attracting for one update and repelling for another, so static landscape labels alone cannot predict algorithmic dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\), whose unique critical point \(x_*=0\) is a strict global minimizer. Consider the two smooth update maps \(T_1(x)=x/2\) and \(T_2(x)=2x\), both fixing \(x_*\). Under \(T_1\), every orbit converges to \(x_*\); under \(T_2\), every nonzero orbit leaves every bounded neighborhood of \(x_*\). The objective-side classification of \(x_*\) is identical in the two systems, but its dynamical stability is opposite. Therefore a static taxonomy based only on critical-point type cannot classify iterative behavior without incorporating the update rule and its local linearization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The static type of \(x_*=0\) does not determine whether \(x_*\) is attracting or repelling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise objective geometry does not determine stability under an unspecified update map.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Benign Landscapes

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Benign Landscapes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic can have a unique minimizer and no saddles yet require arbitrarily many fixed-step gradient iterations as its smallest curvature tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), let \(f_\varepsilon:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f_\varepsilon(x,y)=\tfrac12(x^2+\varepsilon y^2)\). The origin is the unique global minimizer, and there are no other critical points or saddles. The Hessian eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(\varepsilon\), so its condition number is \(\kappa_\varepsilon=1/\varepsilon\). Gradient descent with the fixed step \(\alpha=1\) satisfies \(x_{k+1}=0\) and \(y_{k+1}=(1-\varepsilon)y_k\). For \(0<\delta<1\) and \(y_0\ne0\), the least integer \(k\) for which \(|y_k|\le\delta|y_0|\) is \[k_\delta=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-\varepsilon)}\right\rceil.\] Consequently, for fixed \(\delta\), \(k_\delta=\Theta\!\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\right)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
assumptions_latex: Gradient descent uses the fixed step \(\alpha=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The landscape remains benign while \(\kappa_\varepsilon\to\infty\) and \(k_\delta=\Theta\!\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\right)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strongly convex quadratic family is globally benign while its geometric and convergence constants degenerate.

children.title: Identifiability Failure
children.top_down_role: Global minimizers that do not uniquely encode the intended solution object.

knowledge_statements.title: Identifiability Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because the observation depends only on x², the distinct parameters −1 and 1 are indistinguishable global minimizers; optimization cannot uniquely recover the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the parameter be \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), let the observable map be \(G(x)=x^2\), and suppose the target observation is \(G(x)=1\). The least-squares loss \(f(x)=(G(x)-1)^2=(x^2-1)^2\) has \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}f(x)=\{-1,1\}.\] Both minimizers attain zero loss and generate the same observation, since \(G(-1)=G(1)=1\), although they are distinct parameter values. Thus global optimization identifies only the equivalence class induced by the symmetry \(x\sim -x\), not a unique parameter. Unique recovery requires an identifying constraint, asymmetric observation, or quotient-space formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global minimizer set is \(\{-1,1\}\), so the parameter is identifiable only modulo \(x\sim-x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A symmetry-invariant loss has multiple global minimizers representing indistinguishable parameter values.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The symmetry example is mathematically correct and fits the identifiability-failure container, but the record has no citation for the substantive identifiability and quotient-equivalence interpretation. A statistical inverse-problem or identifiability source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a parameter space, let \(R:\Theta\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a population or deterministic risk, let \(\theta_*\in\Theta\) encode the intended object, and let \(\sim\) be the equivalence relation representing acceptable symmetries.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates optimization success from recovery of the intended object. Nonuniqueness caused solely by declared symmetries is treated as identifiable modulo equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The optimization model is \emph{identifiable modulo \(\sim\)} if \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta)=[\theta_*]_{\sim}.\] It has an \emph{identifiability failure} if this equality fails. In particular, failure occurs when there exists a global minimizer \(\hat\theta\) with \(\hat\theta\not\sim\theta_*\), or when some parameter equivalent to the intended object is excluded from the minimizer set despite equivalence being declared observationally irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identifiability fails when globally minimizing the objective does not select exactly the equivalence class of parameters representing the intended solution object.
assumptions_latex: The intended parameter belongs to \(\Theta\), and its acceptable symmetry class \([\theta_*]_{\sim}\) is specified before optimization.
The global minimizer set is nonempty; otherwise recovery failure is due to nonattainment rather than the stated nonidentifiability condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Theta}R\ne[\theta_*]_{\sim}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When every member of \([\theta_*]_{\sim}\) has the same risk and is minimizing, failure is equivalent to \(\exists\hat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}R\) such that \(\hat\theta\not\sim\theta_*\).
If \(q:\Theta\to\mathcal Z\) is the recovered-object map and \(\theta_1\sim\theta_2\iff q(\theta_1)=q(\theta_2)\), identifiability means \(q(\operatorname*{argmin}R)=\{q(\theta_*)\}\).
special_cases_latex: Label permutations, signs, rotations, or scaling symmetries do not constitute failure when included in \(\sim\).
Two inequivalent global minimizers encoding different recovered objects constitute failure even though both are optimization solutions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convergence to an arbitrary global minimizer does not guarantee recovery of the intended object under identifiability failure.
boundary_notes: A spurious local minimum is not needed: identifiability may fail entirely within the global minimizer set.
Statistical estimation error between an approximate minimizer and \([\theta_*]_{\sim}\) is distinct from exact population identifiability.

notation.meaning: The acceptable equivalence class of the intended parameter.

A precise source locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Phase Transition of Empirical Geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each dimension \(d\), let \(F_{n,d}:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be a random empirical objective based on \(n\) observations, and let \(\mathcal G_{n,d}\) be a measurable event asserting a specified favorable landscape property.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-dimensional probabilistic setting. The geometric event must be fixed before stating the transition; examples include identifiability, absence of spurious minima, or a uniform strict-saddle margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family exhibits a \emph{data-regime phase transition} at sampling ratio \(\rho_c\in(0,\infty)\) for the property \(\mathcal G\) if, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\lim_{\substack{d\to\infty\\ n/d\le\rho_c-\varepsilon}}\mathbb P(\mathcal G_{n,d})=0,\qquad \lim_{\substack{d\to\infty\\ n/d\ge\rho_c+\varepsilon}}\mathbb P(\mathcal G_{n,d})=1.\] The subcritical regime is a geometry-failure regime because the favorable event is asymptotically absent; the supercritical regime is supported because it occurs with probability tending to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data-regime phase transition is a critical sampling ratio below which a stated favorable empirical geometry fails with high probability and above which it holds with high probability.
assumptions_latex: A joint asymptotic sequence \((n,d)\) and a measurable geometric event \(\mathcal G_{n,d}\) are specified.
The transition is stated away from the critical window by an arbitrary fixed margin \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[n/d<\rho_c\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb P(\mathcal G_{n,d})\to0,\qquad n/d>\rho_c\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb P(\mathcal G_{n,d})\to1,\] in the margin-qualified sense of the definition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With failure event \(\mathcal F_{n,d}:=\mathcal G_{n,d}^{c}\), the two limits become \(\mathbb P(\mathcal F_{n,d})\to1\) below threshold and \(\mathbb P(\mathcal F_{n,d})\to0\) above threshold.
special_cases_latex: The ratio may be replaced by another normalized data parameter, such as observations per degree of freedom, provided the scaling variable is specified.
A sharp finite-sample threshold is stronger than this asymptotic definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: A landscape guarantee proved only in the supercritical regime cannot be extrapolated to a subcritical data sequence.
boundary_notes: A gradual degradation without limiting zero-one behavior is not a sharp phase transition under this definition.
The definition does not identify the value of \(\rho_c\) or the width of the critical window.
review_flags: No inspected source was found for the exact zero-one landscape transition convention used here.
The property-specific threshold and scaling variable require application-level sourcing.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Phase Transition of Empirical Geometry
Sampling Phase Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian least squares has a continuum of minimizers below the sample-to-dimension threshold and a unique minimizer at or above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) have independent standard Gaussian entries, let \(b=Ax_\star\), and define \(F_n(x)=\tfrac12\|Ax-b\|^2\). If \(n<d\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) almost surely and \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_n=x_\star+\ker A\), an affine set of dimension \(d-n\). If \(n\ge d\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=d\) almost surely and \(x_\star\) is the unique minimizer. Thus the finite-sample landscape changes at the sampling boundary \(n=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n<d\Rightarrow\dim(\operatorname*{argmin}F_n)=d-n\), whereas \(n\ge d\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}F_n=\{x_\star\}\), almost surely.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identifiability transition for noiseless Gaussian linear regression.

notation.meaning: null space of the sampling matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Gaussian matrices have almost-sure rank equal to the smaller matrix dimension

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian-rank argument and sampling boundary are mathematically precise, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No inspectable source is supplied for the almost-sure rank and identifiability transition.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise Phase Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The double-well landscape collapses at unit noise strength, where two minima merge into one degenerate critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\tau\ge0\), consider \(F_\tau(x)=\tfrac14x^4-\tfrac12(1-\tau)x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), where \(\tau\) represents effective noise strength. When \(0\le\tau<1\), the points \(x=\pm\sqrt{1-\tau}\) are strict local minima and \(x=0\) is a strict local maximum. At \(\tau=1\), these critical points coalesce into the degenerate minimizer \(x=0\). For \(\tau>1\), \(x=0\) is the unique strict global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau=1\) separates a two-minimum regime from a unique-minimum regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional bifurcation under an effective noise parameter.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed polynomial bifurcation follows from its first and second derivatives

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial bifurcation is correct and fits a phase-transition failure boundary, but interpreting the parameter as effective statistical noise is not supported by a cited source.

children.title: Constraint-Induced Spurious Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Induced Spurious Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a linear objective to a parabola creates a strict constrained minimizer even though the ambient objective has none.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f(x,y)=y\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The unconstrained objective has no local minimizer because every point admits a sufficiently small displacement in the negative \(y\)-direction that decreases \(f\). Impose the smooth equality constraint \(c(x,y)=y-x^2=0\). On the feasible set \(C=\{(x,x^2):x\in\mathbb{R}\}\), the restricted objective satisfies \(f(x,x^2)=x^2\), so \((0,0)\) becomes a strict global constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has no unconstrained local minimizer, while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in C}f(x,y)=\{(0,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth equality constraint creates a minimizer absent from the ambient problem.

notation.meaning: objective restricted to the feasible set

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous, let \(C\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f_C:=f|_C\) denote the constrained objective with \(f_C^*:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constrained optimization. The canonical formal core uses new spurious constrained minima; singularity and degeneracy variants require additional constraint regularity notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The restriction to \(C\) creates \emph{constraint-induced spurious geometry} if there exists \(\bar x\in C\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[f(\bar x)\le f(x)\quad\forall x\in C\cap V,\qquad f(\bar x)>f_C^*,\] while \(\bar x\) is not a local minimizer of the ambient objective: \[\forall\text{ neighborhoods }W\ni\bar x\ \exists y\in W:\ f(y)<f(\bar x).\] Thus the structural restriction removes ambient descent directions and creates a nonglobal constrained local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-induced spurious geometry occurs when restricting the feasible set turns a point that is not an ambient local minimum into a feasible local minimum whose value is not globally best on the constraint set.
assumptions_latex: Local constrained comparisons use the relative topology of \(C\).
The strict value gap is measured against the constrained infimum, not the ambient infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\in\operatorname{locmin}_C f\setminus\operatorname*{argmin}_C f,\qquad \bar x\notin\operatorname{locmin}_{\mathbb R^d}f.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The restriction map creates a new local-minimum element: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{locmin}(f|_C)\setminus\bigl(C\cap\operatorname{locmin}f\bigr)\), and this element is constrained-suboptimal.
special_cases_latex: For smooth \(f\) and regular \(C\), the removed ambient descent directions may lie outside the tangent cone \(T_C(\bar x)\).
A disconnected feasible set can create such a minimum even when the ambient objective has no nonglobal local minima.
immediate_consequences_latex: Benign ambient geometry does not imply benign geometry of the restricted problem.
boundary_notes: A constrained global minimizer created by restriction is not spurious under the strict constrained-value criterion.
Constraint qualifications failing at a point without creation of a spurious local minimum are a nearby but distinct degeneracy variant.

children.title: Parameterization-Induced Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Flatness, singularities, and noncompact orbits caused by redundant coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterization-Induced Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bilinear factorization turns one identifiable product into a noncompact minimizer curve with a singular Hessian along its tangent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(u,v)=(uv-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Its global minimizer set is \(M=\{(u,v):uv=1\}\), which is noncompact because \((t,t^{-1})\in M\) for every \(t\ne0\). At each \((u,v)\in M\), the Hessian is \(2(v,u)(v,u)^\top\), hence has rank one and annihilates the tangent direction \((u,-v)\). The represented scalar product is identifiable, but its redundant factor coordinates create a flat direction and unbounded parameter orbits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\{(t,t^{-1}):t\ne0\}\) is noncompact and \(\operatorname{rank}\nabla^2f(u,v)=1\) for every \((u,v)\in M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant bilinear coordinates produce flat, singular, noncompact minimizer orbits.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed minimizer set and Hessian are obtained by direct differentiation

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The minimizer orbit, Hessian formula, tangent null direction, and noncompactness are correct, and counterexample fits the terminal container. No inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy Induced by a Redundant Parameterization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(C^2\), let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), and let \(\phi:\Theta\to X\) be a \(C^2\) parameterization with pulled-back objective \(g:=f\circ\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional parameterized optimization. Degeneracy is attributed to the coordinate map rather than to flatness already present in the intrinsic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The parameterization induces a \emph{degeneracy at \(	heta\in\Theta\)} if there exists \(v
e0\) such that \[D\phi(	heta)v=0.\] If additionally \(
abla f(\phi(	heta))=0\), then \[
abla g(	heta)=0,\qquad v^{\mathsf T}
abla^2g(	heta)v=0,\] so \(v\) is a parameter-space flat direction invisible in the represented object. A global parameterization-induced degeneracy also occurs when a fiber \(\phi^{-1}(x)\) contains a nonconstant unbounded continuous curve, producing a noncompact orbit of equivalent parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterization-induced degeneracy is a nonzero coordinate direction annihilated by the parameterization differential, or a noncompact curve of parameters representing the same object; at intrinsic stationary points such directions become flat directions of the pulled-back objective.
assumptions_latex: The degeneracy direction lies in the tangent space of the parameter domain when \(\Theta\) is not open.
The asserted Hessian flatness is restricted to points where the intrinsic gradient vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\ker D\phi(\theta)\ne\{0\}\quad\text{or}\quad\exists x\in X\ \exists\text{ unbounded nonconstant }c:\mathbb{R}\to\phi^{-1}(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Local differential degeneracy is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rank}D\phi(\theta)<p\).
An exact symmetry action \(a\mapsto a\cdot\theta\) satisfying \(\phi(a\cdot\theta)=\phi(\theta)\) generates fiber directions whenever its orbit has positive dimension.
special_cases_latex: Matrix factorizations may have scaling or change-of-basis orbits that preserve the represented matrix.
Overparameterized models may have positive-dimensional fibers even when the intrinsic solution object is isolated.
immediate_consequences_latex: Isolated intrinsic minimizers can correspond to nonisolated or noncompact parameter-space minimizer sets, weakening local curvature and compactness properties.
boundary_notes: A small but nonzero intrinsic Hessian eigenvalue is ill-conditioning, not exact parameterization degeneracy.
Rank loss of \(D\phi\) need not create a spurious minimum; it defines redundancy or singularity, not global suboptimality.

notation.meaning: The objective expressed in parameter coordinates.
The fiber of parameter values representing the same object.

children.title: Population-to-Empirical Transfer Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure of finite-sample derivatives or critical regions to preserve population geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Population-to-Empirical Transfer Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objectives converge uniformly, but derivative oscillations produce empirical critical points approaching one half rather than the population critical point at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(K=[-1,1]\), let \(F(x)=x^2\) and \(F_n(x)=x^2+n^{-1}\sin(nx)\). Then \(\|F_n-F\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le n^{-1}\to0\), whereas \(F_n'(x)=2x+\cos(nx)\) does not converge uniformly to \(F'(x)=2x\). Moreover, there exist critical points \(x_n\in[-1/2,1/2]\) of \(F_n\) with \(x_n\to1/2\), while the only critical point of \(F\) in \(K\) is \(0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mismatch Between Geometric Certificates and Admissible Algorithmic Actions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be an objective, let \(E_f(x)\subseteq T_xX\) be the set of directions satisfying a stated geometric escape or progress certificate at \(x\), and let \(A_{\mathcal M}(x)\subseteq T_xX\) be the actions available to method \(\mathcal M\) from its oracle information.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Methods at Degenerate Saddles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a quartically flat saddle, gradient descent can converge along an invariant line or escape arbitrarily slowly from nearby points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^4\), the origin is a degenerate saddle with Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(2,0)\). Gradient descent with constant step \(0<\alpha<1\) obeys \(x_{k+1}=(1-2\alpha)x_k\) and \(y_{k+1}=y_k+4\alpha y_k^3\). The invariant initialization set \(y_0=0\) converges to the saddle. When \(0<|y_0|\ll1\), the escape increment is cubic, so no uniform linear saddle-escape rate follows from first-order information near the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_0=0\Rightarrow(x_k,y_k)\to(0,0)\), while transverse escape has leading increment \(4\alpha y_k^3\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient descent can approach or linger near a saddle with zero escape curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Methods with Inexact Information
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric Hessian estimate with operator-norm error delta cannot uniformly distinguish a flat direction from negative curvature whose magnitude is at most delta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) and \(\widehat H\) be symmetric matrices satisfying \(\|\widehat H-H\|_2\le\delta\) for some \(\delta\ge0\). Weyl's inequality gives \(|\lambda_{\min}(\widehat H)-\lambda_{\min}(H)|\le\delta\). Consequently, an oracle with only this error guarantee cannot uniformly distinguish zero curvature from negative curvature of magnitude at most \(\delta\). Indeed, for any unit vector \(v\) and \(\delta>0\), the report \(\widehat H=-\tfrac\delta2vv^\top\) is consistent with both \(H_0=0\) and \(H_1=-\delta vv^\top\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\delta\le\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\) is not uniformly certifiable as negative curvature from \(\widehat H\) under the stated error model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-norm Hessian error imposes a resolution limit on negative-curvature certification.

notation.meaning: exact Hessian or exact symmetric curvature matrix

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(C^2\), let \(H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)\), and let a curvature method use a symmetric approximation \(B(x)\) satisfying \(\|B(x)-H(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional deterministic curvature approximation with an operator-norm error bound. Stochastic estimates require a probability-qualified version of the same inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An approximate negative-curvature certificate at \(x\) is \emph{reliable} when \[\lambda_{\min}(B(x))<-\varepsilon(x),\] because its negativity exceeds the admitted approximation uncertainty. The method has \emph{inexact-curvature ambiguity} at \(x\) when the true Hessian has negative curvature but the approximation does not provide a reliable certificate: \[\lambda_{\min}(H(x))<0,\qquad\lambda_{\min}(B(x))\ge-\varepsilon(x).\] A curvature method suffers information-induced certificate loss when its escape rule requires reliable detected curvature and it encounters such an ambiguous point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact curvature is ambiguous when the true Hessian has a negative eigenvalue but the approximate Hessian’s smallest eigenvalue is not more negative than the known error radius, so its sign cannot reliably certify saddle escape.
assumptions_latex: \(B(x)\) is symmetric, and the approximation error is bounded in spectral norm.
The method’s curvature trigger treats only eigenvalues below \(-\varepsilon(x)\) as reliable negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda_{\min}(H(x))<0\ \wedge\ \lambda_{\min}(B(x))\ge-\varepsilon(x),\] so the available curvature information does not certify the true negative-curvature direction under the stated error model.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A direction \(v\) with \(\|v\|=1\) is reliably negative for the true Hessian whenever \(v^{\mathsf T}B(x)v<-\varepsilon(x)\); ambiguity means no such certified direction is returned despite \(\lambda_{\min}(H(x))<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\varepsilon(x)=0\), ambiguity from approximation vanishes and \(B(x)=H(x)\).
A true eigenvalue in \((-2\varepsilon(x),0)\) can be shifted to a nonnegative approximate eigenvalue while respecting the error bound.
immediate_consequences_latex: Reliable saddle detection requires a negative-curvature margin larger than the curvature-estimation error, or an adaptive reduction of that error.
boundary_notes: An indefinite approximation at a truly positive-semidefinite Hessian is a false-positive phenomenon, distinct from the false-negative ambiguity defined here.
This definition concerns certificate reliability, not convergence or complexity of a particular trust-region, cubic-regularization, or Newton method.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Numerical distortion of asymptotic optimization dynamics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[X\subseteq\mathbb R^n,\qquad x_{k+1}=T(x_k),\qquad \widetilde x_{k+1}=T(\widetilde x_k)+e_k,\quad \|e_k\|\leq\eta_k.\] Here \(X\) is closed, \(T:X\to X\) is the exact iteration map, and every exact or perturbed trajectory under consideration is bounded. For a bounded sequence \(z=(z_k)\), let \(\Omega(z)\) denote its nonempty compact omega-limit set. Let \(Q:\mathcal K(X)\to(Y,d_Y)\) be a chosen qualitative descriptor of a compact limit set, such as its selected critical component, symmetry orbit, or minimizer stratum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns deterministic finite-dimensional iterations represented by an exact map plus admissible additive implementation errors. It measures changes in asymptotic orbit information, not merely a large finite-step forward error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_0\in X\) and an error profile \(\eta=(\eta_k)_{k\geq0}\), define \[\mathcal E_\eta(x_0):=\left\{(\widetilde x_k):\widetilde x_0=x_0,\ \widetilde x_{k+1}=T(\widetilde x_k)+e_k,\ \|e_k\|\leq\eta_k\right\}\] and \[D_{Q,\eta}(x_0):=\sup_{\widetilde x\in\mathcal E_\eta(x_0)}d_Y\!\left(Q(\Omega(\widetilde x)),Q(\Omega((T^kx_0)_{k\geq0}))\right).\] The implemented dynamics exhibit numerical dynamics distortion at \(x_0\), relative to \(Q\) and \(\eta\), precisely when \(D_{Q,\eta}(x_0)>0\). The distortion is persistent under vanishing error when \[\limsup_{\rho\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\substack{\eta_k\leq\rho\ \forall k\\ \eta_k\to0}}D_{Q,\eta}(x_0)>0.\] Thus arbitrarily small admissible perturbations can alter the asymptotic saddle, symmetry, or flat-valley behavior recorded by \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix an exact iteration map \(T\) on a closed subset of \(\mathbb R^n\). A computed trajectory follows the same map with errors \(e_k\) bounded by a prescribed profile \(\eta_k\). Its numerical dynamics distortion is the worst-case distance, measured by \(d_Y\), between the qualitative descriptor \(Q\) of its omega-limit set and that of the exact trajectory from the same initial point. Distortion occurs when this quantity is positive. It is persistent under vanishing error if the distortion remains bounded away from zero along arbitrarily small, asymptotically vanishing error profiles. This distinguishes a change of limiting dynamical behavior from ordinary finite-horizon numerical error.
assumptions_latex: Every trajectory in \(\mathcal E_\eta(x_0)\), as well as \((T^kx_0)_{k\geq0}\), is bounded and remains in \(X\).
\(Q\) is defined on the compact omega-limit sets under consideration and takes values in a metric space \((Y,d_Y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{Numerical dynamics distortion at }x_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{Q,\eta}(x_0)>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[D_{Q,\eta}(x_0)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists\,\widetilde x\in\mathcal E_\eta(x_0):Q(\Omega(\widetilde x))\neq Q(\Omega((T^kx_0)_{k\geq0})).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(Q(K)=K\) and \(Y=\mathcal K(X)\) carries the Hausdorff metric, distortion means that an admissible computed trajectory has an omega-limit set different from that of the exact trajectory.
If \(Q\) records a symmetry orbit or connected component of a minimizer set, positive distortion records numerical selection of a different orbit or component.
immediate_consequences_latex: A small bound on \(\sup_k\|\widetilde x_k-T^kx_0\|\) implies small \(D_{Q,\eta}(x_0)\) only when \(Q\) is suitably continuous on the relevant limit sets.
Persistent distortion identifies a lack of asymptotic robustness of the selected descriptor, even when \(\eta_k\to0\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that floating-point arithmetic always admits a deterministic additive-error model.
Ordinary transient deviation with identical descriptors is not numerical dynamics distortion relative to \(Q\).
Unbounded trajectories require a different limit object and are excluded.

Finite-Precision Effects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient underflow makes a whole neighborhood of nonstationary representable points appear stationary to the computed iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x^2\) and the computed update \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{fl}(x_k-\alpha\operatorname{fl}(2x_k))\). Suppose the arithmetic flushes gradients to zero whenever \(0<|2x|<\eta\). Every representable \(x\) satisfying \(0<|x|<\eta/2\) then obeys \(\operatorname{fl}(2x)=0\) and is a fixed point of the computed iteration, although the exact derivative \(f'(x)=2x\) is nonzero. Exact stationarity is therefore replaced by an arithmetic-dependent stagnation region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<|x_0|<\eta/2\Rightarrow x_k=x_0\) for all \(k\), despite \(f'(x_0)\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient underflow can create nonstationary fixed points in computed dynamics.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the fixed-point implication follows directly from the stated underflow model

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The conditional fixed-point calculation is correct under the stated flush-to-zero model, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A floating-point source is needed to support the arithmetic model and clarify which hardware or execution modes realize it.

knowledge_statements.title: Discretization Effects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable quadratic gradient flow becomes oscillatory or divergent when explicit Euler uses a step at or above one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2\), the gradient flow \(\dot x=-2x\) satisfies \(x(t)=e^{-2t}x(0)\) and converges to zero for every initial value. Explicit Euler discretization with step \(h>0\) gives \(x_{k+1}=(1-2h)x_k\). This discrete trajectory converges to zero exactly when \(0<h<1\); at \(h=1\) it forms a sign-alternating two-cycle unless \(x_0=0\), and for \(h>1\) its magnitude grows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to0\) if and only if \(0<h<1\); stability fails for \(h\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit Euler discretization can destroy gradient-flow stability.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny directional numerical bias selects one direction from an otherwise rotation-symmetric circle of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,y)=(x^2+y^2-1)^2\), whose global minimizers form the rotation-invariant circle \(M=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\}\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), model a persistent numerical bias by \(f_\varepsilon(x,y)=f(x,y)+\varepsilon x\). Every global minimizer of \(f_\varepsilon\) lies on the negative \(x\)-axis, with radius solving \(4r(r^2-1)=\varepsilon\). Thus an arbitrarily small nonsymmetric perturbation collapses the symmetric minimizer orbit to a selected direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Valley Dynamic Distortion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny persistent tangential error accumulates and drives iterates to a valley endpoint that exact gradient descent would not select.

Exact projected gradient descent satisfies \(x_{k+1}=(1-2\alpha)x_k\) and \(y_{k+1}=y_k\), so it preserves the initial representative on the minimizer valley \(M=\{0\}\times[-1,1]\). If each computed step contains a persistent tangential bias \(\varepsilon>0\), then \(y_{k+1}=\Pi_{[-1,1]}(y_k-\alpha\varepsilon)\), which reaches \(-1\) after finitely many steps. Arbitrarily small bias therefore changes trajectory selection along the flat valley.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon=0\Rightarrow y_k=y_0\), while \(\varepsilon>0\Rightarrow y_k=-1\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Benign Landscape without Efficient Navigation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quartic has only one critical point, its global minimizer, yet fixed-step gradient descent approaches it polynomially slowly and needs order inverse-square-root accuracy iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x)=x^4\), and apply gradient descent with constant step size \(\alpha>0\): \(x_{k+1}=x_k-4\alpha x_k^3\). If \(0<4\alpha x_0^2<1\), then every iterate is nonzero, has the sign of \(x_0\), and converges to the unique critical point and global minimizer \(0\). Nevertheless, \(x_k\sim(8\alpha k)^{-1/2}\) and \(f(x_k)\sim(8\alpha k)^{-2}\). Hence reaching \(f(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\) requires order \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\) iterations, so a benign critical-point classification alone supplies neither linear convergence nor logarithmic accuracy complexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to0\), while \(x_k\sim(8\alpha k)^{-1/2}\) and \(f(x_k)\sim(8\alpha k)^{-2}\); thus benign critical points do not imply efficient navigation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional smooth landscape with no spurious critical points but polynomial first-order complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualitatively benign landscape lacking uniform navigation complexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[\mathfrak F=\bigcup_{m\geq1}\mathfrak F_m,\qquad f:\mathbb R^{n(m)}\to\mathbb R,\qquad X_f^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^{n(m)}}f(x)\neq\varnothing.\] Each \(f\in\mathfrak F_m\) is twice continuously differentiable. Fix an algorithmic model \(\mathcal A\), an admissible initialization set \(I_f\), and a stationarity-or-optimality target \(G_f(x)\geq0\) with tolerance \(\varepsilon\). Let \(N_{\mathcal A}(f,x_0,\varepsilon)\) be the number of oracle calls required to produce an iterate satisfying \(G_f(x)\leq\varepsilon\), with value \(+\infty\) on failure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a relative definition for a specified problem family, oracle model, initialization rule, and success criterion. It separates a qualitative critical-point classification from a uniform finite-time complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\mathfrak F\) has a benign strict-saddle landscape when, for every \(m\), there exists \(\gamma_m>0\) such that every \(f\in\mathfrak F_m\) and every critical point \(x\) satisfy \[\nabla f(x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in X_f^*\ \text{ or }\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\leq-\gamma_m.\] It has a benign landscape without efficient navigation for \(\mathcal A\) when this condition holds but no polynomial \(p\) gives the uniform bound \[\sup_{f\in\mathfrak F_m}\ \sup_{x_0\in I_f}N_{\mathcal A}(f,x_0,\varepsilon)\leq p\!\left(m,\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)\] for all \(m\) and all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\). Equivalently, for every polynomial \(p\), some \(m\), \(f\in\mathfrak F_m\), \(x_0\in I_f\), and admissible \(\varepsilon\) violate that bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem family has a benign strict-saddle landscape if every critical point of every instance is either a global minimizer or has a Hessian direction whose curvature is at most \(-\gamma_m\). Relative to an algorithmic and oracle model \(\mathcal A\), the family lacks efficient navigation when there is no polynomial in the instance parameter \(m\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) that uniformly bounds the oracle calls needed from all admissible initial points to reach the prescribed tolerance. The definition therefore permits a favorable classification of all critical points while recording that this classification alone supplies no usable uniform polynomial complexity guarantee.
assumptions_latex: For every \(f\in\mathfrak F_m\), the set \(X_f^*\) is nonempty and \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{n(m)})\).
The algorithmic model \(\mathcal A\), its available oracle, the initialization sets \(I_f\), and the residual \(G_f\) are fixed before complexity is assessed.
The complexity variable \(m\) encodes the selected finite input-size parameter for the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\forall f\in\mathfrak F:\operatorname{Crit}(f)\subseteq X_f^*\cup\{x:\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))<0\}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad \nexists\text{ a uniform polynomial navigation bound for }\mathcal A.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\forall p\in\mathbb R[t_1,t_2],\ \exists(m,f,x_0,\varepsilon):\ N_{\mathcal A}(f,x_0,\varepsilon)>p\!\left(m,\log(1/\varepsilon)\right),\] where the quantification over \(p\) is restricted to polynomials nonnegative on the relevant domain.
special_cases_latex: If \(\gamma_m\downarrow0\) extremely rapidly, the landscapes remain qualitatively strict-saddle while curvature-dependent complexity estimates may become nonuniform; this is a common conditioning mechanism but does not alone establish the navigation condition.

For randomized \(\mathcal A\), \(N_{\mathcal A}\) may instead denote the calls required to reach the target with a fixed success probability such as \(2/3\); that probability must be included in the algorithmic model.
immediate_consequences_latex: The absence of nonglobal local minima does not, by this definition, imply a polynomial-time route to \(X_f^*\).
A critical-point classification and an iteration-complexity statement are logically separate properties of the problem–algorithm pair.
boundary_notes: Failure of one chosen algorithm does not establish hardness for all algorithms or oracle models.
The definition does not claim an unconditional computational lower bound.
Nonsmooth functions and degenerate saddles require a different landscape condition.

notation.meaning: Set of global minimizers of f.
Uniform negative-curvature threshold at nonglobal critical points of size m.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Success without Trajectory Selection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent globally minimizes a convex quadratic with a line of minimizers, but its limit retains the initial flat-direction coordinate and is not uniquely selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(u,v)=u^2\), whose minimizer set is \(M=\{(0,v):v\in\mathbb{R}\}\). Gradient descent with constant step size \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) obeys \(u_{k+1}=(1-2\alpha)u_k\) and \(v_{k+1}=v_k\). Consequently, every trajectory converges globally to a minimizer, namely \((u_k,v_k)\to(0,v_0)\), and \(f(u_k,v_k)\to0\). However, the selected minimizer depends on the initial coordinate \(v_0\); objective convergence and global convergence to the solution set therefore do not determine a trajectory-independent solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u_k,v_k)\to(0,v_0)\in M\), so global success does not determine a unique minimizer independently of initialization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex gradient descent converges globally while retaining an initialization-dependent coordinate along the minimizer set.

notation.meaning: The nonunique set of global minimizers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global convergence to a solution set without point selection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad f^*:=\inf_Xf,\qquad X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\neq\varnothing.\] The domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed. For each initial state \(x_0\in I\subseteq X\), let \(\Gamma(f,x_0)\) be the nonempty family of bounded trajectories permitted by the algorithm, including any admissible tie-breaking, random realization, inexactness, or implementation choice. For a trajectory \(z=(z_k)\), write \(\Omega(z)\) for its omega-limit set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns finite-dimensional global convergence to a possibly non-singleton minimizer set. It distinguishes setwise success from a guarantee selecting one particular minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trajectory family \(\Gamma\) is globally successful on \(I\) when \[\forall x_0\in I\ \forall z\in\Gamma(f,x_0):\qquad \operatorname{dist}(z_k,X^*)\to0\quad\text{and}\quad f(z_k)\to f^*.\] Define its selection set at \(x_0\) by \[\operatorname{Sel}_\Gamma(f,x_0):=\bigcup_{z\in\Gamma(f,x_0)}\Omega(z)\subseteq X^*.\] Global success occurs without trajectory selection when the displayed global-success condition holds and \[\exists x_0\in I:\quad \left|\operatorname{Sel}_\Gamma(f,x_0)\right|>1.\] Equivalently, no single point \(s(f,x_0)\in X^*\) satisfies \(\Omega(z)=\{s(f,x_0)\}\) for every admissible trajectory from that initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of bounded algorithmic trajectories is globally successful if every admissible trajectory from every allowed initial point approaches the global minimizer set and its objective values approach the optimum. Its selection set at \(x_0\) is the union of the omega-limit sets of all admissible trajectories from that same initial point. Global success lacks trajectory selection when this selection set contains more than one minimizer for at least one \(x_0\). Thus the guarantee determines optimality of limiting behavior but does not determine a unique minimizer selected from the nonunique solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed, \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\), and \(X^*\neq\varnothing\).
Every trajectory in \(\Gamma(f,x_0)\) is bounded and remains in \(X\).
The family \(\Gamma(f,x_0)\) includes exactly the admissible trajectory choices covered by the claimed global guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Gamma\text{ is globally successful without trajectory selection}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left[\forall z,\ \operatorname{dist}(z_k,X^*)\to0,\ f(z_k)\to f^*\right]\ \land\ \left[\exists x_0,\ |\operatorname{Sel}_\Gamma(f,x_0)|>1\right].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\exists x_0\in I\ \exists z,w\in\Gamma(f,x_0):\quad \Omega(z)\cup\Omega(w)\text{ contains at least two points of }X^*.\]

When every admissible trajectory converges, the failure of selection is equivalent to the existence of \(x_0\in I\) and trajectories \(z,w\in\Gamma(f,x_0)\) with \(z_k\to x^*\), \(w_k\to y^*\), and \(x^*\neq y^*\) in \(X^*\).
special_cases_latex: If \(X^*=\{x^*\}\), global setwise convergence necessarily selects \(x^*\), so the defined failure cannot occur.
For a minimizer manifold generated by symmetry, different admissible trajectories may converge to different symmetry-equivalent points while attaining the same value \(f^*\).
A single trajectory with a nonsingleton omega-limit set contained in \(X^*\) already yields failure of point selection.
immediate_consequences_latex: The conclusions \(f(z_k)\to f^*\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(z_k,X^*)\to0\) do not imply convergence of \((z_k)\) to one point when \(X^*\) is non-singleton.
Any stronger selection statement requires additional structure, such as uniqueness, a regularizer, an invariant, or a specified tie-breaking rule.
boundary_notes: Different limits caused only by different initial points do not establish failure here; the definition fixes the same \(x_0\) and varies admissible trajectories.
The definition does not rank the selected minimizers or assert implicit bias toward any one of them.
Unbounded trajectories and empty minimizer sets are excluded.

notation.meaning: Family of admissible trajectories for the fixed problem and initial state.
All minimizer limit points selectable by admissible trajectories from x0.

review_flags: The inspected source defines convergence and limit points and shows that common global-convergence conclusions may concern gradients rather than a selected minimizer, but it does not state this exact trajectory-family selection definition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General definition over the objective's domain of interest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:D\to\mathbb{R} and x^*\in D. The point x^* is a global minimizer of f on D if and only if f(x^*)\leq f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an objective f on a domain D, a point x* is a global minimizer when its objective value is no greater than the value at every point in D.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in D,\quad f(x^*)\leq f(x)
